sultan-jahan-begum.s: Sultan Jahan Begum was ruler of Bhopal State from 1901 to 1926, the last of four women who ruled it in succession. She promoted education, especially for women, founded schools and health services, and became the first chancellor of Aligarh Muslim University in 1920.

shimla.s: Shimla, formerly Simla, is a city in the lower Himalaya and the capital of Himachal Pradesh, India. It grew after the Anglo-Nepalese War of 1814–1816 on land taken from the hill states, and from 1864 it was the summer capital of British India.

sambia-peninsula.s: The Sambia Peninsula, or Samland, lies on the Baltic coast of the Kaliningrad Oblast of Russia, between the Curonian and Vistula lagoons. Home of the Sambians, an Old Prussian people, it was conquered by the Teutonic Order in the 1250s and divided with the Bishopric of Samland.

semigallians.s: The Semigallians were a Baltic people of Semigallia, the plain of central Latvia and northern Lithuania. They resisted the German crusaders of Livonia for most of the 13th century, defeating them several times under leaders such as Viesturs and Nameisis, before submitting by…

sefire-steles.s: The Sefire steles are three basalt stelae inscribed in Old Aramaic, found at Sefire near Aleppo in Syria and dating to the mid-8th century BCE. They record a treaty between Bar-Ga'yah, king of KTK, and Mati'ilu, king of Arpad, with long lists of curses on whoever breaks it.

shamash-shum-ukin.s: Shamash-shum-ukin was king of Babylon from 668 to 648 BCE, a son of the Assyrian king Esarhaddon, who made him ruler of Babylonia under his younger brother Ashurbanipal. In 652 BCE he rebelled with the support of Chaldeans, Elamites and Arabs.

samaria.s: Samaria was the capital of the northern Kingdom of Israel, founded by King Omri in the early 9th century BCE on a hill in the central highlands of Palestine. The Assyrians took it in 722 BCE and deported much of the population.

segovesus.s: Segovesus was a legendary Gallic leader, nephew of King Ambigatus of the Bituriges. According to Livy, while his brother Bellovesus led Celtic migrants into Italy around 600 BCE, Segovesus was sent by lot to lead another migration east into the Hercynian Forest of central Europe.

siksika.s: The Siksika, or Blackfoot proper, are one of the nations of the Blackfoot Confederacy of the northern Great Plains, together with the Kainai and the Piikani. Mounted bison hunters of the 18th and 19th centuries, they signed Treaty 7 with Canada in 1877, and today the Siksika…

statute-of-bayonne.s: The Statute of Bayonne was a constitution for Spain approved in July 1808 by an assembly of Spanish notables summoned by Napoleon to Bayonne in France. Granted by Joseph Bonaparte as King Joseph I, it set up a Catholic monarchy with a cortes of estates and limited reforms on…

shehu-of-borno.s: Shehu of Borno is the title of the rulers of Borno in north-eastern Nigeria from the al-Kanemi dynasty, founded by the scholar Muhammad al-Amin al-Kanemi in the early 19th century. The shehus replaced the old Sayfawa kings in 1846, and since British rule they have ruled from…

sindi.s: The Sindi were an ancient people of the Taman peninsula and the lower Kuban in the north-western Caucasus, often counted among the Maeotians. Greek cities such as Gorgippia, modern Anapa, grew in their land, and their kingdom came under the Bosporan kings in the 4th century…

spartocid-dynasty.s: The Spartocid dynasty ruled the Bosporan Kingdom on both sides of the Kerch Strait from 438 BCE until about 108 BCE. Founded by Spartocus I, its rulers called themselves archons of the Greek cities and kings of the native peoples.

spartocus-i.s: Spartocus I was the founder of the Spartocid dynasty of the Bosporan Kingdom, who took power at Panticapaeum in 438 BCE after the Archaeanactids and ruled until 433 BCE, according to Diodorus. His name suggests a Thracian origin.

senat-conservateur.s: The Sénat conservateur was the senate of France under the Consulate and the First Empire, created by the constitution of 1799. Appointed and docile for most of its life, it endorsed Napoleon's rule, but in April 1814, with the allies in Paris, it proclaimed his deposition and…

spartacist-uprising.s: The Spartacist uprising was a general strike and armed rising in Berlin from 5 to 12 January 1919, led by the newly founded Communist Party of Germany and other radicals against the Social Democratic government of Friedrich Ebert. It was crushed by army units and Freikorps…

stanwick-iron-age-fortifications.s: The Stanwick Iron Age Fortifications are a vast series of earthwork ramparts near Stanwick St John in North Yorkshire, enclosing more than 300 hectares. Built and enlarged in the 1st century CE, they were probably a major centre of the Brigantes, possibly linked with…

sidney-shippard.s: Sir Sidney Shippard was a British colonial official and judge in southern Africa. He was administrator of British Bechuanaland from 1885 to 1895 and deputy commissioner for the Bechuanaland Protectorate, and he supported the extension of British influence, and of Cecil…

saya-san.s: Saya San was a Burmese former monk and traditional healer who led a peasant rebellion against British rule in 1930–1932. Beginning in the Tharrawaddy district during the depression, the rising drew on grievances over taxes and land and on Buddhist and royal symbolism.

second-anglo-burmese-war.s: The Second Anglo-Burmese War was fought in 1852–1853 between Britain and the Konbaung kingdom of Burma. Begun by the East India Company over a trade dispute in Rangoon, it ended with the British annexation of the province of Pegu, giving Britain all of Lower Burma.

samuel-auchmuty.s: Sir Samuel Auchmuty was a British general born in New York. He fought in India and Egypt, captured Montevideo in 1807 during the British invasions of the Río de la Plata, and in 1811 commanded the army that conquered Java from the Franco-Dutch forces.

stutterheim.s: Stutterheim is a small town in the Eastern Cape of South Africa, in the former British Kaffraria. It was founded in 1857 as a settlement for soldiers of the British German Legion and named after their commander, Baron Richard von Stutterheim.

samuel-cornish.s: Sir Samuel Cornish was a British admiral. In 1762, during the Seven Years' War, he commanded the naval force from Madras that carried William Draper's troops to Manila and helped capture the city from Spain.

simon-de-anda-y-salazar.s: Simón de Anda y Salazar was a Spanish judge and colonial governor in the Philippines. When the British took Manila in 1762 he escaped to Pampanga, declared himself governor and organised resistance from Bacolor until the British left in 1764.

salt-march.s: The Salt March was a campaign of civil disobedience led by Mahatma Gandhi in British India in 1930. From 12 March to 6 April he and his followers walked about 385 kilometres from Sabarmati to the coastal village of Dandi, where he made salt in defiance of the British salt tax.

santa-isabel-island.s: Santa Isabel is one of the largest islands of the Solomon Islands, lying north-west of Guadalcanal. The Spanish explorer Álvaro de Mendaña named it in 1568.

suitbert.s: Suitbert was an Anglo-Saxon missionary who came to Frisia with Willibrord around 690 and was consecrated a bishop for the mission. He preached among the Bructeri on the lower Rhine until the Saxons overran their land, and then founded a monastery on an island in the Rhine at…

seria.s: Seria is a town in the Belait district of western Brunei, on the coast of the South China Sea. Oil was discovered there in 1929 by the British Malayan Petroleum Company, part of the Shell group, and the Seria oilfield has been the foundation of Brunei's wealth ever since.

schengen-area.s: The Schengen Area is a zone of European countries that have abolished passport and border controls at their common borders. It grew from the Schengen Agreement, signed in 1985 at Schengen in Luxembourg, and the 1990 convention implementing it, which took effect in 1995; it…

semei-kakungulu.s: Semei Kakungulu was a Ganda military leader who served the British in extending colonial rule over eastern Uganda. After fighting against Bunyoro in the 1890s, he conquered much of the region around Mount Elgon and Lake Kyoga, ruling it from Mbale, and in 1906 the British made…

songhua-river.s: The Songhua is a river of north-eastern China, the largest tributary of the Amur. It rises at Heaven Lake on Changbai Mountain and flows north-west and then north-east past Jilin and Harbin to join the Amur on the Russian border.

sousse.s: Sousse is a city on the eastern coast of Tunisia, founded by Phoenicians as Hadrumetum and later the capital of the Roman province of Byzacena. Renamed Justinianopolis under Byzantine rule, it became an Aghlabid naval base after the Arab conquest, with a ribat and a Great…

sufetula.s: Sufetula, modern Sbeitla in central Tunisia, was a Roman town that flourished from the 2nd century CE, known for its well-preserved forum with three temples to the Capitoline gods. In the 7th century it was the seat of the exarch Gregory the Patrician, who was defeated and…

sisebut.s: Sisebut was king of the Visigoths from 612 to 621. He campaigned against the Byzantine province of Spania, taking Málaga and other coastal towns, and against the Basques and Asturians.

suintila.s: Suintila was king of the Visigoths from 621 to 631. Around 624 he expelled the last Byzantine garrisons from Hispania, and Isidore of Seville praised him as the first king to rule the whole peninsula.

san-carlos-pangasinan.s: San Carlos is a city in the province of Pangasinan, on the island of Luzon in the Philippines. Under the name Binalatongan it was a leading town of the pre-colonial polity of Caboloan and the home of Andrés Malong, leader of the revolt of 1660.

santa-maria-ship.s: The Santa María was the largest of the three ships of Christopher Columbus's first voyage in 1492 and served as his flagship. A carrack owned by Juan de la Cosa, it ran aground off the north coast of Hispaniola on Christmas Day 1492.

siege-of-uxellodunum.s: The siege of Uxellodunum in 51 BCE was the last major operation of Julius Caesar's conquest of Gaul. The Cadurcan leader Lucterius and the Senonian Drappes held this hill fortress, probably the Puy d'Issolud in the Lot, until Caesar's troops diverted the spring that supplied…

sarcophagus-of-the-spouses.s: The Sarcophagus of the Spouses is an Etruscan terracotta funerary urn from Caere, made around 520 BCE, showing a married couple reclining together at a banquet. Found in the Banditaccia necropolis in 1881 and now in the National Etruscan Museum of the Villa Giulia in Rome, it…

sonoma-california.s: Sonoma is a town in northern California, north of San Francisco Bay, that grew around the Mission San Francisco Solano, the last of the California missions, founded in 1823. Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo laid out its plaza in 1835.

sackingen-abbey.s: Säckingen Abbey was a house of noble canonesses on the Upper Rhine at Säckingen, in modern Baden-Württemberg, traditionally founded by the Irish missionary Saint Fridolin in the early Middle Ages. It held extensive lands, including the Linth valley of Glarus, whose…

salodurum.s: Salodurum was a Roman settlement on the River Aare in the province of Germania Superior, the origin of the Swiss town of Solothurn. It grew as a roadside village and bridge point on the route between Aventicum and the Rhine.

st-ursus-cathedral.s: St. Ursus Cathedral in Solothurn, Switzerland, is a large early neoclassical church built between 1763 and 1773 to designs by the Ticinese architect Gaetano Matteo Pisoni. It replaced the medieval collegiate church over the shrine of the martyrs Ursus and Victor.

sarnen.s: Sarnen is the capital of the Swiss canton of Obwalden, on the northern shore of Lake Sarnen. Its cantonal archive holds the White Book of Sarnen, written around 1470, which contains the earliest account of the founding of the Swiss Confederacy and the legend of William Tell.

stans.s: Stans is the capital of the Swiss canton of Nidwalden, at the foot of the Stanserhorn south of Lake Lucerne. In 1481 the Diet of Stans, helped by the mediation of the hermit Niklaus von Flüe, settled a crisis that threatened to split the Confederacy.

santa-maria-capua-vetere.s: Santa Maria Capua Vetere is a town in Campania, Italy, on the site of ancient Capua, once the largest city of southern Italy. Its remains include a great Roman amphitheatre, second in size only to the Colosseum, and a painted Mithraeum.

sicels.s: The Sicels were an ancient people of eastern Sicily, who gave the island its name. They lived in hill towns of the interior when Greek colonists arrived in the 8th century BCE, and were gradually Hellenised by cities such as Syracuse, Catana and Gela.

simeto.s: The Simeto, the ancient Symaethus, is the river with the largest basin in Sicily. It rises in the Nebrodi mountains, flows around the western and southern flanks of Mount Etna, and reaches the Ionian Sea south of Catania.

salento.s: Salento is the peninsula at the south-eastern tip of Italy, the 'heel' of the Italian boot, in Apulia, with Lecce as its main city. Under Byzantine rule until the 11th century it kept Greek religious and cultural traditions much longer than the rest of Apulia.

st-albans.s: St Albans is a city in Hertfordshire, England, north of London, beside the site of the Roman town of Verulamium. It grew around the abbey built at the shrine of Saint Alban, traditionally Britain's first Christian martyr, whose church is now the cathedral.

siege-of-akhulgo.s: The siege of Akhulgo was a Russian siege of Imam Shamil's mountain fortress in Dagestan in the summer of 1839. A Russian force under General Pavel Grabbe stormed the fortress in August after some eighty days, at a heavy cost on both sides, and most of the defenders and their…

soria.s: Soria is a city in Castile and León, north-central Spain, capital of the province of the same name on the upper Douro. The province covers the heartland of the ancient Arevaci, including the ruins of Numantia just north of the city.

selbach-mac-ferchair.s: Selbach mac Ferchair was a king of Dál Riata from the Cenél Loairn, who died in 730. A son of Ferchar Fota, he destroyed the fortress of Dunollie in 701 and fought the rival Cenél nGabráin, losing to them in 719 in one of the earliest recorded sea battles in British waters.

segre.s: The Segre is a river of north-eastern Spain, about 265 km long, rising in the French part of Cerdanya and flowing south-west through Catalonia past La Seu d'Urgell and Lleida to join the Ebro at Mequinenza. Its valleys were home to Iberian peoples such as the Cerretani and…

sara-people.s: The Sara are a group of related peoples of southern Chad and the north of the Central African Republic, speaking Central Sudanic languages, and form the largest ethnic group in Chad. Long raided for slaves by the northern sultanates, they were drawn into French colonial cotton…

siwana.s: Siwana is a town in western Rajasthan, India, dominated by a hill fort on the edge of the Thar Desert. Held by the Chauhans of Jalor, the fort was besieged by Alauddin Khalji in 1308; its commander Sitaladeva was killed and the fort fell before the Delhi army moved on to Jalor.

sambhar-salt-lake.s: Sambhar Salt Lake is India's largest inland salt lake, about 80 km west of Jaipur in Rajasthan. Salt from it supported the early medieval Chahamana dynasty, which tradition says was founded by Vasudeva, the lake's legendary discoverer, and whose homeland Shakambhari takes its…

somadeva-suri.s: Somadeva Suri was a 10th-century Jain monk and scholar who lived at the court of the Vemulavada Chalukyas, feudatories of the Rashtrakutas. His Sanskrit romance Yashastilaka, completed in 959, is a major work of Jain literature, and his Nitivakyamrita is a treatise on…

sahil-varman.s: Sahil Varman was a 10th-century raja of Chamba in the western Himalayas who moved his capital from Brahmapura (Bharmour) down the Ravi valley and founded the town of Chamba, named by tradition after his daughter Champavati. He is credited with building the Lakshmi Narayan…

shrichandra.s: Shrichandra was the most powerful king of the Chandra dynasty of south-eastern Bengal, ruling in the mid-10th century. Son of Trailokyachandra, he moved the capital to Vikramapura near Dhaka and ruled a kingdom independent of the Pala Empire, covering Vanga, Samatata and…

san-pedro-cactus.s: The San Pedro cactus, Echinopsis pachanoi, is a fast-growing columnar cactus native to the Andes of Peru and Ecuador. It contains mescaline and has been used in Andean healing and religious ceremonies for at least 3,000 years; it appears in the art of Chavín de Huántar, where…

shishupala.s: Shishupala is a king of Chedi in the Mahabharata, a cousin and enemy of Krishna. At the royal consecration sacrifice (rajasuya) held by Yudhishthira he objected to the honour given to Krishna and insulted him repeatedly, until Krishna killed him with his discus.

sequoyah.s: Sequoyah (c. 1770–1843) was a Cherokee silversmith who created the Cherokee syllabary, a writing system of 85 characters for the Cherokee language, completed around 1821. Although he could not read any other language, his invention was adopted by the Cherokee Nation in 1825,…

scilurus.s: Scilurus was a king of the Scythians in the Crimea in the 2nd century BCE, who ruled from Scythian Neapolis near modern Simferopol. He revived Scythian power, issued coins at Olbia and pressed the Greek cities of the region, notably Chersonesus.

segestes.s: Segestes was a nobleman of the Cherusci in the early 1st century CE and a leading supporter of Rome. He warned the governor Varus of Arminius' plans before the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest in 9 CE, but was ignored.

sacred-cenote.s: The Sacred Cenote is a large natural sinkhole at Chichen Itza in Yucatán, Mexico, linked to the city's main plaza by a raised causeway. The Maya threw offerings into it, including gold, jade, copal, pottery and human victims, as gifts to the rain god Chaac, and pilgrims still…

shaan-gan-ning-border-region.s: The Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region was the Chinese Communist base area in northern Shaanxi and parts of Gansu and Ningxia, with its capital at Yan'an, from 1937 to 1950. Formed from the soviet area reached by the Long March, it was recognised as a special region by the…

second-united-front.s: The Second United Front was the alliance between the Chinese Nationalist Party (Kuomintang) and the Chinese Communist Party against the Japanese invasion, formed in 1937 after the Xi'an Incident of December 1936. The Communists placed their forces under nominal Nationalist…

songkhla.s: Songkhla is a city in southern Thailand, on a narrow strip of land between the Gulf of Thailand and the Songkhla Lake lagoon. Early in the 17th century a Muslim ruler, Dato Mogol, founded a fortified port at Singora on the hills nearby, which traded with the Dutch and English…

sudak.s: Sudak is a town on the south-east coast of the Crimea, on the Black Sea. As Soldaia it was a major trading port from the Byzantine era; it was attacked by the Seljuks around 1222 and by the Mongols, and Venetian merchants kept a consulate there.

shimonoseki.s: Shimonoseki is a city at the south-western tip of Honshu, Japan, on the Kanmon Strait facing Kyushu. Off its shore the Battle of Dan-no-ura ended the Genpei War in 1185.

sanuki-province.s: Sanuki Province was an old province of Japan in north-eastern Shikoku, corresponding to modern Kagawa Prefecture. It was the birthplace of the monk Kūkai and home of the Konpira shrine.

satto.s: Satto was king of Chūzan on Okinawa from 1350 to 1395, ruling from Urasoe castle. In 1372 he answered the call of the Ming Hongwu Emperor and opened tribute relations with China, gaining access to Chinese trade and goods, and he also sent missions to Korea.

shunten.s: Shunten is the legendary first king of Ryukyu, said in the Chūzan Seikan chronicle to have reigned from 1187 to 1237. Later tradition made him a son of the Japanese warrior Minamoto no Tametomo and a local woman, a story used to tie the Ryukyuan royal line to Japan.

sati-beg.s: Sati Beg was a Mongol princess of the Ilkhanate, a daughter of Öljaitü and sister of Abu Sa'id. She was married first to the emir Chupan and later to Arpa Ke'un.

sadiya.s: Sadiya is a town in Tinsukia district in the far east of Assam, India, on the plain of the upper Brahmaputra near the border with Arunachal Pradesh. It was the centre of the medieval Chutia kingdom and, after the Ahom conquest of 1523–24, the seat of the Ahom frontier…

suhungmung.s: Suhungmung (r. 1497–1539) was a king of the Ahom kingdom in Assam, also known by the Hindu title Swarganarayan and as Dihingia Raja. He greatly enlarged the kingdom, annexing the Chutia kingdom in 1523–24, pressing the Dimasa Kacharis and repelling invasions from the Bengal…

sillustani.s: Sillustani is a pre-Inca burial ground on the shores of Lake Umayo near Puno in southern Peru. It is known for its chullpas, tall cylindrical stone funerary towers built by the Colla and later by the Incas, some reaching about 12 metres.

sydney-nova-scotia.s: Sydney is the main town of Cape Breton Island in Nova Scotia, Canada. It was founded in 1785 by Joseph Frederick Wallet DesBarres as the capital of the separate colony of Cape Breton, which was merged into Nova Scotia in 1820.

sydney.s: Sydney is the capital of New South Wales and the largest city in Australia, on Port Jackson on the south-east coast. It grew from the penal settlement founded at Sydney Cove by the First Fleet under Arthur Phillip in January 1788, the first British colony in Australia.

suva.s: Suva is the capital and largest city of Fiji, on the south-east coast of Viti Levu. It replaced Levuka as the capital of the British colony in 1882 and remained the capital at independence in 1970.

samuel-sharpe.s: Samuel Sharpe was an enslaved Baptist deacon in Jamaica who planned and led the Christmas Rebellion of 1831–1832, known as the Baptist War. He intended a peaceful general strike for wages, which turned into a widespread armed revolt across western Jamaica.

shimaore.s: Shimaore is a Bantu language spoken in Mayotte, one of the varieties of Comorian and closely related to Swahili. It is the native language of most of the island's population and has absorbed many words from Arabic, Malagasy and French.

sydney-cove.s: Sydney Cove is a small bay on the southern shore of Port Jackson, at the heart of modern Sydney, Australia. The First Fleet under Arthur Phillip landed there on 26 January 1788 to found a penal colony, the first British settlement in Australia, an event marked as Australia Day.

samuel-gorton.s: Samuel Gorton was an English religious dissenter and early settler of New England. Expelled from Plymouth, Portsmouth and Providence for his radical views and defiance of authority, he bought land from the Narragansett and founded Shawomet, later renamed Warwick, in 1642.

scarborough-tobago.s: Scarborough is the capital and main port of Tobago, in Trinidad and Tobago, on the island's southern coast. Founded by the British after they gained the island in 1763, it was the seat of the colonial government, overlooked by Fort King George, built in the 1770s.

shoshone.s: The Shoshone are a Native American people of the Great Basin, the Snake River plain and the Rocky Mountains, speaking a Numic language of the Uto-Aztecan family. The Comanche split from them around 1700 and moved onto the southern Plains.

sinaloa.s: Sinaloa is a state on the Pacific coast of north-western Mexico, with its capital at Culiacán. Under Spanish rule it was a frontier province of New Spain, linked with Sonora and evangelised by Jesuit missions from the 1590s.

sonora.s: Sonora is a state of north-western Mexico bordering Arizona, with its capital at Hermosillo. A frontier province of New Spain, it was settled through Jesuit missions and presidios among the Opata, Pima, Yaqui and Seri, and was a base for expeditions to Alta California.

scaliger.s: The Scaliger, or della Scala, were a family who ruled Verona as lords from the 1260s to 1387. Mastino I della Scala was chosen leader of the commune in 1259, and under Cangrande I and Mastino II the family dominated north-eastern Italy, ruling Vicenza, Padua, Treviso and for a…

sordello.s: Sordello da Goito was an Italian troubadour from near Mantua who wrote in Occitan. After an affair with Cunizza da Romano, sister of Ezzelino III, he left Italy for Provence and later served Charles of Anjou, following him to southern Italy.

scrovegni-chapel.s: The Scrovegni Chapel in Padua was built for the banker Enrico Scrovegni and consecrated in 1305. Giotto covered its interior with a fresco cycle of the lives of the Virgin and Christ and the Last Judgement, under a deep blue vault.

san-michele-maggiore-pavia.s: San Michele Maggiore is a Romanesque basilica in Pavia, Lombardy, rebuilt in sandstone in the early 12th century on the site of a Lombard church. It was used for royal coronations, and Frederick Barbarossa was crowned king of Italy there in 1155.

san-pietro-in-ciel-doro.s: San Pietro in Ciel d'Oro is a Romanesque basilica in Pavia, Lombardy, rebuilt in the 12th century and named after its once gilded ceiling. It holds the tomb of Saint Augustine of Hippo, whose relics the Lombard king Liutprand brought from Sardinia in the 8th century, and the…

sesia.s: The Sesia is a river of Piedmont in north-western Italy, about 138 km long, rising on the glaciers of Monte Rosa and flowing south through the Valsesia past Vercelli to join the Po. Its plain, irrigated by canals, is a major rice-growing area, and in the Middle Ages it lay…

siege-of-vicksburg.s: The Siege of Vicksburg, from May to 4 July 1863, ended with the surrender of the Confederate fortress on the Mississippi River in Mississippi to Union forces under Ulysses S. Grant. Its fall gave the Union control of the Mississippi and split the Confederacy in two.

shwenankyawshin.s: Shwenankyawshin, also known as Narapati II, was king of Ava in Upper Burma from 1501 to 1527. His reign was spent fighting rebel vassals, including Toungoo and Prome, and Shan states to the north.

saint-lizier.s: Saint-Lizier is a small town in Ariège in the French Pyrenees, the Roman Lugdunum Consoranorum, chief town of the Consoranni. It later took the name of its early bishop Lycerius and was the seat of the bishops of Couserans until 1801.

suniti-devi.s: Suniti Devi was Maharani of Cooch Behar, the daughter of the reformer Keshab Chandra Sen and wife of Maharaja Nripendra Narayan, whom she married in 1878. Her marriage, contrary to her father's campaign against child marriage, divided the Brahmo Samaj.

skibbereen.s: Skibbereen is the largest town in West Cork, Ireland, on the River Ilen. It grew in the 17th century in a district long held by Gaelic families such as the O'Driscolls, MacCarthys and O'Donovans.

saint-corentin.s: Saint Corentin is a Breton saint venerated as the first bishop of Quimper, in Cornouaille in western Brittany, probably in the 5th or 6th century. Legend says he lived as a hermit fed by a miraculous fish that renewed itself each day, and that King Gradlon gave him land for…

shropshire.s: Shropshire is a rural county in the West Midlands of England, on the Welsh border and crossed by the River Severn, with Shrewsbury as its county town. It was the heartland of the Iron Age Cornovii, whose Roman capital was Viroconium at Wroxeter, and later part of Powys and…

staffordshire.s: Staffordshire is a county in the West Midlands of England, in the upper Trent valley, with Stafford as its county town. The area lay in the heartland of the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Mercia, whose bishopric was at Lichfield and whose wealth is reflected in the Staffordshire Hoard…

san-millan-de-la-cogolla.s: San Millán de la Cogolla is a village in La Rioja, Spain, with two monasteries, Suso and Yuso, that grew from the hermitage of the 6th-century saint Aemilian (Millán). The monastery was a major religious and landowning centre of medieval Castile and Navarre, and the Glosas…

saint-pierre-martinique.s: Saint-Pierre is a town on the north-west coast of Martinique, founded in 1635 by Pierre Belain d'Esnambuc as the first French settlement on the island. It became the commercial and cultural capital of the colony, known as the 'Paris of the Caribbean'.

sergius-iv-of-naples.s: Sergius IV was duke of Naples from about 1002 to around 1036. Driven from his city in 1027 by Pandulf IV of Capua, he recovered it in 1029 with the help of Norman mercenaries, and in 1030 granted their leader Rainulf Drengot the town of Aversa, the first Norman lordship in…

sant-pere-de-besalu.s: Sant Pere de Besalú is a former Benedictine monastery in Besalú, Catalonia, founded in 977 by Miró Bonfill, who was both count of Besalú and bishop of Girona. Its Romanesque church, of the 12th century, survives with an ambulatory around the apse, carved capitals and a large…

stephen-count-of-blois.s: Stephen-Henry was count of Blois and Chartres and a leader of the First Crusade. He deserted the siege of Antioch in 1098 and returned home in disgrace, then set out again in 1101 and was killed at the Second Battle of Ramla in 1102.

stephen-king-of-england.s: Stephen was king of England from 1135 to 1154, a grandson of William the Conqueror through his mother Adela and a son of Stephen-Henry, Count of Blois. He became count of Boulogne by marrying its heiress Matilda and seized the English throne on the death of Henry I, against…

steigerwald.s: The Steigerwald is a wooded range of low hills in Franconia, northern Bavaria, Germany, between Bamberg and Würzburg. Its western slopes, overlooking the Main valley, carry vineyards of the Franconian wine region.

sant-marti-del-canigo.s: Sant Martí del Canigó is a Benedictine monastery high on the slopes of the Canigó massif in the eastern Pyrenees, now in the French department of Pyrénées-Orientales. Count Wifred II of Cerdanya founded it, its church was consecrated in 1009, and he later retired there as a monk.

sunifred-of-urgell.s: Sunifred was a 9th-century Frankish count who ruled Urgell and Cerdanya from about 834 and also Barcelona, Girona and other counties of the Spanish March from 844 until his death in 848. He was the father of Wilfred the Hairy and the ancestor of the House of Barcelona, which…

semois.s: The Semois is a river of the Ardennes, about 210 kilometres long, rising near Arlon in the Belgian province of Luxembourg and winding west through deep meanders past Chiny and Bouillon into France, where it joins the Meuse as the Semoy. Its wooded valley held small medieval…

sisteron.s: Sisteron is a town in the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence department of France, at a narrow gap where the Durance cuts through the mountains between Provence and the Dauphiné. Its position made it a key fortress of the counts of Forcalquier and Provence, and its citadel was rebuilt in…

soca.s: The Soča, in Italian Isonzo, is a river about 140 kilometres long that rises in the Julian Alps of Slovenia and flows past Gorizia into the Adriatic. Theodoric the Great defeated Odoacer on its banks in 489 on his way into Italy.

sarine.s: The Sarine, in German Saane, is a river of western Switzerland, about 125 kilometres long and a tributary of the Aare. It rises in the Bernese Alps, flows through Saanen and the Gruyère region and past the city of Fribourg, founded on a bend of the river in 1157.

saanen.s: Saanen is a municipality in the canton of Bern, Switzerland, in the upper valley of the Sarine (Saane), and includes the resort of Gstaad. Once part of the County of Gruyère, it passed to Bern when the indebted county was divided in 1555, and its German-speaking inhabitants…

schleusingen.s: Schleusingen is a small town in southern Thuringia, Germany, at the southern edge of the Thuringian Forest. From the 13th century it was the main residence of the counts of Henneberg-Schleusingen, whose Bertholdsburg castle still stands.

schmalkalden.s: Schmalkalden is a town in south-western Thuringia, Germany, on the south-western slopes of the Thuringian Forest, long known for iron and steel working. Shared for centuries between the counts of Henneberg and the landgraves of Hesse, it gave its name to the Schmalkaldic…

schleswig.s: Schleswig is a historical region and former duchy in southern Jutland, divided since a plebiscite of 1920 between Denmark (North Schleswig) and Germany (South Schleswig). Ruled by Danish royal princes and from 1386 by the counts of Holstein, it was joined with Holstein under…

stormarn.s: Stormarn is a historical region and present-day district in Schleswig-Holstein, Germany, between Hamburg and Lübeck. In the early Middle Ages it was one of the three Saxon districts north of the Elbe, alongside Holstein and Dithmarschen, with Hamburg as its chief centre.

sankt-goar.s: Sankt Goar is a small town on the left bank of the Middle Rhine in Rhineland-Palatinate, Germany, opposite St. Goarshausen and near the Lorelei rock. It grew around the cell of the 6th-century hermit Saint Goar and became a toll station of the counts of Katzenelnbogen, who…

sudetes.s: The Sudetes are a mountain range of central Europe along the border of the Czech Republic and Poland, with a small part in Germany, stretching about 300 km from Lusatia to the Moravian Gate. The highest peak is Sněžka in the Giant Mountains.

simon-august-count-of-lippe-detmold.s: Simon August (1727–1782) was Count of Lippe-Detmold from 1734, succeeding as a child. An enlightened ruler, he reformed schools, poor relief and agriculture and improved the administration of his small Westphalian county.

senne.s: The Senne (Dutch Zenne) is a small river of central Belgium, about 100 km long, flowing north through Brussels to join the Dijle near Mechelen. Brussels grew up on and around an island in the Senne in the 10th century.

siegfried-count-of-luxembourg.s: Siegfried (c. 922–998) was a Lotharingian count regarded as the founder of Luxembourg. In 963 he acquired the rocky promontory of Lucilinburhuc above the Alzette from St Maximin's Abbey at Trier and built a castle there, around which the city of Luxembourg grew.

siegen.s: Siegen is a university city in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany, on the Sieg in the Siegerland. Held by the House of Nassau from the 13th century, it was the residence of the Nassau-Siegen line from 1606, whose Upper and Lower Castles still stand.

saarland.s: The Saarland is a state of south-western Germany bordering France and Luxembourg, with its capital at Saarbrücken. Formed as the Territory of the Saar Basin under League of Nations administration in 1920, it voted to return to Germany in 1935, came under French control after…

sophie-of-brabant.s: Sophie of Brabant (1224–1275) was a daughter of Saint Elizabeth of Hungary and Landgrave Louis IV of Thuringia, and the wife of Duke Henry II of Brabant. When the Ludowingian line died out in 1247 she claimed the Thuringian inheritance for her son Henry and fought the Wettin…

stedingen.s: Stedingen is a marshland district on the lower Weser north-west of Bremen, settled by free peasant farmers in the 12th century. When the Stedinger refused tithes and dues to the archbishop of Bremen, they were declared heretics and a crusade was preached against them, ending…

santa-maria-de-mur.s: Santa Maria de Mur is a Romanesque church and former house of canons near the castle of Mur in the Pallars Jussà district of Catalonia. It was founded in 1069 by Count Ramon IV of Pallars Jussà and his wife Valença.

sort.s: Sort is a town in the province of Lleida, Catalonia, capital of the Pallars Sobirà district on the Noguera Pallaresa. In the Middle Ages it was the main seat of the counts of Pallars Sobirà, whose castle ruins stand above the town.

sparrenburg.s: The Sparrenburg is a castle on a ridge of the Teutoburg Forest above Bielefeld, built by the counts of Ravensberg in the first half of the 13th century. It was the administrative seat of the county and was rebuilt as a fortress with bastions in the 16th century.

sant-andreu-de-sureda.s: Sant Andreu de Sureda, in French Saint-André-de-Sorède, is a former Benedictine abbey in the foothills of the Albères in Roussillon, southern France. Its church has a carved marble lintel of the early 11th century, made by the same workshop as the dated lintel of nearby Sant…

sant-genis-de-fontanes.s: Sant Genís de Fontanes, in French Saint-Génis-des-Fontaines, is a former Benedictine abbey in Roussillon, founded in the early 9th century. Its marble lintel, carved with Christ in Majesty among the apostles and dated by its inscription to 1019–1020, is the oldest dated work…

saldana.s: Saldaña is a town on the Carrión river in the north of the province of Palencia, Castile and León. In the 10th and 11th centuries it was the seat of the counts of the Banu Gómez family, powerful frontier lords of the Kingdom of León.

sayn-abbey.s: Sayn Abbey is a former Premonstratensian monastery in Bendorf, near Koblenz, founded in 1202 by Count Henry II of Sayn. It served as the burial place of the counts of Sayn, and its church keeps a medieval arm reliquary of the apostle Simon.

siegerland.s: The Siegerland is a hilly region around the upper Sieg river in the south of North Rhine-Westphalia, centred on Siegen. Rich in iron ore, it was one of Germany's oldest mining and iron-working areas, worked from Celtic times until the 1960s.

stadthagen.s: Stadthagen is a town in the Schaumburg district of Lower Saxony, founded by the counts of Schaumburg in the 13th century. It was long their main residence, and the mausoleum of Prince Ernst, built in the early 17th century with bronze sculptures by Adriaen de Vries, adjoins…

schwarza-saale.s: The Schwarza is a river in Thuringia, about 50 km long, a left tributary of the Saale that flows through a deep, wooded valley on the edge of the Thuringian Forest. Schwarzburg castle above the valley gave its name to the counts of Schwarzburg in the 12th century.

sondershausen.s: Sondershausen is a town in northern Thuringia, below the Hainleite hills. It was the residence of the counts, later princes, of Schwarzburg-Sondershausen from 1599 until 1918, and their palace keeps rooms from the Renaissance to neoclassical periods.

schwaz.s: Schwaz is a town in the Inn valley of Tyrol, Austria, east of Innsbruck. In the 15th and 16th centuries its silver and copper mines were among the richest in Europe, financing the Habsburgs and the Fugger bankers who leased them.

spessart.s: The Spessart is a range of low, densely wooded hills in north-western Bavaria and southern Hesse, Germany, enclosed on three sides by the River Main. For centuries it was a hunting forest of the archbishops of Mainz, and the region around Aschaffenburg formed part of their…

stuttgart.s: Stuttgart is the capital of the German state of Baden-Württemberg, lying in a basin beside the Neckar. It probably began as a stud farm (Stuotgarten) in the 10th century, became the residence of the counts of Württemberg in the 14th century and was later the capital of the…

sea-beggars.s: The Sea Beggars (Watergeuzen) were Dutch Protestant privateers who fought Spanish rule in the Low Countries from 1568, sailing under letters of marque from William of Orange. Expelled from English ports, they captured Brielle on 1 April 1572 and then Flushing, setting off…

schwalm.s: The Schwalm is a river in northern Hesse, Germany, about 97 km long, rising in the Vogelsberg and flowing north past Alsfeld and Schwalmstadt (Treysa and Ziegenhain) to join the Eder near Felsberg. Its marshy valley around Ziegenhain gave its name to the Schwalm region, known…

san-gervasio.s: San Gervasio is a Maya archaeological site in the interior of the island of Cozumel, off the coast of Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula. Occupied from the Classic period and flourishing in the Postclassic, it was the island's main political and religious centre and is associated with…

sevastopol.s: Sevastopol is a port city in south-western Crimea, founded by the Russian Empire in 1783 as the base of the Black Sea Fleet, near the ruins of Greek Chersonesus. It withstood long sieges in the Crimean War (1854–1855) and the Second World War (1941–1942).

sandakan.s: Sandakan is a city on the north-east coast of Sabah, Malaysia. Founded in 1879 and renamed from Elopura, it was the capital of British North Borneo from 1884 until much of it was destroyed in the Second World War, when the Japanese held prisoners of war there; the Sandakan…

sibu.s: Sibu is a town on the lower Rajang River in central Sarawak, Malaysia. It grew under the Brooke rajahs, especially after the settlement of Foochow Chinese immigrants from 1901, and became a major river port and commercial centre for the Rajang basin.

sharukan.s: Sharukan was a Cuman khan of the late 11th century, a leader of the tribes on the Donets steppe. He raided the lands of Kievan Rus' and was defeated with other khans by the Rus' princes on the Sula river in 1107.

sudetenland.s: The Sudetenland was the name used in the 20th century for the border regions of Bohemia, Moravia and Czech Silesia inhabited mainly by German speakers. Claimed by German Austria in 1918, it was ceded to Nazi Germany under the Munich Agreement of 1938.

sari-iran.s: Sari is the capital of Mazandaran province in northern Iran, on the plain between the Alborz mountains and the Caspian Sea. It was a seat of the Dabuyid ispahbads of Tabaristan and later of local dynasties such as the Bavandids and the Marashis.

sadaham.s: Sadaham was a young hwarang, a member of the elite youth corps of Silla, in the 6th century. According to the Samguk sagi he fought with distinction at about the age of fifteen in Isabu's conquest of Daegaya in 562, refused rewards of land and captives, and died of grief soon…

seomjin-river.s: The Seomjin River is a river in south-western South Korea, about 220 km long, rising in North Jeolla and flowing south into the sea near Gwangyang. In the Three Kingdoms period its valley was contested between Baekje and the Gaya states, and its lower course gave access to the…

shengle.s: Shengle was the early centre of the Tuoba Xianbei, near modern Horinger in Inner Mongolia, China. Tradition says the Tuoba leader Liwei settled there in 258, and it served as a capital of the state of Dai and of the early Northern Wei before the court moved to Pingcheng…

saint-comgall.s: Saint Comgall was an Irish abbot of the Dál nAraidi who founded the monastery of Bangor in County Down around 558. Under his rule it became famous for strict discipline, learning and the singing of psalms, with very large numbers of monks, and it trained missionaries including…

senchus-fer-n-alban.s: The Senchus fer n-Alban ('history of the men of Scotland') is an early medieval Irish text describing the kingdom of Dál Riata in western Scotland. It gives the genealogies of its main kindreds, the Cenél nGabráin, Cenél Loairn and Cenél nÓengusa, with the number of houses in…

stirlingshire.s: Stirlingshire is a historic county in central Scotland, centred on Stirling at the head of the Forth estuary. Its control of the lowest crossing of the Forth gave it great strategic importance, and the battles of Stirling Bridge (1297) and Bannockburn (1314) were fought there.

serampore.s: Serampore is a town on the Hooghly River in West Bengal, India, north of Kolkata. As Frederiksnagore it was a Danish trading settlement from 1755 to 1845.

serampore-college.s: Serampore College is a college in Serampore, West Bengal, India, founded in 1818 by the Baptist missionaries William Carey, Joshua Marshman and William Ward. In 1827 the King of Denmark granted it a charter to award degrees, and it still confers theology degrees on colleges…

sivas.s: Sivas is a city in central Anatolia, Turkey, on the upper Kızılırmak. As ancient Sebasteia it was a Roman and Byzantine city; after 1071 it became a Danishmendid capital and then passed to the Seljuks of Rum, who built celebrated madrasas there.

stolac.s: Stolac is a small town in Herzegovina, in southern Bosnia and Herzegovina, on the Bregava river. Its surroundings are rich in archaeological remains, including the Illyrian hillfort of Daorson and the medieval necropolis of Radimlja, whose decorated tombstones (stećci) are…

scupi.s: Scupi was an ancient city on the upper Vardar, just north-west of modern Skopje in North Macedonia. Originally a centre of the Dardani, it became a Roman legionary base and then, under the Flavian emperors, a colony of veterans, later serving as capital of the province of…

skopje.s: Skopje is the capital and largest city of North Macedonia, on the Vardar river. It grew near Roman Scupi and became a royal city of medieval Serbia, where Stefan Dušan was crowned emperor in 1346.

sila-calabria.s: The Sila is a high forested plateau in Calabria, in the toe of southern Italy, rising to about 1,900 metres. In antiquity its pine forests supplied the Bruttii and later Rome with timber and pitch, used for shipbuilding and waterproofing.

sila-region.s: Sila is a region of south-eastern Chad, on the border with Sudan, with its capital at Goz Beïda. It corresponds to the old sultanate of Dar Sila, ruled by a dynasty related to that of Darfur from about the 17th century until the 20th.

salapia.s: Salapia was an ancient Daunian town on the Adriatic coast of northern Apulia, near the lagoon later called the Salpi lake. It was a busy port and minted its own coins.

sipontum.s: Sipontum was an ancient port on the Gulf of Manfredonia in northern Apulia, said in legend to have been founded by Diomedes. Rome planted a colony there in 194 BCE, and it later became an early Christian bishopric whose basilica of Santa Maria di Siponto survives.

suzhou.s: Suzhou is a city in southern Jiangsu, China, on the Grand Canal near Lake Tai, famous for its canals, classical gardens and silk. Called Pingjiang under the Song and Yuan, it was the capital of the rebel Zhang Shicheng from 1356 until Zhu Yuanzhang, the future Hongwu Emperor…

shandwick-stone.s: The Shandwick Stone, or Clach a' Charridh, is a Pictish cross-slab of around 800 CE standing above the village of Shandwick in Easter Ross, Scotland. One side carries a large cross with raised bosses, the other Pictish symbols, a hunting scene and a panel of intricate spiral…

saur-revolution.s: The Saur Revolution was the coup of 27–28 April 1978 in which army units loyal to the People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan overthrew and killed President Mohammad Daoud Khan. Named after the Afghan month in which it took place, it brought a communist government under Nur…

songhai-people.s: The Songhai are a people of West Africa living along the middle Niger in Mali and Niger, around towns such as Gao, Timbuktu and Niamey. They speak the Songhay languages and are traditionally farmers, fishermen and traders.

satpura-range.s: The Satpura Range is a range of hills in central India, running east to west between the Narmada and Tapti rivers through Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat. Its highest point, Dhupgarh near Pachmarhi, reaches about 1,350 metres.

salihiyya.s: The Salihiyya is a Sufi order founded in Mecca in the late 19th century by Muhammad Salih, a disciple in the Ahmadiyya tradition of Ahmad ibn Idris. It spread in Somalia, where its strict teaching, including a ban on tobacco and qat, won followers.

shpata-family.s: The Shpata were an Albanian noble family that ruled parts of Epirus and Aetolia in the late 14th and early 15th centuries. Their leader Gjin Bua Shpata took Angelokastron, Lepanto and later Arta, ruling as despot.

serres.s: Serres is a city in the region of Macedonia in northern Greece, in the fertile valley of the Strymon. Stefan Dušan took it from Byzantium in 1345, and after his death it became the seat of his widow Helena and of the despot Jovan Uglješa.

sonargaon.s: Sonargaon, the old Suvarnagrama, is a historic town near Narayanganj in central Bangladesh. It was a capital of eastern Bengal under the Deva dynasty and then of Muslim governors and the Sultan Fakhruddin Mubarak Shah in the 14th century.

sisodia.s: The Sisodia are a Rajput clan that ruled the kingdom of Mewar, with capitals at Chittorgarh and later Udaipur, from the 14th century until 1947. A branch of the earlier Guhila dynasty, they were famous for their long resistance to the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals under…

shizhaishan.s: Shizhaishan is a low hill near Jinning, by the southern shore of Lake Dian in Yunnan, China, site of a royal cemetery of the Dian kingdom. Excavations from 1955 uncovered tombs rich in bronze drums, weapons and cowrie containers topped with lively scenes of figures.

shuwa-arabs.s: The Shuwa Arabs are an Arabic-speaking people of the Lake Chad region, living in north-eastern Nigeria, northern Cameroon and Chad, and a branch of the wider Baggara Arabs. They descend from Arab groups who moved west across the Sahel over several centuries from about the 14th…

saar-bahrain.s: Saar is an archaeological site in northern Bahrain with the remains of an Early Dilmun settlement of about 2000 BCE. Excavations by the London–Bahrain Archaeological Expedition from 1990 uncovered a temple, a main street and dozens of stone houses, along with seals and pottery.

saar-river.s: The Saar is a river of north-eastern France and western Germany, about 246 kilometres long, which rises in the Vosges and flows north past Saarbrücken to join the Moselle near Trier. Its valley and the surrounding coal basin gave their name to the Saar region, separated from…

serbian-patriarchate-of-pec.s: The Serbian Patriarchate of Peć was the patriarchate of the Serbian Orthodox Church, seated at the Patriarchal Monastery of Peć in present-day Kosovo. The Serbian archbishopric was raised to a patriarchate in 1346, when Stefan Dušan was crowned emperor; after lapsing under…

slovakia.s: Slovakia is a landlocked country in Central Europe, with its capital at Bratislava, bordered by Poland, Ukraine, Hungary, Austria and Czechia. From the 11th century until 1918 its lands formed the northern part of the Kingdom of Hungary, and they then became part of…

syagrius.s: Syagrius was the last Roman ruler in northern Gaul, governing the region around Soissons after the death of his father Aegidius in 464 or 465. Gregory of Tours calls him 'king of the Romans'.

s-w-r-d-bandaranaike.s: S. W. R. D. Bandaranaike was Prime Minister of Ceylon from 1956 until his assassination in 1959. He founded the Sri Lanka Freedom Party in 1951 and won the 1956 election on a Sinhalese nationalist programme, passing the Sinhala Only Act, which made Sinhala the sole official…

sinhala-only-act.s: The Sinhala Only Act, formally the Official Language Act No. 33 of 1956, was passed by the Parliament of Ceylon under Prime Minister S. W. R. D. Bandaranaike. It replaced English with Sinhala as the sole official language, excluding Tamil, and many Tamil-speaking public…

social-security-act-1938.s: The Social Security Act 1938 was a New Zealand law passed by the first Labour government under Michael Joseph Savage. It created a comprehensive system of state support, including old-age, invalid and widows' benefits, family allowances and free hospital treatment, funded by a…

saint-malo.s: Saint-Malo is a walled port city on the Channel coast of Brittany, France, at the mouth of the Rance. Named after the Welsh monk Malo, who founded a monastery at neighbouring Aleth in the 6th century, it became famous for its seafarers, privateers and explorers, including…

saint-pol-de-leon.s: Saint-Pol-de-Léon is a town in Finistère, north-western Brittany, near the Channel coast. It takes its name from Paul Aurelian, a Welsh monk held to have founded the bishopric of Léon there in the 6th century.

starocherkasskaya.s: Starocherkasskaya is a Cossack village on the lower Don in Rostov oblast, Russia, known until 1805 as Cherkassk. From the mid-17th century it was the capital of the Don Cossack Host, built on an island exposed to spring floods.

shengzong-of-liao.s: Emperor Shengzong of Liao, Yelü Longxu, was the sixth emperor of the Khitan Liao dynasty, reigning from 982 to 1031. During his long reign, at first under the regency of his mother, Empress Dowager Xiao Chuo, Liao reached its height: the Chanyuan Treaty of 1005 secured annual…

swabia-bavaria.s: Swabia is an administrative region of Bavaria, Germany, often called Bavarian Swabia, with its capital at Augsburg. It covers the Swabian lands between the Iller and the Lech, including Augsburg, Kempten and Memmingen, which the Kingdom of Bavaria acquired in 1803–1810 from…

saint-gall.s: Saint Gall was a missionary monk, traditionally said to be an Irish companion of Saint Columbanus, who around 612 settled as a hermit in the Steinach valley south of Lake Constance. The Abbey of Saint Gall was founded on the site of his cell by Otmar in 719 and became one of…

saint-odile.s: Saint Odile was the daughter of Adalrich, Duke of Alsace, and founder of the convent of Hohenburg on the mountain now called Mont Sainte-Odile. According to her legend she was born blind, rejected by her father and given her sight at baptism.

sundgau.s: The Sundgau is a hilly region in the south of Alsace, France, between Mulhouse and the Swiss border near Basel. Originally the southern of the two counties into which Alsace was divided around 740, it passed to the Habsburgs and belonged to Further Austria until France…

straubing.s: Straubing is a town on the Danube in Lower Bavaria, at the centre of the fertile Gäuboden plain. From 1353 to 1425 it was the capital of the Duchy of Bavaria-Straubing, whose dukes also ruled Hainaut and Holland and built its ducal castle, and in 1435 Agnes Bernauer was…

santa-sofia-benevento.s: Santa Sofia is a church in Benevento, southern Italy, founded around 760 by the Lombard duke Arechis II as the national shrine of the southern Lombards. Its unusual star-shaped plan, with a central hexagon of ancient columns, makes it one of the most original surviving early…

schloss-burg.s: Schloss Burg is a castle above the Wupper river within the city of Solingen in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. Built in the 12th century by the counts of Berg, it was their main seat until the court moved to Düsseldorf in the late 14th century.

solingen.s: Solingen is a city in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany, in the hills of the Bergisches Land above the Wupper river. Known since the Middle Ages for its blades, it became the leading German centre for swords, knives and scissors, and its name is legally protected as a mark of…

s-hertogenbosch.s: 's-Hertogenbosch, also called Den Bosch, is the capital of the Dutch province of North Brabant. Duke Henry I of Brabant granted it town rights around 1185, and it became one of the four chief towns of the duchy, a prosperous trading town and the home of the painter Hieronymus…

saint-sever.s: Saint-Sever is a town in the Landes department of south-western France, above the Adour river. It grew around a Benedictine abbey founded in 988 by Duke William Sánchez of Gascony, whose scriptorium produced the illuminated Saint-Sever Beatus in the 11th century, a major work…

swidnica.s: Świdnica is a town in Lower Silesia, Poland, at the foot of the Sudetes. From the 1290s it was the capital of a Piast duchy, the last independent one in Silesia, and it grew rich from trade and brewing.

stanislaw-of-masovia.s: Stanisław of Masovia (1501–1524) was one of the last Piast dukes of Masovia, ruling jointly with his brother Janusz III, at first under the regency of their mother, Anna Radziwiłł. He died young and without heirs in 1524, and after Janusz III's death in 1526 Masovia was…

strelitz.s: Strelitz was a small town in the Lordship of Stargard in Mecklenburg, which became the residence of the dukes of Mecklenburg-Strelitz after the partition of 1701. After its palace burned in 1712, Duke Adolphus Frederick III built the new residence town of Neustrelitz nearby,…

somes.s: The Someș (Hungarian: Szamos) is a river of north-western Romania and eastern Hungary, a left tributary of the Tisza. It is formed at Dej by the union of the Someșul Mare and the Someșul Mic, which flows past Cluj-Napoca, and runs north-west past Satu Mare into Hungary.

sergius-i-of-naples.s: Sergius I (d. 864) was Duke of Naples from 840 and founder of a hereditary dynasty that ruled the duchy for three centuries. Elected by the citizens, he allied with neighbouring powers against Saracen raiders, and a Neapolitan fleet under his son Caesarius fought at the naval…

sergius-vii-of-naples.s: Sergius VII (d. 1137) was the last independent Duke of Naples, ruling from the early 1120s. He opposed Roger II of Sicily and resisted a long siege of Naples in 1135–1137, but then made peace and submitted to him.

sorrento.s: Sorrento is a town on the Sorrento Peninsula in Campania, southern Italy, overlooking the Bay of Naples. Known in antiquity as Surrentum, it was a self-governing duchy under Byzantine and Neapolitan influence in the early Middle Ages before falling to the Normans in the 12th…

silvius-i-nimrod-duke-of-wurttemberg-oel.n: Silvius I Nimrod, Duke of Württemberg-Oels
silvius-i-nimrod-duke-of-wurttemberg-oel.s: Silvius I Nimrod (1622–1664) was a prince of the House of Württemberg who in 1647 married Elisabeth Marie, heiress of the last Poděbrady duke of Oleśnica, and so became Duke of Oleśnica (Oels). He founded the Württemberg-Oels line, which ruled the Silesian duchy until it…

sisak.s: Sisak is a town in central Croatia at the confluence of the Kupa and the Sava, on the site of Roman Siscia, an important city and mint of Pannonia. In the 9th century it was the seat of the dukes of Pannonian Croatia.

slavonia.s: Slavonia is a historical region of eastern Croatia between the Drava, the Sava and the Danube, centred on Osijek. In the Middle Ages the name covered the lands between the Drava and Sava ruled by Hungary through a ban, and most of it fell to the Ottomans in the 16th century.

stralsund.s: Stralsund is a port city in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Germany, on the Strelasund opposite the island of Rügen. Granted town rights in 1234 by Prince Wizlaw I of Rügen, it became one of the leading Hanseatic towns and gave its name to the Treaty of Stralsund of 1370, which…

szczecin.s: Szczecin (German: Stettin) is a port city in north-western Poland on the lower Oder, near the Baltic. A Slavic stronghold and trading centre, it became the residence of the Griffin dukes of Pomerania and a Hanseatic town.

slupsk.s: Słupsk (German: Stolp) is a city in the Pomeranian Voivodeship of northern Poland, on the Słupia river near the Baltic coast. A Slavic stronghold and later a town of the Griffin dukes, it was the seat of the Duchy of Pomerania-Stolp in the 14th and 15th centuries.

swina.s: The Świna (German: Swine) is a strait in north-western Poland connecting the Szczecin Lagoon with the Baltic Sea between the islands of Usedom and Wolin. The port of Świnoujście stands at its mouth, and it carries the main shipping channel to Szczecin.

sambor-i.s: Sambor I (c. 1150–c. 1207) was the first prince of the Samboride dynasty in Gdańsk Pomerania (Pomerelia), which he governed for the Polish dukes. In 1186 he founded the Cistercian abbey of Oliwa near Gdańsk and endowed it with lands.

samborides.s: The Samborides were a dynasty that ruled Pomerelia, the region around Gdańsk on the lower Vistula, from the 12th century until 1294. At first governors for the Polish dukes, they became independent under Świętopełk II, who took the ducal title in 1227.

swietopelk-ii-duke-of-pomerania.s: Świętopełk II the Great (c. 1195–1266) was Duke of Pomerelia, the most powerful of the Samborides. In 1227 he threw off Polish overlordship and was involved in the killing of the Polish high duke Leszek the White at Gąsawa.

siemowit-vi-of-masovia.s: Siemowit VI of Masovia was a Piast duke who, with his younger brother Władysław II, inherited the lands of Płock, Rawa, Gostynin and other districts of western Masovia as a child in 1455, at first under the regency of their mother. He died unmarried on 1 January 1462, and his…

sandalj-hranic-kosaca.s: Sandalj Hranić Kosača was a Bosnian magnate who held the title of Grand Duke of Bosnia and ruled Hum and the Adriatic hinterland as a nearly independent lord. He played kings of Bosnia, Hungary and the Ottomans against one another and had close but difficult dealings with…

skat.s: Skat is a three-player trick-taking card game developed in Altenburg in Thuringia around 1810–1820, drawing on older games such as Schafkopf and Tarock. It spread through Germany during the nineteenth century and became the country's national card game, with standard rules…

saalfeld.s: Saalfeld is a town on the Saale river in Thuringia, Germany. An old mining and trading town, it was the residence of the dukes of Saxe-Saalfeld and then of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld until 1826, when it passed to Saxe-Meiningen.

seeberg-observatory.s: The Seeberg Observatory was an astronomical observatory built on the Kleiner Seeberg hill near Gotha by Duke Ernest II of Saxe-Gotha-Altenburg and completed in 1791. Under its first director, Franz Xaver von Zach, it became a leading centre of European astronomy and hosted the…

schlei.s: The Schlei is a long, narrow inlet of the Baltic Sea in Schleswig-Holstein, northern Germany, reaching about 40 kilometres inland. The Viking Age town of Hedeby stood near its western end, and the town of Schleswig, later capital of the Duchy of Schleswig, grew up on its shore.

scinawa.s: Ścinawa is a small town on the Oder river in Lower Silesia, Poland, between Głogów and Wrocław. In the late thirteenth and fourteenth centuries it was the seat of a small duchy held by branches of the Silesian Piasts.

sieradz-voivodeship.s: The Sieradz Voivodeship was a province of the Kingdom of Poland and the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, formed after the Duchy of Sieradz was incorporated into the Crown in 1339. Its seat was Sieradz on the Warta, and it included the Wieluń land.

sophia-olelkovich.s: Sophia Olelkovich was the last heiress of the Olelkovich princes of Slutsk. In 1600 she married Janusz Radziwiłł on condition that her lands remain Orthodox, and she defended the Orthodox faith in Slutsk after the Union of Brest.

slutsk.s: Slutsk is a town in the Minsk Region of Belarus, south of Minsk. It was the seat of the Olelkovich princes and later of the Radziwiłłs, who made it a fortified town with schools and churches.

strzelce-opolskie.s: Strzelce Opolskie (German Groß Strehlitz) is a town in the Opole Voivodeship of southern Poland, east of Opole. From 1313 it was the seat of a small Silesian Piast duchy, and it later followed Silesia under Bohemian and Habsburg rule.

sunan-ampel.s: Sunan Ampel, born Raden Rahmat, was one of the Wali Songo, the nine saints credited with spreading Islam in Java. Said to have come from Champa, he settled at Ampel Denta in Surabaya in the fifteenth century, where he founded a religious school that trained other preachers.

svitrigaila.s: Švitrigaila was a son of Algirdas and Grand Duke of Lithuania from 1430 to 1432. Supported by Orthodox Ruthenian nobles, he was overthrown by Sigismund Kęstutaitis and fought a civil war until his defeat at Wiłkomierz in 1435.

sauerland.s: The Sauerland is a hilly, wooded upland region in North Rhine-Westphalia and northern Hesse, Germany, south of the Ruhr valley. Much of it belonged to the County of Arnsberg and from 1368 to the Duchy of Westphalia ruled by the archbishops of Cologne, remaining Catholic.

soest.s: Soest is a town in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany, east of Dortmund. In the Middle Ages it was one of the largest towns of Westphalia and a leading member of the Hanseatic League, whose town law influenced many others.

somerset.s: Somerset is a county of south-west England, between the Bristol Channel and Dorset, with its county town at Taunton. Its low-lying Somerset Levels include the island of Athelney, where Alfred the Great sheltered from the Danes in 878, and the town of Glastonbury with its…

suetonius.s: Suetonius was a Roman biographer and imperial official who served as a secretary to the emperors Trajan and Hadrian. His Lives of the Twelve Caesars, covering Julius Caesar to Domitian, is a main source for the early Roman Empire and records details such as Vespasian's…

sadozai.s: The Sadozai are a clan of the Popalzai branch of the Abdali or Durrani Pashtuns of Afghanistan. Ahmad Shah Durrani, founder of the Durrani Empire in 1747, belonged to it, and his descendants ruled the empire until the Barakzai family took Kabul in the 1820s.

sindh.s: Sindh is a province of south-eastern Pakistan on the lower course of the Indus River, with its capital at Karachi. It was a centre of the Indus Valley Civilisation, whose city of Mohenjo-daro lies there.

sergipe.s: Sergipe is the smallest state of Brazil, on the north-eastern Atlantic coast between Bahia and Alagoas, with its capital at Aracaju. The Portuguese conquered the area from its Indigenous inhabitants in 1590 and developed cattle ranching and sugar there.

simon-van-der-stel.s: Simon van der Stel was commander and then the first governor of the Dutch Cape Colony from 1679 to 1699. He founded the town of Stellenbosch in 1679, encouraged settlement and wine-growing, and settled French Huguenot refugees in the colony from 1688.

sadras.s: Sadras, now Sadurangapattinam, is a coastal village south of Chennai in Tamil Nadu, India. In the 17th century the Dutch East India Company built a fortified trading post there to buy cotton textiles woven in the area.

sarekat-islam.s: Sarekat Islam was an Indonesian organisation founded in 1912 out of an association of Muslim batik traders, and under Oemar Said Tjokroaminoto it became the first mass political movement in the Dutch East Indies, with hundreds of thousands of members by 1919. It called for…

siraya-people.s: The Siraya are an Austronesian Indigenous people of the south-western plains of Taiwan, around modern Tainan. They were among the first Taiwanese peoples to deal with the Dutch East India Company, whose missionaries learned their language and wrote it in Latin letters.

stadthuys.s: The Stadthuys is a red-painted building in the centre of Malacca, Malaysia, built by the Dutch after their conquest of the city in 1641 and completed around 1660. It served as the residence of the Dutch governor and the seat of administration, and is regarded as the oldest…

si-thep.s: Si Thep is an ancient city in Phetchabun province in central Thailand, with a double moated town and monuments of the Dvaravati period and later Khmer influence, from roughly the 6th to the 13th century. Its Buddhist and Hindu sculpture and brick monuments such as Khao Klang…

siward-earl-of-northumbria.s: Siward was an earl of Scandinavian origin who governed York under Cnut and his successors from the 1030s. In 1041 he killed Eadwulf of Bamburgh and brought all of Northumbria under his rule.

sweyn-haakonsson.s: Sweyn Haakonsson was a Norwegian earl of Lade, a son of Håkon Sigurdsson. After the Battle of Svolder in 1000 he and his brother Eric governed Norway for the kings of Denmark and Sweden.

sunnmore.s: Sunnmøre is the southernmost traditional district of the county of Møre og Romsdal on the west coast of Norway, with Ålesund as its main town. Its fjords include the Geirangerfjord, a World Heritage Site.

st-magnus-cathedral.s: St Magnus Cathedral in Kirkwall, Orkney, was founded in 1137 by Earl Rögnvald Kali Kolsson in honour of his uncle, the martyred Earl Magnus. Built in red and yellow sandstone in the Romanesque style, it is the most northerly cathedral in Britain and the finest surviving…

senguttuvan.s: Senguttuvan was a Chera king of the Sangam age in southern India, praised in the fifth decade of the Patirruppattu for his campaigns. In the epic Silappatikaram he leads an expedition to the Himalayas to bring a stone for an image of Kannagi, the heroine of the poem,…

silappatikaram.s: The Silappatikaram, or Tale of the Anklet, is a Tamil epic attributed to Ilango Adigal and usually dated to around the 5th century CE. It tells of Kannagi, whose husband Kovalan is wrongly executed in Madurai, and of her revenge and deification, moving across the lands of the…

saqqara.s: Saqqara is a vast ancient burial ground west of Memphis in Egypt, used for over 3,000 years. It holds large mastaba tombs of First Dynasty officials and the Step Pyramid of Djoser, built by Imhotep around 2650 BCE, the earliest monumental stone building.

second-dynasty-of-egypt.s: The Second Dynasty of Egypt ruled from about 2890 to 2686 BCE, the second line of kings of the Early Dynastic period. Its rulers included Hotepsekhemwy, Nynetjer, Peribsen and Khasekhemwy, and the period seems to have seen internal division before Khasekhemwy reunited the…

seth.s: Seth was an ancient Egyptian god of storms, the desert, foreign lands and disorder. In myth he murdered his brother Osiris and fought Osiris's son Horus for the throne, but he also defended the sun god against the serpent Apophis.

sangam-literature.s: Sangam literature is the earliest body of Tamil poetry, composed roughly between 300 BCE and 300 CE and collected in the Eight Anthologies and the Ten Idylls. Its poems deal with love and with war, kings and patronage, and they are a main source for the early Chera, Chola and…

samguk-sagi.s: The Samguk sagi, or History of the Three Kingdoms, is the oldest surviving history of Korea, compiled in Classical Chinese by Kim Busik and other scholars and presented to King Injong of Goryeo in 1145. It covers Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla, with annals, tables and biographies.

samguk-yusa.s: The Samguk yusa, or Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms, is a collection of Korean histories, legends and Buddhist tales compiled by the monk Iryeon in the 1280s. It preserves material missing from the Samguk sagi, including the foundation myth of Dangun and the traditions of…

szekesfehervar.s: Székesfehérvár is a city in central Hungary, between Lake Balaton and Budapest. Developed as a royal centre by Grand Prince Géza and King Stephen I, it was the coronation and burial place of Hungarian kings for some five centuries, centred on its royal basilica.

siege-of-yanmen.s: The Siege of Yanmen was the encirclement of Emperor Yang of Sui by the Eastern Turkic ruler Shibi Khagan in 615, at Yanmen commandery in northern Shanxi. Caught on a tour of the northern frontier, the emperor was besieged for about a month until relief armies approached and…

sa-caleta.s: Sa Caleta is the site of a Phoenician settlement on the south coast of Ibiza, occupied in the 7th century BCE and abandoned around 600 BCE, when its people probably moved to the site of the city of Ibiza. Its excavated houses, streets and workshops are among the best-preserved…

sodeke.s: Sodeke was an Egba war leader who led refugees from the towns destroyed in the Yoruba wars to Olumo Rock around 1830, where they founded Abeokuta. As the city's leading figure until his death in the 1840s, he united the displaced townships in one settlement, organised its…

seventh-dynasty-of-egypt.s: The Seventh Dynasty of Egypt is a dynasty listed by the historian Manetho, who described it as 'seventy kings in seventy days' at Memphis after the end of the Old Kingdom. Modern scholars generally regard it as fictitious, perhaps an echo of the confusion of the period, and…

shams-al-din-eldiguz.s: Shams al-Din Eldiguz was a former Kipchak slave who founded the Eldiguzid dynasty of atabegs of Azerbaijan. Around 1136 the Seljuk sultan Mas'ud made him governor of Arran and guardian of the prince Arslan Shah, whose widowed mother he married.

schleissheim-palace.s: Schleissheim Palace is a group of three palaces at Oberschleissheim, north of Munich. Beside an early 17th-century country residence of Duke William V and Elector Maximilian I, Elector Max Emanuel built the small Lustheim garden palace and, from 1701, the large Baroque New…

schmalkaldic-war.s: The Schmalkaldic War of 1546–1547 was fought between Emperor Charles V and the Schmalkaldic League of Lutheran princes and cities in the Holy Roman Empire. Allied with the Protestant Duke Maurice of Saxony, Charles defeated and captured Elector John Frederick of Saxony at the…

san-pedro-martir-river.s: The San Pedro Mártir is a river of northern Guatemala and south-eastern Mexico that flows west from the Petén lowlands into Tabasco to join the Usumacinta. In the Classic period it was a trade route between the Gulf lowlands and the central Petén, guarded by the Maya city of…

sampsigeramus-i.s: Sampsigeramus I was an Arab chieftain who founded the priest-kingdom of Emesa, modern Homs, in Syria, controlling the Orontes valley and the town of Arethusa as the Seleucid Empire collapsed in the 1st century BCE. He submitted to Pompey in 64 BCE and was recognised as a…

second-anglo-afghan-war.s: The Second Anglo-Afghan War was fought from 1878 to 1880 between British India and the Emirate of Afghanistan, after the emir Sher Ali Khan received a Russian mission. British forces occupied much of the country and imposed the Treaty of Gandamak in 1879, but the murder of the…

sawdan.s: Sawdan was the third and last emir of Bari, ruling from about 857 to 871. He raided widely in southern Italy, including the lands of the abbey of Monte Cassino, and obtained recognition from the Abbasid caliph through the governor of Egypt.

sharaf-khan-bidlisi.s: Sharaf Khan Bidlisi was a Kurdish emir of Bitlis and historian, born in 1543 and raised at the Safavid court. After serving the Safavids he went over to the Ottomans, who restored him as ruler of his family's emirate of Bitlis in 1578.

sharafnama.s: The Sharafnama is a history of the Kurdish dynasties and principalities written in Persian by Sharaf Khan Bidlisi, emir of Bitlis, and completed in 1597. It surveys the ruling families of Kurdistan, their genealogies and their relations with the Ottoman and Safavid empires,…

saud-ibn-abd-al-aziz.s: Saud ibn Abd al-Aziz was ruler of the Emirate of Diriyah, the first Saudi state, from 1803 to 1814. As commander and then ruler he led the state to its greatest extent: his forces sacked Karbala in 1802, took Mecca in 1803 and Medina soon after, and raided Iraq, Syria and Oman.

salghurids.s: The Salghurids were a Turkmen dynasty of atabegs who ruled Fars in southern Iran from Shiraz between 1148 and 1282. Nominally subject first to the Seljuks and later to the Khwarazmshahs and Mongols, they extended their power over the Persian Gulf, conquering Kish in 1229.

siraf.s: Siraf was a port on the Iranian coast of the Persian Gulf, near modern Bandar Taheri in Bushehr province. In the 9th and 10th centuries it was the Gulf's leading harbour, trading with India, East Africa and China.

siculo-arabic.s: Siculo-Arabic was the variety of Arabic spoken in Sicily and Malta from the Islamic conquest in the 9th century. It remained in use among Sicily's Muslims, Christians and Jews under Norman rule but died out on the island in the later Middle Ages.

sakanoue-no-tamuramaro.s: Sakanoue no Tamuramaro was a Japanese general and court noble of the early Heian period. Appointed seii taishōgun in 797, he led the campaigns against the Emishi of northern Honshu, built Isawa Castle in 802 and received the surrender of the Emishi leader Aterui that year.

sumela-monastery.s: Sumela Monastery is a Greek Orthodox monastery built into a cliff in the Pontic Mountains near Maçka, south of Trabzon in north-eastern Turkey. Dedicated to the Virgin, it was by tradition founded in the 4th century and flourished under the emperors of Trebizond, who granted…

samuel-pepys.s: Samuel Pepys was an English naval administrator and member of parliament, best known for the diary he kept from 1660 to 1669, describing the Restoration court, the Great Plague and the Great Fire of London. As Secretary to the Admiralty he helped reform the navy.

sanctuary-of-asclepius-at-epidaurus.s: The Sanctuary of Asclepius at Epidaurus, in the north-eastern Peloponnese, was the most celebrated healing centre of the ancient Greek world. From the late 5th century BCE the sick came to sleep in its halls hoping for healing dreams, and inscriptions record their cures.

saint-louis-senegal.s: Saint-Louis is a city in north-western Senegal, built on an island at the mouth of the Senegal River. Founded by the French in 1659, it was their main trading post in West Africa, the capital of the colony of Senegal and, until 1902, of French West Africa; it also served as…

seton-lloyd.s: Seton Lloyd was a British archaeologist who worked in Iraq and Turkey for much of the 20th century. As adviser to the Iraqi Directorate of Antiquities he excavated Tell Hassuna, Eridu and other sites with Fuad Safar.

seydisehir.s: Seydişehir is a town in Konya Province in central Turkey, south of Lake Beyşehir. In the late Middle Ages it belonged to the Eshrefid and then the Hamidid beyliks before passing to the Karamanids and the Ottomans.

sees.s: Sées is a small town in the Orne department of Normandy, north-western France. It grew from the Roman-era centre of the Gallic Sagii and has been the seat of a bishopric since late antiquity.

santona.s: Santoña is a coastal town in Cantabria, northern Spain, on the estuary of the Asón river, known for its anchovy canning and its fortifications. In August 1937, during the Spanish Civil War, Basque troops surrendered there to Italian forces fighting for Franco under the Santoña…

shuqra.s: Shuqra is a small port town on the Gulf of Aden in the Abyan Governorate of southern Yemen, east of Aden. From the late 17th century it was the chief town of the Fadhli Sultanate, whose sultans controlled the coast and hinterland of Abyan.

stanley-falkland-islands.s: Stanley is the capital and only town of the Falkland Islands, on the east coast of East Falkland. It replaced Port Louis as the seat of government in 1845 and grew as a harbour serving ships rounding Cape Horn.

sheberghan.s: Sheberghan is a city in northern Afghanistan, the capital of Jowzjan Province on the plain between the Hindu Kush foothills and the Amu Darya. Medieval geographers knew it as Shiburghan, one of the towns of the region of Guzgan.

sushila-karki.s: Sushila Karki is a Nepalese jurist who became the first woman to serve as chief justice of Nepal, in 2016–2017, known for rulings against corruption. In September 2025, after youth-led protests forced the resignation of K. P. Sharma Oli, she was appointed interim prime…

spina.s: Spina was an Etruscan port on the Po delta near modern Comacchio, in north-eastern Italy, founded in the late 6th century BCE. It was a major trading centre between the Etruscans of the Po plain and the Greek world, and its cemeteries, uncovered during land drainage in the…

sabha-libya.s: Sabha is the largest city of the Fezzan region in south-western Libya, an oasis town on the old caravan routes across the Sahara. Under Italian rule it was a military post, and after the Second World War it served as the centre of the French-administered territory of Fezzan.

st-andrews.s: St Andrews is a town on the coast of Fife in eastern Scotland, known earlier as Cennrigmonaid. A Pictish church there received relics of Saint Andrew by tradition in the 8th century, and it became the seat of Scotland's chief bishop, raised to an archbishopric in 1472.
