sir-john-kerr.s: Sir John Kerr was Governor-General of Australia from 1974 to 1977. On 11 November 1975, after the opposition-controlled Senate had blocked the government's budget, he dismissed the prime minister Gough Whitlam and appointed Malcolm Fraser as caretaker until an election.

societe-anversoise-du-commerce-au-congo.n: Société Anversoise du Commerce au Congo
societe-anversoise-du-commerce-au-congo.s: The Société Anversoise du Commerce au Congo was an Antwerp company that held a concession for rubber in the Mongala basin of the Congo Free State, in which the state had a large interest. Like ABIR, it extracted rubber through armed agents, quotas and violence, and its…

stairs-expedition-to-katanga.s: The Stairs Expedition was a Congo Free State expedition of 1891–1892 to Katanga led by the Canadian-born British officer William Stairs. Its aim was to secure the copper-rich region before Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company.

st-donatians-cathedral.s: St Donatian's Cathedral was the principal church of Bruges, standing on the Burg square beside the counts' residence. A collegiate church dedicated to Saint Donatian of Reims, it was where Count Charles the Good was murdered in 1127, and it became the cathedral of the new…

saint-waltrude.s: Saint Waltrude was a Frankish noblewoman who founded a religious community at Mons in Hainaut in the seventh century, around which the town grew. Married to Vincent Madelgarius and the mother of children also venerated as saints, she withdrew to a life of prayer.

schalksburg.s: The Schalksburg was a castle on a hill near Balingen and Albstadt in the Swabian Jura, in Baden-Württemberg, Germany. From the late thirteenth century it was the seat of a branch of the counts of Zollern, the Schalksburg line, whose lordship included Balingen.

saint-dominic.s: Saint Dominic, born Domingo de Guzmán at Caleruega in Castile, was the founder of the Order of Preachers, the Dominicans. Sent to Languedoc to preach against the Cathars, he founded a house for converted women at Prouille and in 1215 a community of preachers in Toulouse.

saint-gilles-gard.s: Saint-Gilles is a town in the Gard department of southern France, on the edge of the Camargue near the Rhône delta. It grew around the abbey holding the tomb of Saint Giles, a major pilgrimage goal and a stop on the road to Santiago de Compostela, and was the ancestral seat of…

santiago-de-compostela.s: Santiago de Compostela is the capital of Galicia in north-western Spain. It grew around the shrine where the remains of the apostle Saint James were believed to have been found in the ninth century, and its cathedral became one of the three great pilgrimage goals of medieval…

simon-de-montfort-6th-earl-of-leicester.n: Simon de Montfort, 6th Earl of Leicester
simon-de-montfort-6th-earl-of-leicester.s: Simon de Montfort, 6th Earl of Leicester, was a French-born noble, a son of the leader of the Albigensian Crusade, who became leader of the baronial opposition to Henry III of England. He defeated the king at Lewes in 1264 and governed England, summoning in 1265 a parliament…

song-of-the-albigensian-crusade.s: The Song of the Albigensian Crusade is an Occitan epic poem of nearly 10,000 lines describing the crusade against the Cathars from 1208 to 1219. The first part, by William of Tudela, favours the crusaders; an anonymous continuator wrote the rest from the side of the counts of…

sahib-i-giray.s: Sahib I Giray was khan of Kazan from 1521 to 1524 and khan of Crimea from 1532 to 1551. Installed in Crimea with Ottoman support, he used Ottoman troops and firearms to strengthen the khan's power over the great clans and built up Bakhchysarai as his capital, with its palace.

sahin-giray.s: Şahin Giray was the last khan of Crimea, ruling from 1777 to 1783 with Russian support after the khanate became nominally independent in 1774. His centralising, European-style reforms of the army and administration provoked revolts that Russian troops put down.

selim-iii-giray.s: Selim III Giray was khan of Crimea in 1764–1767 and again in 1770–1771. During his second reign, in the Russo-Turkish War of 1768–1774, Russian forces under Vasily Dolgorukov stormed the Perekop lines and overran Crimea in 1771, and he fled to Istanbul.

siete-partidas.s: The Siete Partidas, or Seven-Part Code, is a law code compiled in Castile under Alfonso X, drawing on Roman and canon law. It covered government, the church, family, property and crime, but gained force of law only through the Ordinance of Alcalá of 1348.

santa-hermandad.s: The Santa Hermandad, or Holy Brotherhood, was a peacekeeping force created by Isabella I and Ferdinand II at the Cortes of Madrigal in 1476, built on the older brotherhoods of Castilian towns. Paid for by local levies, it pursued robbers and rebels in the countryside and…

school-of-salamanca.s: The School of Salamanca was a group of 16th-century Spanish theologians and jurists, led by Francisco de Vitoria and including Domingo de Soto, Luis de Molina and Francisco Suárez. Reviving Thomist natural law, they debated the rights of the conquered peoples of the Americas,…

spanish-inquisition.s: The Spanish Inquisition was a church tribunal under royal control, authorised by Pope Sixtus IV in 1478 at the request of Isabella I and Ferdinand II. Its first targets were converted Jews suspected of secret Judaism; it later pursued Moriscos, Protestants and other dissenters…

sudeten-german-party.s: The Sudeten German Party was the political party of the German minority in Czechoslovakia, founded by Konrad Henlein in 1933 as the Sudeten German Home Front and renamed in 1935. Winning more votes than any other party in the 1935 elections, it was increasingly directed and…

sudeten-germans.s: The Sudeten Germans were the German-speaking inhabitants of Bohemia, Moravia and Czech Silesia, about three million people in interwar Czechoslovakia. Their grievances were exploited by Nazi Germany, which annexed the mainly German border areas, the Sudetenland, under the…

scoti.s: Scoti was the Latin name for the Gaels of Ireland, first used by Roman writers in the fourth century, when they raided Roman Britain. Some settled in western Britain, and Gaels from Ireland and the kingdom of Dál Riata spread their language across northern Britain.

synod-of-whitby.s: The Synod of Whitby was a church council held in 664 at the abbey of Whitby, presided over by King Oswiu of Northumbria. Wilfrid argued for Roman practice and Bishop Colmán for the Irish tradition of Iona in calculating the date of Easter; Oswiu chose Rome.

soteria.s: The Soteria was a festival at Delphi founded after the defence of the sanctuary against the Gauls of Brennus in 279 BCE, honouring Zeus Soter and Apollo for the city's deliverance. Controlled by the Aetolian League, which had led the defence, it was reorganised in the…

second-sacred-war.s: The Second Sacred War was a brief conflict around 449–448 BCE over control of the sanctuary of Delphi. Sparta sent an army that took the sanctuary from the Phocians and handed it to the Delphians, after which Athens under Pericles marched in and returned it to the Phocians.

scanian-war.s: The Scanian War was fought from 1675 to 1679 between Denmark-Norway and Sweden, as part of the wider Franco-Dutch War. Denmark-Norway invaded Scania to recover the provinces lost in 1658 and won at sea under Niels Juel, but lost the Battle of Lund in 1676.

saint-hilaire-le-grand.s: Saint-Hilaire-le-Grand is a Romanesque church in Poitiers built over the tomb of Saint Hilary, the fourth-century bishop of the city. The present building was consecrated in 1049 and was served by a powerful chapter of canons whose abbots were the counts of Poitou and dukes of…

saint-jean-dangely.s: Saint-Jean-d'Angély is a town in the Charente-Maritime department of western France, in the old province of Saintonge. It grew around a Benedictine abbey founded in the early ninth century by Pepin I of Aquitaine, which claimed to hold the head of John the Baptist and drew…

siegfried-of-westerburg.s: Siegfried of Westerburg was archbishop of Cologne from 1275 until his death in 1297. He opposed John I of Brabant in the War of the Limburg Succession, but was defeated and captured at the Battle of Worringen in 1288.

sack-of-antwerp-1576.s: The Sack of Antwerp, known as the Spanish Fury, took place on 4 November 1576, when mutinous, long-unpaid Spanish troops of the Army of Flanders stormed and plundered the city for three days. Several thousand inhabitants were killed and much of the city was burned.

states-brabant.s: States Brabant (Staats-Brabant) was the northern part of the Duchy of Brabant conquered by the Dutch Republic in the Eighty Years' War, around 's-Hertogenbosch, Breda and Bergen op Zoom. Confirmed to the Republic by the Peace of Münster in 1648, it was governed directly by the…

saint-florentin.s: Saint-Florentin is a small town in the Yonne department of Burgundy, where the Armance meets the Armançon. Near it in 898 Richard the Justiciar, count of Autun, defeated a Viking army, a victory that strengthened his claim to lead the region that became the Duchy of Burgundy.

sainte-marie-aux-mines.s: Sainte-Marie-aux-Mines is a town in a valley of the Vosges in the Haut-Rhin department of Alsace, north-eastern France. In the sixteenth century its silver mines were among the richest in Europe, and the valley was divided between the dukes of Lorraine and the lords of…

saint-nicolas-de-port.s: Saint-Nicolas-de-Port is a town on the Meurthe near Nancy in north-eastern France. It grew around a relic of Saint Nicholas brought from Bari in the late eleventh century and became the chief pilgrimage centre and fair town of the Duchy of Lorraine.

sarreguemines.s: Sarreguemines is a town in the Moselle department of north-eastern France, at the confluence of the Saar and the Blies on the border with Germany. In the Duchy of Lorraine it was the seat of the German-speaking bailliage d'Allemagne.

santa-maria-delle-grazie-milan.s: Santa Maria delle Grazie is a Dominican church and convent in Milan, built from 1463 to designs by Guiniforte Solari. Ludovico Sforza had its east end rebuilt with a large domed tribune, attributed to Donato Bramante, as a family mausoleum.

senate-of-milan.s: The Senate of Milan was the supreme court and highest council of the Duchy of Milan, created by Louis XII of France in 1499 after his conquest of the duchy. It survived under the last Sforza dukes and under Spanish rule, registering and interpreting laws and guarding local…

saint-valery-sur-somme.s: Saint-Valery-sur-Somme is a small port on the estuary of the Somme in Picardy, northern France. In late September 1066 Duke William of Normandy's invasion fleet sailed from there, after waiting weeks for a favourable wind, and landed at Pevensey in England, leading to the…

siege-of-turin.s: The Siege of Turin was the French attempt in 1706 to capture the capital of Victor Amadeus II of Savoy during the War of the Spanish Succession. After a siege of nearly four months, a relief army under Prince Eugene of Savoy joined the duke and defeated the French besiegers on…

savoie.s: Savoie is a department of south-eastern France in the Alps, with its prefecture at Chambéry, the old capital of the counts of Savoy. Together with Haute-Savoie it was formed from the historic Duchy of Savoy, which the Kingdom of Sardinia ceded to France by the Treaty of Turin…

shroud-of-turin.s: The Shroud of Turin is a linen cloth bearing the faint image of a man, venerated by many as the burial cloth of Jesus. It is first documented at Lirey in France in the 1350s, was acquired by the house of Savoy in 1453 and moved from Chambéry to Turin in 1578.

statuta-sabaudiae.s: The Statuta Sabaudiae were the general statutes issued by Duke Amadeus VIII of Savoy in 1430. They codified the law, the courts and the administration of his lands on both sides of the Alps, regulated social ranks, dress and expenditure, and organised the ducal council.

sachsenspiegel.s: The Sachsenspiegel ('Mirror of the Saxons') is a law book compiled by Eike von Repgow between about 1220 and 1235, recording the customary land law and feudal law of Saxony in Middle Low German. The most influential German law book of the Middle Ages, it was copied in…

sutan-sjahrir.s: Sutan Sjahrir was an Indonesian nationalist and socialist leader from West Sumatra. Exiled by the Dutch to Boven-Digoel and Banda Neira in the 1930s, he refused to collaborate with the Japanese during the occupation.

second-stadtholderless-period.s: The Second Stadtholderless Period was the era from 1702 to 1747 when most provinces of the Dutch Republic left the office of stadtholder vacant after the death of William III. Regent oligarchies governed under grand pensionaries such as Anthonie Heinsius, while the costs of…

simon-stevin.s: Simon Stevin was a Flemish mathematician and engineer who settled in the Dutch Republic and served Maurice of Nassau as tutor, adviser and quartermaster. He popularised decimal fractions in De Thiende (1585), contributed to statics and hydrostatics, and designed fortifications…

southern-netherlands.s: The Southern Netherlands were the provinces of the Low Countries that remained under Habsburg rule after the Dutch Revolt, corresponding roughly to modern Belgium and Luxembourg. Ruled by Spain until 1714 and then by Austria, they were also called the Spanish and Austrian…

sengge-dzungar-ruler.s: Sengge was ruler of the Dzungars from 1653 to 1670, the son and successor of Erdeni Batur. His reign was troubled by disputes with his half-brothers over the inheritance, and he clashed with Russian outposts in southern Siberia over tribute from local peoples.

shangqing.s: Shangqing ('Highest Clarity') is a school of Daoism based on revelations received in the 360s by Yang Xi, who wrote down scriptures dictated, he said, by perfected immortals, for an aristocratic family near Jiankang. Emphasising meditation, visualisation and individual…

shishuo-xinyu.s: The Shishuo Xinyu (A New Account of the Tales of the World) is a Chinese collection of anecdotes compiled about 430 under Liu Yiqing, a prince of the Liu Song dynasty. Its more than a thousand short episodes record the sayings and conduct of scholars, officials and aristocrats…

sima-yuanxian.s: Sima Yuanxian was a prince of the Eastern Jin dynasty and son of Sima Daozi, whom he displaced as the effective ruler of the court in 399 under the disabled Emperor An. His conscription of the dependants of eastern landholders provoked the rebellion of Sun En.

su-jun.s: Su Jun was a general of the Eastern Jin dynasty who led a rebellion in 327–329. A northern refugee commander posted north of the Yangtze, he rose with Zu Yue against the regent Yu Liang, who had tried to take away his troops, and captured the capital Jiankang in 328, holding…

sodom-and-gomorrah.s: Sodom and Gomorrah are two cities of the Hebrew Bible, described in the Book of Genesis as destroyed by God with fire and brimstone for the wickedness of their inhabitants. Their location, traditionally placed near the Dead Sea, is unknown.

song-of-release.s: The Song of Release is a Hurrian poem preserved in a bilingual Hurrian–Hittite version on tablets from Hattusa, dating from the fifteenth century BCE. It tells how the city of Ebla refused the storm god Teshub's demand to free captives from the town of Igingallis and was…

sapienza-university-of-rome.s: Sapienza University of Rome is a public university in Rome, founded in 1303 by Pope Boniface VIII as a studium for the papal city. One of the largest universities in Europe, it is known for archaeology and Near Eastern studies; its mission under Paolo Matthiae began excavating…

synod-of-dort.s: The Synod of Dort was an international assembly of the Reformed churches held at Dordrecht in the Dutch Republic in 1618–1619. Called to settle the dispute between the Arminians (Remonstrants) and strict Calvinists, it rejected the Arminian position, adopted the Canons of Dort…

sistine-madonna.s: The Sistine Madonna is an oil painting by Raphael, made about 1512–1513 for the church of San Sisto in Piacenza. It shows the Virgin and Child on clouds between Pope Sixtus II and Saint Barbara, with two winged putti leaning on a ledge below.

saxon-retablissement.s: The Rétablissement was the programme of reconstruction in the Electorate of Saxony after the Seven Years' War, begun in 1762–1763 under Elector Frederick Christian and continued under the regency and reign of Frederick Augustus III. Led by officials such as Thomas von Fritsch,…

saxe-merseburg.s: Saxe-Merseburg was a duchy created in 1656–1657 for Christian, a younger son of Elector John George I of Saxony, and centred on Merseburg on the Saale. It was one of three Albertine secondary lines, with Saxe-Weissenfels and Saxe-Zeitz, whose dukes remained under the…

saxe-weissenfels.s: Saxe-Weissenfels was a duchy created in 1656–1657 for Augustus, a younger son of Elector John George I of Saxony, with its residence at Weissenfels on the Saale from 1680. Its court was noted for music, and Johann Sebastian Bach held the honorary title of Kapellmeister to the…

schneeberg-saxony.s: Schneeberg is a mining town in the Ore Mountains of Saxony, Germany. It grew rapidly after rich silver finds from 1470 into one of the wealthiest towns of the Saxon silver boom, which financed the Wettin rulers.

st-thomas-church-leipzig.s: St Thomas Church in Leipzig is a late Gothic Lutheran church, home of the Thomanerchor boys' choir founded in 1212. Johann Sebastian Bach was its cantor from 1723 until his death in 1750, and his remains have rested in the church since 1950.

sierra-nevada-spain.s: The Sierra Nevada is a mountain range in Andalusia, southern Spain, in the provinces of Granada and Almería, rising to 3,479 metres at Mulhacén, the highest peak of the Iberian Peninsula. Its snowmelt fed the irrigation of the Vega of Granada and the Alpujarras, and the range…

stoicism.s: Stoicism is a school of Hellenistic philosophy founded by Zeno of Citium in Athens around 300 BCE, named after the Painted Stoa where he taught. It held that virtue, living in agreement with nature and reason, is the only true good and that passions arising from false…

sonsonate.s: Sonsonate is a city in western El Salvador and capital of the department of the same name. In the colonial period it was the seat of a separate alcaldía mayor and a centre of the cacao trade.

siege-of-dorostolon.s: The Siege of Dorostolon took place from April to July 971 at Dorostolon, now Silistra, on the lower Danube. The Byzantine emperor John I Tzimiskes besieged Prince Sviatoslav I of Kiev, who had invaded Bulgaria, until hunger and losses forced him to make peace and withdraw.

silistra.s: Silistra is a town on the lower Danube in north-eastern Bulgaria, on the border with Romania. As Roman Durostorum it was a legionary base on the Danube frontier, and as Byzantine Dorostolon and Bulgarian Drastar it was an important fortress and bishop's seat.

salic-law.s: The Salic law, or Pactus Legis Salicae, is the law code of the Salian Franks, probably first issued under Clovis I in the early 6th century. Written in Latin, it consists mainly of fines, including the wergild owed for killing free Franks, Romans and the half-free.

saint-remigius.s: Saint Remigius (c. 437–533) was bishop of Reims for more than seventy years. He wrote to Clovis I on his accession, implying that the young Frankish king exercised Roman authority in Belgica Secunda, and later baptised Clovis at Reims, an event variously dated between 496 and…

salian-franks.s: The Salian Franks were the Frankish groups of the north-west, first recorded in Toxandria, in the present-day southern Netherlands, in the 4th century. In the 5th century their kings ruled from Tournai and Cambrai, and under Clovis I, king of the Salian Franks of Tournai, they…

stilicho.s: Flavius Stilicho (c. 359–408) was a Roman general of Vandal descent who effectively governed the western empire for the young emperor Honorius from 395. He fought the Visigoths of Alaric in Greece and Italy, defeated the invasion of Radagaisus in 406 and kept the Frankish…

sunno.s: Sunno was a Frankish king of the late 4th century who, together with Marcomer, raided Roman territory across the lower Rhine in 388. The Frankish general Arbogast, serving Rome, campaigned against them in 392.

speicherstadt.s: The Speicherstadt is a warehouse district in the port of Hamburg, built from 1883 after the city agreed to join the German customs union while keeping a free port. Its red-brick Gothic Revival warehouses, standing on oak piles between canals, form the largest such complex in…

ss-kaiser-wilhelm-der-grosse.s: SS Kaiser Wilhelm der Grosse was a transatlantic liner of Norddeutscher Lloyd, built at Stettin and launched in 1897. The first liner with four funnels, she won the Blue Riband for the fastest Atlantic crossing in 1897, ending British dominance of the record.

sidi-bel-abbes.s: Sidi Bel Abbès is a city in north-western Algeria, south of Oran, that grew from a French military post established in the 1840s. It became the depot and headquarters of the French Foreign Legion, which remained there until Algerian independence in 1962, when the Legion moved…

spahis.s: The Spahis were light cavalry regiments of the French Army recruited mainly among the Arab and Berber populations of North Africa, first organised in Algeria in 1834. Their name came from the Ottoman sipahi cavalry.

statute-of-algeria.s: The Statute of Algeria was a French law of September 1947 that defined Algeria as a group of departments with its own Algerian Assembly. The assembly was elected by two separate colleges, one mainly of European settlers and one of Muslim Algerians, each with the same number of…

sisophon.s: Sisophon is a town in north-western Cambodia, the capital of Banteay Meanchey Province, on the main road and railway between Phnom Penh and the Thai border. With Battambang and Siem Reap, it was returned by Siam to Cambodia under the Franco-Siamese treaty of 1907, and it was…

six-articles-1832.s: The Six Articles were repressive measures adopted by the Federal Assembly of the German Confederation on 28 June 1832, after the Hambach Festival. Promoted by Metternich, they restricted the rights of state parliaments to refuse taxes or legislate against federal law and set…

siemens.s: Siemens is a German engineering company founded in Berlin in 1847 by Werner von Siemens and Johann Georg Halske as a telegraph manufacturer. It built telegraph lines across Europe and to India, and expanded into electric power, lighting and railways, becoming one of the…

sanai.s: Sana'i was a Persian poet of Ghazni who lived at the court of the late Ghaznavid sultans. After early panegyric verse he turned to religious and mystical poetry, and his Hadiqat al-Haqiqa, dedicated to Bahram Shah, was the first great Sufi didactic poem in Persian.

sayf-al-din-suri.s: Sayf al-Din Suri was a prince of the Ghurid dynasty of Ghor. After his brother Qutb al-Din Muhammad was poisoned at the Ghaznavid court, he seized Ghazni in 1148 and drove out Sultan Bahram Shah.

seo-hui.s: Seo Hui was a Korean statesman and diplomat of the Goryeo period. In 993, when a Khitan army of the Liao dynasty invaded, he negotiated with its commander and secured its withdrawal.

seon-buddhism.s: Seon is the Korean form of Chan or Zen Buddhism, which stresses meditation and direct insight. Introduced from Tang China in the eighth and ninth centuries, it spread through the Nine Mountain schools of late Silla.

seongjong-of-goryeo.s: Seongjong of Goryeo was king of Goryeo from 981 to 997. Following the advice of Choe Seung-ro, he governed on Confucian principles, created twelve provincial governorships in 983 and founded the national academy, the Gukjagam, in 992.

seongjong-of-joseon.s: Seongjong of Joseon was king of Joseon from 1469 to 1494. In 1485 he promulgated the Gyeongguk daejeon, the National Code that formed the legal basis of the Joseon state.

sin-don.s: Sin Don was a Korean Buddhist monk who became the chief adviser of King Gongmin of Goryeo from 1365. He led a commission that returned land seized by powerful families and freed people wrongly held as slaves, earning popular support and the hostility of the aristocracy.

slave-review-act.s: The Slave Review Act was a law issued in 956 by King Gwangjong of Goryeo. It ordered the review of the status of slaves and freed many people who had been wrongly enslaved during the wars of the Later Three Kingdoms.

ssang-gi.s: Ssang Gi was a Chinese official of the Later Zhou dynasty who came to Korea with an embassy in 956 and stayed in the service of King Gwangjong of Goryeo. On his advice Goryeo introduced civil service examinations on the Chinese model in 958, and he supervised the first of them.

ssangseong-prefecture.s: Ssangseong Prefecture was an administrative district set up by the Mongols in 1258 in north-eastern Korea, around modern Kumya and Yonghung, after local Korean officials defected to them. It remained under Yuan control for almost a century.

statutes-of-lithuania.s: The Statutes of Lithuania were three law codes of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, issued in 1529, 1566 and 1588 and written in Ruthenian. They codified the rights of the nobility, courts and procedure and were among the most advanced legal codes of their time.

sapieha-family.s: The Sapiehas are a Lithuanian and Polish magnate family of Ruthenian origin that rose to prominence in the sixteenth century. Lew Sapieha was chancellor of Lithuania and editor of the Third Statute of 1588.

schengen-agreement.s: The Schengen Agreement is a treaty signed on 14 June 1985 at Schengen in Luxembourg by Belgium, France, West Germany, Luxembourg and the Netherlands to abolish checks at their common borders gradually. A convention of 1990 implemented it, and checks were lifted from 1995.

ses-s-a.s: SES is a satellite telecommunications company founded in Luxembourg in 1985 as the Société Européenne des Satellites, with the Luxembourg state as a major shareholder. Its first Astra satellite, launched in 1988, pioneered direct-to-home satellite television across Europe, and…

shuisky-family.s: The Shuiskys were a Russian princely family descended from the Rurikid princes of Suzdal and Nizhny Novgorod, who entered Muscovite service in the fifteenth century. During the minority of Ivan IV they led the boyar factions that struggled for power after 1538, ruling by…

sergius-of-radonezh.s: Sergius of Radonezh was a Russian monk who founded the Trinity Monastery north-east of Moscow around the 1340s and became the most venerated saint of medieval Russia. He revived communal monastic life, and his disciples founded dozens of monasteries across the northern forests.

severia.s: Severia was a historical region in the basin of the Desna and Seim rivers, now divided between north-eastern Ukraine and south-western Russia, named after the East Slavic Severians. Its towns included Novgorod-Seversky, Starodub, Putivl and Rylsk.

sophia-palaiologina.s: Sophia Palaiologina was a Byzantine princess, niece of the last emperor Constantine XI, who married Ivan III of Moscow in 1472. Brought up in Rome after the fall of Constantinople, she came to Moscow through papal mediation, though hopes of drawing Moscow into union with Rome…

sudebnik-of-1497.s: The Sudebnik of 1497 was the first law code of the unified Muscovite state, issued by Ivan III. Drawing on earlier Russian law, it standardised court procedure and fees, defined the powers of officials and set penalties for crimes.

senate-of-forty-eight.s: The Senate of Forty-Eight was a council created in Florence in 1532, when the republic was abolished and Alessandro de' Medici became hereditary duke. Its members, chosen for life from leading families, formally kept the right to elect the duke and to approve major decisions,…

state-of-the-presidi.s: The State of the Presidi was a group of fortified coastal places in southern Tuscany, including Orbetello, Porto Ercole, Porto Santo Stefano and Talamone, kept by Spain when it granted Siena to Cosimo I de' Medici in 1557. Garrisoned to guard the sea route between Spain's…

sushruta-samhita.s: The Sushruta Samhita is an ancient Sanskrit treatise on medicine and surgery attributed to Sushruta, one of the foundational texts of Ayurveda. Compiled over several centuries and probably reaching its surviving form in the early centuries CE, it describes many surgical…

salzkammergut.s: The Salzkammergut is an Alpine lake district in Upper Austria, Styria and Salzburg, named after the salt mines and the Habsburg chamber that administered them. Salt had been mined at Hallstatt since prehistoric times, and under the Habsburgs the region was a closely controlled…

sharif-of-mecca.s: The Sharif of Mecca was the ruler of Mecca and much of the Hejaz, chosen from among the descendants of the Prophet Muhammad through his grandson Hasan, from the 10th century until 1925. The sharifs usually acknowledged the overlordship of a stronger Muslim power, such as the…

steelyard.s: The Steelyard was the Hanseatic League's trading base, or Kontor, in London, a walled compound on the north bank of the Thames near Dowgate. Its German merchants enjoyed customs and legal privileges, and the Treaty of Utrecht of 1474 gave the Hansa ownership of the site.

sharahbil-yafur.s: Sharahbil Ya'fur was a king of Himyar in south Arabia in the mid-5th century, a son of Abikarib As'ad. A long inscription records his major repairs to the Marib Dam in the 450s, after a breach.

siling-vandals.s: The Siling Vandals were one of the two main branches of the Vandals, whose name may survive in that of Silesia. In 409 they crossed the Pyrenees with the Hasding Vandals, Alans and Suebi and settled in Baetica.

shabdamanidarpana.s: The Shabdamanidarpana, "jewel-mirror of grammar", is a grammar of the Kannada language written by the poet Kesiraja around 1260, in the Hoysala period. Composed in verse with explanatory prose, it describes the literary language of the earlier Kannada poets.

sri-vaishnavism.s: Sri Vaishnavism is a Hindu tradition devoted to the god Vishnu and his consort Lakshmi, or Sri, which grew from the Tamil devotional hymns of the Alvars. It was systematised by Ramanuja in the 11th and 12th centuries, and its main centres include the temples of Srirangam,…

sacred-ensembles-of-the-hoysalas.s: The Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas is a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Karnataka, inscribed in 2023. It comprises three temples of the 12th and 13th centuries: the Chennakeshava temple at Belur, the Hoysaleswara temple at Halebidu and the Chennakeshava temple at…

shantala-devi.s: Shantala Devi was the queen of the Hoysala king Vishnuvardhana, celebrated in inscriptions as an accomplished dancer and musician. A devout Jain, she endowed Jain shrines at Shravanabelagola, while her husband patronised Vaishnava temples.

sadashivrao-bhau.s: Sadashivrao Bhau was a Maratha general and cousin of the Peshwa Balaji Baji Rao. He defeated the Nizam of Hyderabad at Udgir in 1760, gaining large territories, and then commanded the Maratha army against Ahmad Shah Durrani.

salabat-jung.s: Salabat Jung was a son of Asaf Jah I who became Nizam of Hyderabad in 1751 with the support of the French under the Marquis de Bussy. Dependent on French troops, he assigned the Northern Circars to France in 1753, and his army was defeated by the Marathas at Udgir in 1760.

salar-jung-i.s: Salar Jung I, born Mir Turab Ali Khan, was chief minister of Hyderabad State from 1853 until his death in 1883. He reorganised revenue collection, created modern district administration, courts, police and schools, and restored the state's finances.

salar-jung-iii.s: Salar Jung III, born Mir Yousuf Ali Khan, was a Hyderabad noble, grandson of Salar Jung I, who served briefly as prime minister of the state in 1912–1914. He spent much of his fortune collecting art, manuscripts and objects from Asia and Europe, which after his death formed…

salar-jung-museum.s: The Salar Jung Museum in Hyderabad houses the collection of Salar Jung III, including paintings, sculpture, manuscripts, arms, textiles and decorative arts from India, the Middle East, Europe and East Asia. It opened in 1951 and was declared a museum of national importance in…

secunderabad.s: Secunderabad is the twin city of Hyderabad in Telangana, India, named after Sikandar Jah, the third Nizam. It grew around the British cantonment established there in the early 19th century under the subsidiary alliance, which housed the troops that guaranteed the Nizam's…

sunderlal-committee.s: The Sunderlal Committee was a goodwill mission sent by the Indian government in late 1948, led by the Congress politician Pandit Sunderlal, to investigate violence in Hyderabad after its annexation. Its report estimated that between 27,000 and 40,000 Muslims had been killed…

sudirman.s: Sudirman was the first commander-in-chief of the Indonesian armed forces during the war of independence against the Netherlands. A former schoolteacher, he was elected commander in November 1945 at the age of 29.

susilo-bambang-yudhoyono.s: Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono is a retired Indonesian general and politician who served as president from 2004 to 2014. A former security minister, he founded the Democratic Party and won the country's first direct presidential election in 2004.

shangjing-of-liao.s: Shangjing, the Supreme Capital, was the principal capital of the Khitan Liao dynasty, founded by Abaoji in 918 in present-day Bairin Left Banner, Inner Mongolia. It had a northern city for the Khitan court and a southern city for Han Chinese and other subjects.

singapore-strait.s: The Singapore Strait is a channel about 100 kilometres long between the Strait of Malacca and the South China Sea, separating Singapore from the Riau Islands of Indonesia. One of the busiest shipping lanes in the world, it carries much of the trade between the Indian Ocean and…

sulaiman-badrul-alam-shah.s: Sulaiman Badrul Alam Shah was sultan of Johor and Riau from 1722 to 1760. A son of Abdul Jalil IV, he was placed on the throne by Bugis warriors who drove out Raja Kecil of Siak.

sangpyeong-tongbo.s: The Sangpyeong tongbo was a copper coin of Joseon Korea, cast in large numbers from 1678 under King Sukjong as the country's standard currency. Earlier attempts to introduce coins had failed, but the growth of markets after the Uniform Land Tax Law allowed this one to…

sejo-of-joseon.s: Sejo was the seventh king of Joseon, ruling from 1455 to 1468. A son of Sejong, as Grand Prince Suyang he seized power in 1453 from ministers serving his young nephew Danjong and forced him to abdicate in 1455.

seonjo-of-joseon.s: Seonjo was the fourteenth king of Joseon, ruling from 1567 to 1608. His reign saw a flowering of Neo-Confucian scholarship but also the split of officials into rival factions.

suwon.s: Suwon is a city about 30 kilometres south of Seoul and the capital of Gyeonggi Province, South Korea, with more than a million inhabitants. In the 1790s King Jeongjo moved the tomb of his father there and built Hwaseong Fortress around a new town, which he hoped would become a…

state-council-of-joseon.s: The State Council (Uijeongbu) was the highest deliberative body of the Joseon government, created in 1400 and led by the chief state councillor and his left and right colleagues. It advised the king and oversaw the six ministries, though its power varied as kings such as…

sayram.s: Sayram is an ancient town in southern Kazakhstan, east of Shymkent, on the site usually identified with medieval Isfijab. It was an oasis town on the Silk Road route along the middle Syr Darya and a centre of Islamic learning, and is known as the birthplace of the Sufi master…

sighnaq.s: Sighnaq, also written Sygnak, is a ruined medieval city on the middle Syr Darya in southern Kazakhstan. In the fourteenth century it was the capital of the White Horde, and in the fifteenth it was the seat of the Uzbek khan Abu'l-Khayr.

sermon-on-law-and-grace.s: The Sermon on Law and Grace is a work by Hilarion, later metropolitan of Kiev, composed between about 1037 and 1050. Contrasting the Law of the Old Testament with the grace of the New, it celebrates the conversion of Rus' and praises Vladimir the Great and Yaroslav the Wise,…

san-julian-de-los-prados.s: San Julián de los Prados is a church in Oviedo built under Alfonso II of Asturias in the early ninth century. It is the largest surviving church of Asturian pre-Romanesque architecture and is known for its wall paintings of architectural motifs, inspired by Roman decoration.

san-miguel-de-lillo.s: San Miguel de Lillo is a church on Mount Naranco above Oviedo, built under Ramiro I of Asturias around 842–850, near the hall of Santa María del Naranco. Only part of the original building survives, with carved door jambs showing circus scenes copied from a Byzantine consular…

santa-maria-del-naranco.s: Santa María del Naranco is a building on Mount Naranco above Oviedo, built as a royal hall for Ramiro I of Asturias and dated by an inscription of 848; it was later turned into a church. A two-storey hall with barrel vaults, external loggias and carved medallions, it is the…

st-vitus-cathedral.s: St Vitus Cathedral is the cathedral of Prague, within Prague Castle. Begun in 1344 under Charles IV by Matthias of Arras and continued by Peter Parler, it was left unfinished during the Hussite Wars and completed only in 1929.

semakookiro.s: Semakookiro was kabaka of Buganda around the turn of the nineteenth century. He seized the throne from his brother Junju, whom he had killed, and completed the conquest of Buddu from Bunyoro.

sese-islands.s: The Sese Islands are an archipelago of some eighty-four islands in the north-west of Lake Victoria, forming Kalangala District of Uganda. They were the main home of the cult of the lake god Mukasa, and their canoe-builders and fishermen supplied the fleets of the Kingdom of…

suna-ii.s: Suna II was kabaka of Buganda from about 1832 to 1856. A powerful ruler, he led frequent military expeditions against neighbouring peoples and kept a tight hold on the chiefs.

samuel-baker.s: Samuel Baker was an English explorer who in 1864, with his partner Florence, reached Lake Albert and saw the waterfall he named Murchison Falls. From 1869 to 1873 he served the Khedive Ismail as governor of Equatoria, trying to suppress the slave trade and extend Egyptian rule…

solomon-gafabusa-iguru-i.s: Solomon Gafabusa Iguru I is the omukama of Bunyoro-Kitara, crowned in 1994 after the monarchy was restored as a cultural institution without governmental powers. He is a son of Tito Winyi IV.

sepulveda.s: Sepúlveda is a small historic town in the province of Segovia in Castile, Spain, set on a rock above the gorges of the Duratón. Fortified by the counts of Castile in the tenth century, it received in 1076 from Alfonso VI a fuero, or local charter, granting settlers freedom,…

second-schleswig-war.s: The Second Schleswig War was fought in 1864 between Denmark and the allied German powers Prussia and Austria. It began after Denmark adopted a constitution binding Schleswig more closely to the kingdom, contrary to earlier agreements.

soren-kierkegaard.s: Søren Kierkegaard was a Danish philosopher and theologian, regarded as the first existentialist. Writing often under pseudonyms, in works such as "Either/Or" (1843) and "Fear and Trembling" (1843), he explored faith, choice, anxiety and the individual's relation to God.

sweyn-ii-of-denmark.s: Sweyn II Estridsen was King of Denmark from 1047 to 1076, a nephew of Cnut the Great through his mother Estrid. After years of war with Magnus the Good and Harald Hardrada of Norway, he secured the Danish throne and founded the dynasty that ruled Denmark until the late…

suger.s: Suger was abbot of Saint-Denis near Paris from 1122 and an adviser to the French kings Louis VI and Louis VII, serving as regent while Louis VII was on the Second Crusade. His rebuilding of the abbey church of Saint-Denis in the 1140s, with its pointed arches, rib vaults and…

suleymanshah-ii.s: Süleymanshah II, Rukn al-Din, was sultan of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum in Anatolia from 1196 to 1204. He took the throne from his brother Kaykhusraw I, reunited lands divided among his brothers and annexed the Saltukid principality of Erzurum.

samuel-johnson.s: Samuel Johnson was an English writer, critic and lexicographer. His Dictionary of the English Language of 1755, compiled largely alone over nine years, was the most influential English dictionary until the Oxford English Dictionary.

samuel-richardson.s: Samuel Richardson was an English printer and novelist. His novels Pamela (1740) and Clarissa (1748), told in the form of letters, explored the feelings and moral struggles of their heroines and won a huge readership across Europe.

septennial-act-1716.s: The Septennial Act 1716 was a law of the Parliament of Great Britain that extended the maximum life of a parliament from three to seven years. Passed by the Whig government soon after the Jacobite rising of 1715, it postponed an election the Whigs feared to lose and helped…

south-sea-bubble.s: The South Sea Bubble was a financial crisis in Britain in 1720 caused by speculation in shares of the South Sea Company, which had taken over much of the national debt in exchange for trading rights in Spanish America. The share price rose about tenfold before collapsing in…

syros.s: Syros is a Greek island in the Cyclades in the Aegean Sea. Its town, Ermoupoli, founded by refugees from Chios and Psara during the War of Independence, was the leading port and commercial centre of Greece in the mid-nineteenth century, with shipyards and textile mills.

saint-beuno.s: Saint Beuno was a Welsh abbot and missionary of the seventh century, one of the most important saints of north Wales. Tradition holds that he founded a monastery at Clynnog Fawr on the Llŷn peninsula and that he restored his niece Saint Winefride to life.

saint-deiniol.s: Saint Deiniol was a sixth-century Welsh churchman, traditionally regarded as the founder of the monastery of Bangor in Gwynedd and its first bishop. According to tradition he was consecrated by Saint Dyfrig with the support of Maelgwn Gwynedd, who granted the land.

saint-emeric-of-hungary.s: Saint Emeric was the son and heir of Stephen I of Hungary, to whom his father addressed the Admonitions on Christian kingship. He was killed by a boar while hunting in 1031, which left Stephen without a surviving son and led to the succession struggles after 1038.

sajo.s: The Sajó, Slovak Slaná, is a river about 230 kilometres long that rises in the Slovak Ore Mountains and flows south-east through north-eastern Hungary to join the Tisza. On its banks near the village of Muhi the Mongols destroyed the army of Béla IV at the Battle of Mohi in…

samuel-aba.s: Samuel Aba was king of Hungary from 1041 to 1044. A magnate of the Aba kindred and brother-in-law of Stephen I, he was raised to the throne when the nobles expelled Peter Orseolo.

simon-of-keza.s: Simon of Kéza was a Hungarian cleric at the court of King Ladislaus IV who wrote the Gesta Hunnorum et Hungarorum in the early 1280s. His chronicle traced the Hungarians back to the Huns of Attila and presented the nobility as the heirs of a free warrior people, ideas that…

sabac.s: Šabac is a city in western Serbia on the Sava river. Its fortress was built by the Ottomans in 1471, taken by Matthias Corvinus in 1476 and held by Hungary as part of its southern defences until Suleiman the Magnificent captured it, together with Belgrade, in 1521.

second-battle-of-kosovo.s: The Second Battle of Kosovo was fought on 17–20 October 1448 on the Kosovo plain, where the Ottoman army of Murad II defeated a Hungarian and Wallachian army under John Hunyadi. It ended Hunyadi's hope of reversing the defeat at Varna, and on his retreat he was briefly held…

spis.s: Spiš, Hungarian Szepes and German Zips, is a historical region of north-eastern Slovakia below the High Tatras. Settled by many German colonists from the thirteenth century, it formed a county of the Kingdom of Hungary, and in 1412 King Sigismund pledged thirteen of its towns…

szekelys.s: The Székelys, or Szeklers, are a Hungarian-speaking people living mainly in south-eastern Transylvania, in present-day Romania. In the medieval Kingdom of Hungary they served as frontier guards and light cavalry and held collective liberties as one of the three privileged…

svetitskhoveli-cathedral.s: Svetitskhoveli Cathedral is the principal Orthodox cathedral of Mtskheta, the ancient capital of Iberia, standing on the site of the first church built after the conversion of King Mirian III in the fourth century. The present building was completed around 1029 by the…

shorapani.s: Shorapani is a village on the Kvirila river in the Imereti region of western Georgia, site of a medieval fortress on a rocky hill. Known in antiquity as Sarapana, a fortified point on the road from Colchis to Iberia, it guarded the route between western and eastern Georgia and…

solomon-i-of-imereti.s: Solomon I was king of Imereti in western Georgia from 1752 to 1784, with an interruption in the 1760s. He defeated an Ottoman army in 1757, curbed the power of his great vassals and banned the slave trade that had drained the kingdom's population.

samerina.s: Samerina was the Assyrian province created from the former Kingdom of Israel after the fall of Samaria in 722–720 BCE, with Samaria as its seat. Sargon II deported part of the population and settled people from Babylonia, Syria and elsewhere in their place.

shallum-of-israel.s: Shallum was king of Israel for one month around 752 BCE, according to the Bible. He seized the throne by murdering Zechariah, the last king of the dynasty of Jehu, and was himself killed by Menahem.

syro-ephraimite-war.s: The Syro-Ephraimite War was a conflict of about 735–732 BCE in which Rezin of Aram-Damascus and Pekah of Israel, or Ephraim, attacked Judah after its king Ahaz refused to join their alliance against Assyria. Ahaz appealed to Tiglath-pileser III, who took Damascus, annexed much…

safed.s: Safed is a city in the mountains of Upper Galilee in northern Israel. The Knights Templar rebuilt its castle in the 1240s, but the Mamluk sultan Baybars captured it in 1266 and executed the garrison.

sibylla-queen-of-jerusalem.s: Sibylla was Queen of Jerusalem from 1186 to 1190, daughter of Amalric I and sister of the leper king Baldwin IV. Against much of the nobility she had her husband Guy of Lusignan crowned with her, and their reign saw the disastrous defeat at Hattin and the loss of Jerusalem to…

sancho-i-of-leon.s: Sancho I, called the Fat, was King of León from 956 to 958 and again from 960 to 966. Deposed by the nobility, he travelled with his grandmother Queen Toda of Navarre to Córdoba, where the Jewish physician Hasdai ibn Shaprut treated his obesity, and with the help of the caliph…

sahagun.s: Sahagún is a town in the province of León in north-western Spain, on the pilgrimage road to Santiago de Compostela. Its Benedictine monastery of San Benito, richly endowed by Alfonso VI and reformed on the model of Cluny, was one of the most powerful in medieval León, and…

san-esteban-de-gormaz.s: San Esteban de Gormaz is a town on the Duero river in the province of Soria, Spain. In the 10th century it was a frontier stronghold contested between the Kingdom of León and the Caliphate of Córdoba, near the great caliphal fortress of Gormaz.

sancha-of-leon.s: Sancha was Queen of León, the daughter of Alfonso V and sister of Bermudo III, the last king of the old Leonese line. After her husband Ferdinand, count of Castile, killed Bermudo at Tamarón in 1037, he became king of León by right of her inheritance.

sparda.s: Sparda was the Achaemenid Persian satrapy of Lydia, created after Cyrus the Great conquered the kingdom of Croesus around 546 BCE, with its seat at Sardis. Sardis became the main Persian capital in western Anatolia and the western end of the Royal Road from Susa.

shudra.s: Shudra is the fourth of the four varnas, the classes of traditional Hindu society described in Vedic and later Sanskrit texts, below the Brahmins, Kshatriyas and Vaishyas. Shudras were assigned the duty of serving the other three classes and were excluded from Vedic study and…

stafford.s: Stafford is the county town of Staffordshire in the English Midlands. Æthelflæd, Lady of the Mercians, fortified it as a burh in 913 during her campaigns against the Danes, and it became the centre of the shire created around it in the 10th century. After the Norman Conquest a…

staffordshire-hoard.s: The Staffordshire Hoard is the largest hoard of Anglo-Saxon gold and silver metalwork yet found, discovered by a metal detectorist in a field near Lichfield in 2009. It contains several thousand pieces, mostly fittings stripped from swords and other war gear of the 7th…

second-anglo-mysore-war.s: The Second Anglo-Mysore War (1780–1784) began when Hyder Ali invaded the Carnatic and destroyed a British detachment at Pollilur in 1780. Eyre Coote checked him at Porto Novo in 1781, and after Hyder's death in 1782 his son Tipu Sultan, aided for a time by the French, carried…

sacro-regio-consiglio.s: The Sacro Regio Consiglio was the supreme court of the Kingdom of Naples, created by Alfonso V of Aragon after his conquest of the kingdom in 1442. Presided over by a senior jurist, it heard appeals from the kingdom's other courts and became the centre of Neapolitan legal…

sancho-iii-of-castile.s: Sancho III (c. 1134–1158) was king of Castile from 1157 to 1158, the eldest son of Alfonso VII, who divided his realms between Sancho, who received Castile, and Ferdinand II, who received León. In his short reign he granted the fortress of Calatrava to the Cistercians, leading…

sancho-vi-of-navarre.s: Sancho VI (1132–1194), called the Wise, was king of Navarre from 1150 to 1194 and the first to use the title king of Navarre consistently instead of king of Pamplona. He defended the kingdom against Castile and Aragon, accepting the arbitration of Henry II of England in 1177,…

sino-nepalese-war.s: The Sino-Nepalese War (1788–1792) began with Nepalese invasions of Tibet over trade and coinage disputes, culminating in the sack of the Tashilhunpo monastery in 1791. The Qianlong Emperor sent a Qing army under Fuk'anggan, which drove the Nepalese out of Tibet and advanced to…

stainmore.s: Stainmore is a high pass across the Pennines between the Eden valley in Cumbria and Teesdale, followed by a Roman road and the modern A66. In the early Middle Ages it marked a frontier of the Northumbrian and Cumbrian lands, and the stump of the Rey Cross stands on the summit.

skule-bardsson.s: Skule Bårdsson was a Norwegian earl and later duke who governed Norway as regent for the young Haakon IV and was the most powerful noble of his time. Rivalry with Haakon grew, and in 1239 Skule had himself proclaimed king.

second-mithridatic-war.s: The Second Mithridatic War (83–81 BCE) was a short conflict between Rome and Mithridates VI of Pontus. It began when Lucius Licinius Murena, the Roman governor of Asia, invaded Pontus on his own initiative.

saint-tysilio.s: Saint Tysilio was a Welsh saint of the seventh century, said in tradition to be a son of Brochwel Ysgithrog, king of Powys. He is associated above all with Meifod, the mother church of Powys, and churches dedicated to him are found across Wales, including Llandysilio on the…

second-silesian-war.s: The Second Silesian War (1744–1745) was fought between Prussia and Austria, with Saxony, as part of the War of the Austrian Succession. Fearing Austria would retake Silesia, Frederick II invaded Bohemia in 1744 and then won the battles of Hohenfriedberg, Soor and Kesselsdorf…

shairum-awtar.s: Sha'irum Awtar was a king of Saba and Dhu Raydan in the early third century CE, ruling from Marib. His inscriptions record victories over Hadramawt, including the capture and burning of its capital Shabwa, and campaigns against Himyar and the Aksumite forces then active in…

sa-die-de-sa-sardigna.s: Sa die de sa Sardigna ('Sardinia's Day') is the regional holiday of Sardinia, held on 28 April. It commemorates the uprising of 28 April 1794 in Cagliari, when the people drove out the Piedmontese viceroy and officials after the court in Turin rejected the island's demands for…

scottish-reformation-parliament.s: The Scottish Reformation Parliament met in Edinburgh in August 1560, after the Treaty of Edinburgh had removed French and English troops. Without the consent of the absent Mary, Queen of Scots, it abolished the pope's authority in Scotland, forbade the celebration of Mass and…

stuart-restoration.s: The Stuart Restoration was the return of the monarchy in England, Scotland and Ireland in 1660, when Charles II came back from exile after the collapse of the Commonwealth and Protectorate. In Scotland it revived the separate parliament, Privy Council and bishops, leading to…

scottish-enlightenment.s: The Scottish Enlightenment was the flourishing of philosophy, science and scholarship in eighteenth-century Scotland, centred on the universities of Edinburgh, Glasgow and Aberdeen. Its figures included David Hume, Adam Smith, Adam Ferguson, Thomas Reid and the geologist James…

second-war-of-scottish-independence.s: The Second War of Scottish Independence began in 1332 when Edward Balliol, backed by the 'Disinherited' nobles and later by Edward III of England, invaded Scotland against the young David II. The Scots suffered heavy defeats at Dupplin Moor, Halidon Hill and Neville's Cross,…

stone-of-scone.s: The Stone of Scone, or Stone of Destiny, is a block of red sandstone on which Scottish kings were inaugurated at Scone. Edward I took it to Westminster Abbey in 1296 as a sign of his conquest, and it was built into the Coronation Chair used for English and British monarchs.

saltsjobaden-agreement.s: The Saltsjöbaden Agreement was signed on 20 December 1938 at Saltsjöbaden near Stockholm between the Swedish Trade Union Confederation and the Swedish Employers' Association. It set rules for collective bargaining and for limiting strikes and lockouts, leaving the labour…

sigtuna.s: Sigtuna is a town on Lake Mälaren north-west of Stockholm, founded around 980 as a royal centre. King Olof Skötkonung struck the first Swedish coins there around 995, modelled on English pennies, and in the eleventh century it became an early bishop's seat and a base for the…

sten-sture-the-elder.s: Sten Sture the Elder was regent of Sweden from 1470 to 1497 and again from 1501 to 1503, during the Kalmar Union. His victory over Christian I of Denmark at the Battle of Brunkeberg in 1471 secured his power, and he governed with the support of the peasants and miners against…

stockholms-banco.s: Stockholms Banco was a Swedish bank founded by Johan Palmstruch in 1657 under royal charter. In 1661 it issued the first banknotes in Europe, credit notes that could be exchanged for heavy copper plate money.

stones-of-mora.s: The Stones of Mora was the place in a meadow south-east of Uppsala where medieval Swedish kings were elected and acclaimed by representatives of the provinces. Royal elections are recorded there from the late thirteenth to the fifteenth century.

swedish-academy.s: The Swedish Academy was founded by King Gustav III in 1786 to promote the purity and strength of the Swedish language, on the model of the Académie française. It has eighteen members elected for life and publishes a great dictionary and the official word list of Swedish.

systema-naturae.s: Systema Naturae is the work in which Carl Linnaeus set out his classification of nature into the three kingdoms of animals, plants and minerals, divided into classes, orders, genera and species. First published at Leiden in 1735 as a short folio, it grew through many editions,…

st-ninians-isle.s: St Ninian's Isle is a small island off the west coast of mainland Shetland, joined to it by a sand bar. In 1958 excavations at its ruined chapel uncovered the St Ninian's Isle Treasure, a hoard of 28 silver objects, including bowls and penannular brooches, buried around 800.

shetland.s: Shetland is an archipelago in the North Atlantic north-east of mainland Scotland, the most northerly part of the United Kingdom. Inhabited by Picts in the early Middle Ages, it was settled by Norse colonists from the ninth century and ruled from Norway until 1469, when…

siyannu.s: Siyannu was a small Late Bronze Age kingdom on the Syrian coast south of Ugarit, around modern Tell Siyannu near Jableh. Long a dependency of Ugarit, it was detached from Ugaritic control by the Hittite king Mursili II in the late fourteenth century BCE and placed under the…

semiramis.s: Semiramis is a legendary queen of Assyria in Greek tradition, credited with founding Babylon, building great works and leading campaigns as far as India. The legend probably drew on Shammuramat, the mother of Adad-nirari III, who was influential at the Assyrian court around…

shivini.s: Shivini was the sun god of Urartu, third in rank of the state pantheon after Haldi and the storm god Teisheba. He was probably derived from the Hurrian sun god Shimige, and his consort was the goddess Tushpuea.

southampton.s: Southampton is a port city on the south coast of England, at the head of Southampton Water. In the eighth century the trading settlement of Hamwic on its site was one of the main emporia of Anglo-Saxon England, dealing with the Frankish world, and the later town gave its name…

swindon.s: Swindon is a large town in Wiltshire, south-west England. Nearby Wroughton is the probable site of the Battle of Ellendun in 825, when Ecgberht of Wessex defeated Mercia.

supayalat.s: Supayalat was the last queen of Burma, the daughter of King Mindon and Queen Hsinbyumashin and the wife of King Thibaw, her half-brother. She dominated Thibaw's court and is held responsible, with her mother's faction, for the massacre of royal relatives in 1879.

surkh-kotal.s: Surkh Kotal is an archaeological site in Baghlan Province, northern Afghanistan, where a hilltop dynastic sanctuary of the Kushan kings stood. French archaeologists excavated it from 1952, uncovering monumental stairways, royal statues and a long inscription in Bactrian…

sam-fang-kaen.s: Sam Fang Kaen was a king of Lan Na who ruled from about 1402 to 1441. His long reign was largely stable, but in 1441 he was overthrown by his son Tilokarat, who exiled him and went on to lead the kingdom to the height of its power.

sumana-thera.s: Sumana Thera was a Buddhist monk from Sukhothai who, at the invitation of King Kue Na, came to Chiang Mai in 1369. He established there a monastic ordination lineage derived from Sri Lanka, based at the new monastery of Wat Suan Dok, and tradition credits him with enshrining…

samsenthai.s: Samsenthai, born Oun Heuan, was the second king of Lan Xang, ruling from 1373 to 1416 after the nobles deposed his father, Fa Ngum. His regnal name, "three hundred thousand Tai", is traditionally linked to a census of his male subjects.

sinxay.s: Sinxay is a Lao epic poem attributed to the poet Pangkham and traditionally dated to the reign of Sourigna Vongsa in the 17th century. It tells of the hero Sinxay and his journey to rescue his aunt from a giant, and it is regarded as the masterpiece of classical Lao…

sea-of-japan.s: The Sea of Japan is the marginal sea of the western Pacific between the Japanese archipelago, Sakhalin, the Korean Peninsula and the Russian Far East. Its coasts formed the eastern edge of empires based in Manchuria, such as Balhae and the Liao, and its name is disputed by…

shulu-ping.s: Shulü Ping was the wife of Abaoji, founder of the Liao dynasty, and a powerful figure in its early history. After his death in 926 she secured the throne for her second son, Yelü Deguang, over the eldest, Yelü Bei, and according to tradition cut off her own hand to place in…

sande-society.s: The Sande society is a women's initiation society of Liberia, Sierra Leone, Guinea and Côte d'Ivoire, the female counterpart of the Poro. It prepares girls for adulthood and upholds moral and social order, and its masks, worn by women, are among the few in Africa danced by women.

sherbro-island.s: Sherbro Island is an island off the southern coast of Sierra Leone. In 1820 the American Colonization Society landed its first settlers of free African Americans there, but disease killed many of them, and the survivors moved in 1821–1822 to Cape Mesurado, where the colony…

sao-cucufate.s: São Cucufate is the site of a large Roman villa near Vila de Frades, in the Vidigueira municipality of the Alentejo in southern Portugal. Founded in the 1st century CE and rebuilt on a grand scale in the 4th century, its two-storey residence with vaulted halls survives to an…

santarem.s: Santarém is a city on the Tagus in central Portugal, the main town of the Ribatejo. As Scallabis, later Scallabis Praesidium Iulium, it was a Roman colony and the seat of one of the three judicial districts (conventus) of Lusitania.

setubal.s: Setúbal is a port city on the estuary of the Sado in southern Portugal, south of Lisbon. In Roman times the area was a centre of fish-salting, and at Tróia, across the estuary, archaeologists have excavated one of the largest fish-salting complexes known in the Roman world,…

shakanda.s: Shakanda was a king of Makuria in Nubia, installed by the Mamluks in 1276. A relative of King David, he sought the support of Sultan Baybars, whose army defeated David near Dongola and placed Shakanda on the throne as a vassal bound by oath to pay an annual tribute.

shemamun.s: Shemamun was a king of Makuria in Nubia in the late 13th century, repeatedly deposed and restored. Mamluk armies sent by Sultan Qalawun in the late 1280s installed rival princes at Dongola, but Shemamun regained the throne each time the Egyptian troops withdrew.

second-battle-of-dongola.s: The Second Battle of Dongola was the siege of Old Dongola, capital of the Nubian kingdom of Makuria, by the Arab army of Abdallah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh, governor of Egypt, in 652. The Arabs bombarded the city with a catapult and damaged its church, but Nubian archers inflicted…

sudan-national-museum.s: The Sudan National Museum in Khartoum, opened in 1971, is the largest museum in Sudan. Its collections span Sudanese history from prehistory through the kingdoms of Kerma and Kush to the Christian Nubian kingdoms, including wall paintings from Faras cathedral.

sheraton-move.s: The Sheraton Move was the political manoeuvre of February 2020 that brought down Malaysia's Pakatan Harapan government. Defecting members of parliament and opposition parties met at the Sheraton hotel in Petaling Jaya, Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad resigned, and Muhyiddin…

south-korea.s: South Korea (the Republic of Korea) is a state in the southern part of the Korean peninsula, established in 1948. After the Korean War of 1950–1953 it grew under authoritarian governments, above all that of Park Chung-hee, into one of the world's leading industrial economies,…

straits-settlements.s: The Straits Settlements were a British colony on the Strait of Malacca made up of Penang, Malacca and Singapore. Formed in 1826 under the East India Company, they became a Crown colony in 1867 and were the base of British trade and influence in the Malay Peninsula.

seventh-crusade.s: The Seventh Crusade was the crusade led by King Louis IX of France against Ayyubid Egypt in 1248–1254. After taking Damietta in 1249, the crusaders advanced on Cairo but were checked at al-Mansura, and in 1250 Louis and much of his army were captured during the retreat.

second-northern-war.s: The Second Northern War (1655–1660) was fought between Sweden under Charles X Gustav and its adversaries, Poland–Lithuania, Russia, Denmark, the Habsburg monarchy and Brandenburg. The Great Elector changed sides from Sweden to Poland and won full sovereignty over the Duchy of…

sorbs.s: The Sorbs are a West Slavic people of Lusatia in eastern Germany, living in Saxony and Brandenburg. Descendants of Slavs who settled between the Elbe and the Oder in the early Middle Ages, they survived the German colonisation of the region and keep their own Upper and Lower…

spandau.s: Spandau is a district of Berlin, Germany, at the confluence of the Havel and the Spree. A town first recorded in 1197, with a castle of the margraves of Brandenburg, it was where Elector Joachim II took communion in both kinds in 1539, marking Brandenburg's adoption of the…

spilberk-castle.s: Špilberk Castle stands on a hill above Brno in Moravia. Founded in the thirteenth century as a royal castle, it withstood a Swedish siege in 1645, was rebuilt as a baroque fortress and from the eighteenth century served as a notorious Habsburg prison for political prisoners,…

statue-of-ebih-il.s: The statue of Ebih-Il is an alabaster figure of a seated worshipper from the temple of Ishtar at Mari, made around 2400 BCE. It shows Ebih-Il, a superintendent of Mari, wearing a sheepskin skirt, with inlaid eyes of shell and lapis lazuli.

shibtu.s: Shibtu was the queen of Zimri-Lim, king of Mari, in the eighteenth century BCE, and a daughter of Yarim-Lim I of Yamhad. Her letters in the Mari archives show her running the palace and its administration, reporting on affairs and consulting prophets and omens while the king…

simalites.s: The Sim'alites (Bin-Sim'al, 'sons of the left') were a confederation of Amorite pastoral tribes of the middle Euphrates and Khabur region in the early second millennium BCE. Zimri-Lim of Mari belonged to them, and their mobile herders, the Hana, formed a major part of his…

saka-era.s: The Saka era is a calendar era beginning in 78 CE, used widely in India and in Hindu-Buddhist Java and Bali to date inscriptions and chronicles. Its origin is traditionally linked to a Saka or Kushan ruler.

semarang.s: Semarang is the capital of Central Java province, Indonesia, and a major port on the north coast of Java. Ceded by Mataram to the Dutch East India Company in the late 1670s in return for military help, it became the Company's main base on the north coast in the eighteenth…

special-region-of-yogyakarta.s: The Special Region of Yogyakarta is a province of Indonesia in south-central Java, with its capital at the city of Yogyakarta. It keeps its special status in recognition of the Sultanate of Yogyakarta's support for the Indonesian Republic during the war of independence: the…

second-javanese-war-of-succession.s: The Second Javanese War of Succession (1719–1723) followed the death of Pakubuwana I of Mataram, when brothers and uncles of his son Amangkurat IV rebelled against the new king. The Dutch East India Company supported Amangkurat IV, defeated the rebels and exiled several princes.

suvarnagiri.s: Suvarnagiri, 'golden mountain', was a city of the Maurya Empire in southern India, named in Ashoka's minor rock edicts as the seat of a prince who governed the southern province. Many scholars identify it with Kanakagiri in Karnataka, near the gold-bearing country around Maski…

serabit-el-khadim.s: Serabit el-Khadim is an ancient site in south-western Sinai where Egyptians mined turquoise from the Middle Kingdom onwards. Its temple of Hathor, 'Lady of Turquoise', was enlarged over many centuries.

shechem.s: Shechem was an ancient city of the central hill country of Canaan, at Tell Balata near modern Nablus in the West Bank. Probably the Sekmem named on the stele of the Egyptian officer Khusobek, it was a major Middle Bronze Age town and appears in the Amarna letters.

semna-dispatches.s: The Semna Dispatches are copies of reports sent from Egyptian fortresses in Nubia, such as Semna, to the administration at Thebes in the reign of Amenemhat III. Preserved on a papyrus found in a tomb at Thebes and now in the British Museum, they record patrols, the movements…

senusret-i.s: Senusret I was the second king of the Twelfth Dynasty of Egypt, son of Amenemhat I, reigning about 45 years in the twentieth century BCE. He conquered Lower Nubia to the Second Cataract, building the fortress at Buhen, and undertook major building works throughout Egypt.

senusret-ii.s: Senusret II was a king of the Twelfth Dynasty of Egypt in the nineteenth century BCE. He began the large-scale development of the Faiyum, controlling the waters of the Bahr Yusuf, and built his pyramid at el-Lahun with the planned town of Kahun for its workers and priests.

shalfak.s: Shalfak was a Middle Kingdom Egyptian fortress in Lower Nubia, built on a granite outcrop above the Nile in the Second Cataract region. One of the chain of forts erected in the Twelfth Dynasty, probably under Senusret III, it guarded the river passage and the desert routes.

shedet.s: Shedet was the chief town of the Faiyum in ancient Egypt, on the site of modern Faiyum city, and the main cult centre of the crocodile god Sobek. The Greeks called it Crocodilopolis and later Arsinoe.

sithathoriunet.s: Sithathoriunet was an Egyptian princess of the Twelfth Dynasty, probably a daughter of Senusret II, buried near his pyramid at el-Lahun. Her tomb, excavated by Flinders Petrie and Guy Brunton in 1914, contained a treasure of jewellery, including a gold pectoral bearing the…

sobek.s: Sobek was the ancient Egyptian crocodile god, associated with the Nile, fertility and the power of the pharaoh. His main cult centres were Shedet in the Faiyum and Kom Ombo in Upper Egypt.

sobekhotep-iv.s: Sobekhotep IV was a king of the Thirteenth Dynasty of Egypt in the mid-eighteenth century BCE, brother of Neferhotep I, and one of the most powerful rulers of the dynasty. Monuments in his name are known across Egypt, and he campaigned in Nubia.

sobekneferu.s: Sobekneferu was the last ruler of the Twelfth Dynasty of Egypt, reigning for nearly four years in the late nineteenth century BCE. Probably a daughter of Amenemhat III, she succeeded Amenemhat IV and is the first woman known for certain to have taken the full royal titles of a…

sadyattes.s: Sadyattes was a king of Lydia of the Mermnad dynasty, son of Ardys and father of Alyattes, who reigned in the later 7th century BCE from his capital at Sardis. Herodotus records that he began the long war against Miletus, invading its territory every year at harvest time to…

single-whip-reform.s: The Single Whip reform was a fiscal reform of Ming China that combined the land tax and labour service obligations into a single payment, largely in silver. Tried locally from the 1530s, it was extended across the empire in the 1570s and 1580s under the grand secretary Zhang…

shattuara-ii.s: Shattuara II was the last known king of Mitanni, or Hanigalbat, in the 13th century BCE. Allied with the Hittites and the Ahlamu, he rebelled against Assyria but was defeated by Shalmaneser I, who claimed to have blinded 14,400 captives and annexed his kingdom.

shuttarna-ii.s: Shuttarna II was a king of Mitanni in the early 14th century BCE, son of Artatama I. He continued the alliance with Egypt that his father had sealed and sent his daughter Gilukhipa to marry Pharaoh Amenhotep III.

segeju.s: The Segeju are a Bantu-speaking people of the coast on the Kenya–Tanzania border, south of Mombasa. Portuguese and Swahili sources of the late 16th century describe them as warlike allies of Malindi who helped defeat the Zimba raiders in 1589 and attacked Mombasa around 1592,…

s-n-goenka.s: S. N. Goenka was a Burmese-born Indian teacher of vipassana meditation. Born into an Indian business family in Mandalay, he learned meditation from the lay teacher Sayagyi U Ba Khin in Rangoon and from 1969 taught in India.

saffron-revolution.s: The Saffron Revolution was a wave of protests in Myanmar in August–October 2007, named after the robes of the Buddhist monks who led them. Sparked by a sharp rise in fuel prices, the marches grew to tens of thousands in Yangon and other cities before the military government…

state-law-and-order-restoration-council.n: State Law and Order Restoration Council
state-law-and-order-restoration-council.s: The State Law and Order Restoration Council was the military junta that seized power in Burma on 18 September 1988 after crushing the pro-democracy uprising. It renamed the country Myanmar in 1989, refused to recognise the National League for Democracy's victory in the 1990…

socialist-republic-of-the-union-of-burma.n: Socialist Republic of the Union of Burma
socialist-republic-of-the-union-of-burma.s: The Socialist Republic of the Union of Burma was the official name of Burma under the one-party constitution of 1974. Under Ne Win and the Burma Socialist Programme Party the state followed the 'Burmese Way to Socialism', with nationalised industry and isolation from the…

state-counsellor-of-myanmar.s: The State Counsellor of Myanmar was a post created in April 2016 for Aung San Suu Kyi, who was barred from the presidency by the 2008 constitution because her sons held foreign citizenship. Comparable to a prime minister, it gave her leadership of the government and the right…

strength-through-joy.s: Strength Through Joy was the leisure organisation of the German Labour Front, founded in November 1933. It offered workers cheap holidays, cruises, concerts, sport and theatre, aiming to win support for the regime and raise productivity, and it began the giant seaside resort…

sinti.s: The Sinti are a Romani people of Central Europe, settled in German-speaking lands since the 15th century. Persecuted by the Nazi regime as racially alien, together with the Roma they were deported to camps and murdered in the genocide known as the Porajmos, in which hundreds…

sobibor-extermination-camp.s: Sobibor was a Nazi extermination camp in eastern German-occupied Poland, built as part of Operation Reinhard. From May 1942 to October 1943 some 170,000 to 250,000 Jews were murdered there in gas chambers.

shu-sin.s: Shu-Sin was the fourth king of the Third Dynasty of Ur, who reigned for about nine years in the late 21st century BCE. He campaigned in the Zagros and against Shimashki, and built a long fortification wall, called 'Repeller of the Tidnum', to keep Amorite nomads out of Sumer.

schenectady-new-york.s: Schenectady is a city in New York State on the Mohawk River, founded by Dutch settlers in 1661. On the night of 8–9 February 1690, during King William's War, a French and Native raiding party from Montreal surprised and burned the village, killing about 60 people.

seminaire-de-quebec.s: The Séminaire de Québec is a Catholic seminary founded in 1663 by François de Laval, first bishop of Quebec, to train priests for New France. It became the centre of the colonial church and of education in Canada, and in 1852 it founded Université Laval, the first…

stadacona.s: Stadacona was a St Lawrence Iroquoian village on the site of present-day Quebec City, visited by Jacques Cartier in 1535. Its chief Donnacona traded with the French, and Cartier wintered nearby in 1535–1536 before taking Donnacona to France.

san-juan-de-ulua.s: San Juan de Ulúa is a fortress on an island off the port of Veracruz, Mexico. Built from the sixteenth century to guard the main harbour of New Spain and the treasure fleets, it was the scene of a defeat of John Hawkins and Francis Drake in 1568.

sor-juana-ines-de-la-cruz.n: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz
sor-juana-ines-de-la-cruz.s: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz was a Hieronymite nun, poet and scholar of New Spain and the outstanding writer of the Spanish baroque in the Americas. Her works include the long poem Primero sueño, plays, love poetry and the Respuesta a Sor Filotea of 1691, a defence of women's…

southeast-asia-treaty-organization.s: The Southeast Asia Treaty Organization was a collective defence organisation created by the Manila Pact of September 1954 to contain communism in Southeast Asia after the French defeat in Indochina. Its members were the United States, Britain, France, Australia, New Zealand,…

sidney-holland.s: Sidney Holland was Prime Minister of New Zealand from 1949 to 1957, leading the First National Government. His government abolished the Legislative Council with effect from 1951, broke the 1951 waterfront dispute with emergency regulations and signed the ANZUS Treaty with…

south-pacific-nuclear-free-zone-treaty.n: South Pacific Nuclear Free Zone Treaty
south-pacific-nuclear-free-zone-treaty.s: The South Pacific Nuclear Free Zone Treaty, or Treaty of Rarotonga, was signed at Rarotonga in the Cook Islands on 6 August 1985 by members of the South Pacific Forum, including Australia and New Zealand. It bans the manufacture, possession, stationing and testing of nuclear…

statute-of-westminster-adoption-act-1947.s: The Statute of Westminster Adoption Act 1947 was passed by the New Zealand Parliament under Peter Fraser's Labour government to adopt the Statute of Westminster 1931. Together with a British act passed at New Zealand's request, it gave the New Zealand Parliament full power to…

shelon-river.s: The Shelon is a river of north-western Russia, about 250 kilometres long, flowing north-east through the Pskov and Novgorod regions into Lake Ilmen. Its valley lay in the heart of the lands of the Novgorod Republic.

sergei-eisenstein.s: Sergei Eisenstein was a Soviet film director and theorist whose use of montage made him one of the most influential figures in the history of cinema. His films include Battleship Potemkin (1925), October (1928), Alexander Nevsky (1938), celebrating the victory on Lake Peipus,…

staraya-russa.s: Staraya Russa is a town in the Novgorod region of Russia, south of Lake Ilmen, first recorded in the eleventh century. In the Middle Ages it was the second town of the Novgorod Republic and a centre of salt production.

sicca-veneria.s: Sicca Veneria was an ancient town in north-western Tunisia, on the site of modern El Kef, named after its sanctuary of a goddess identified with Venus. Under Carthage it was where mercenaries gathered before the Mercenary War of 241 BCE, and it later belonged to the Numidian…

sadocus.s: Sadocus was a son of the Odrysian king Sitalces. When Athens made his father an ally at the start of the Peloponnesian War in 431 BCE, it granted Sadocus Athenian citizenship.

seuthes-i.s: Seuthes I was king of the Odrysian Thracians from 424 BCE, succeeding his uncle Sitalces. Thucydides records that under him the yearly tribute from the Thracian tribes and the Greek cities reached about 400 talents of gold and silver, with gifts of equal value, the height of…

seuthes-ii.s: Seuthes II was an Odrysian Thracian ruler who held the lands near the Propontis in the late fifth and early fourth centuries BCE, while Medocus ruled the interior. In 400–399 BCE he hired the survivors of the Ten Thousand, as Xenophon, their commander, describes in the…

schollenen-gorge.s: The Schöllenen Gorge is a narrow gorge of the Reuss River in the canton of Uri, Switzerland, between Göschenen and Andermatt on the route to the Gotthard Pass. The building of a bridge through it in the early thirteenth century, later called the Devil's Bridge, opened the…

sempach-charter.s: The Sempach Charter was an agreement of 1393 among the eight Swiss Confederate cantons and Solothurn setting common rules for conduct in war. It forbade plundering before victory was secure and unauthorised flight from battle, and protected churches, convents and women.
