stans-agreement.s: The Stans Agreement of 22 December 1481 settled a dispute among the Swiss cantons after the Burgundian Wars, between the city cantons and the rural cantons, over the division of booty and the admission of Fribourg and Solothurn. Reached with the advice of the hermit Niklaus…

swiss-guards.s: Swiss Guards were Swiss mercenary units serving as bodyguards and palace troops at foreign courts from the late fifteenth century. In France the Hundred Swiss and the Swiss Guards regiment served the kings, and hundreds of the regiment died defending the Tuileries Palace on 10…

shin-chapata.s: Shin Chapata was a Buddhist monk of the Pagan Kingdom who was ordained in Sri Lanka in the Mahavihara tradition and returned to Pagan around 1190 with four other monks. With the support of King Narapatisithu they founded a Sinhalese order of monks, which divided the Burmese…

sawlu.s: Sawlu was king of Pagan from 1077 to 1084, the son and successor of Anawrahta. An inexperienced ruler, he inherited a large but loosely integrated realm and appointed his boyhood companion Nga Yaman Kan governor of Pegu.

somapura-mahavihara.s: Somapura Mahavihara is the ruin of a great Buddhist monastery at Paharpur in Naogaon District, Bangladesh, founded by the Pala king Dharmapala in the late eighth century. Its square court of 177 monastic cells surrounds a cruciform temple whose plan influenced Buddhist…

suvarnadvipa.s: Suvarnadvipa, Sanskrit for 'island of gold', was the Indian name for a land in maritime Southeast Asia, usually identified with Sumatra or more broadly with the Malay Peninsula and archipelago. In Pala inscriptions it denotes the realm of the Shailendra king Balaputradeva, and…

shivaskandavarman.s: Shivaskandavarman was one of the earliest known kings of the Pallava dynasty, ruling in the fourth century CE from Kanchipuram. His copper-plate charters in Prakrit, such as the Mayidavolu and Hirahadagalli grants, record gifts of land in the Andhra country and the Bellary…

south-india.s: South India is the southern part of the Indian peninsula, usually taken to include the states of Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Telangana. Largely Dravidian-speaking, it was the home of the Pallavas, Cholas, Pandyas, Chalukyas and Vijayanagara, whose…

savona.s: Savona is a port city on the Ligurian coast of north-western Italy, west of Genoa. A rival of Genoa in the Middle Ages, it was subdued by the Genoese in 1528.

sistine-chapel.s: The Sistine Chapel is a chapel in the Apostolic Palace in Vatican City, built between 1473 and 1481 for Pope Sixtus IV, after whom it is named. Its walls were painted by Botticelli, Perugino and others, and Michelangelo painted its ceiling between 1508 and 1512 for Julius II…

surena.s: Surena was a Parthian general of the House of Suren in the service of King Orodes II. In 53 BCE at Carrhae, using horse archers kept supplied with arrows by a camel train and heavy cataphract cavalry, he destroyed a much larger Roman army under Marcus Licinius Crassus, who was…

shining-path.s: The Shining Path is a Maoist insurgent organisation in Peru, founded around 1969 by the philosophy professor Abimael Guzmán in Ayacucho. It launched an armed struggle in 1980, and the conflict with the state cost some 70,000 lives by official estimates.

shenzhen.s: Shenzhen is a city in Guangdong province in southern China, bordering Hong Kong. In 1980 it became one of China's first Special Economic Zones under Deng Xiaoping's reforms, and it grew from a small market town into a metropolis of more than 17 million people, a centre of…

sino-soviet-split.s: The Sino-Soviet split was the breakdown of relations between the People's Republic of China and the Soviet Union. Beginning with ideological disputes after Khrushchev's denunciation of Stalin in 1956, it led to the withdrawal of Soviet advisers in 1960 and an open break by the…

standard-chinese.s: Standard Chinese, or Standard Mandarin, is the official language of the People's Republic of China, based on the pronunciation of Beijing and the grammar of modern vernacular Mandarin literature. Promoted as Putonghua ('common speech') from 1956, it is also an official…

sigismund-iii-vasa.s: Sigismund III Vasa was king of Poland and grand duke of Lithuania from 1587 to 1632, and king of Sweden from 1592 until he was deposed in 1599. A zealous Catholic, he moved the royal residence from Kraków to Warsaw and fought long wars with Sweden, Russia and the Ottomans;…

stanislaw-august-poniatowski.s: Stanisław August Poniatowski was the last king of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, elected in 1764 with the backing of Catherine the Great. A patron of the arts and of reform, he supported the Constitution of 3 May 1791, but he could not prevent the three partitions of…

societe-libre-d-emulation.s: The Société libre d'Émulation is a learned society founded in Liège in 1779 under the patronage of Prince-Bishop François-Charles de Velbruck to encourage the arts, sciences and letters. A centre of the Enlightenment in the principality, it held competitions and exhibitions…

seraing.s: Seraing is an industrial town on the Meuse just upstream of Liège, Belgium. In 1817 John Cockerill set up ironworks and engineering shops in the former summer palace of the prince-bishops there, and the Cockerill works became one of the largest industrial enterprises of…

sentence-of-guadalupe.s: The Sentence of Guadalupe was an arbitral ruling issued by Ferdinand II of Aragon at the monastery of Guadalupe on 21 April 1486. It ended the War of the Remences by allowing Catalan remença peasants to redeem the 'evil customs' that bound them to their lords, and it abolished…

sant-climent-de-taull.s: Sant Climent de Taüll is a Romanesque church in the Vall de Boí in the Catalan Pyrenees, consecrated in 1123. Its apse fresco of Christ in Majesty, now in the National Art Museum of Catalonia, is a masterpiece of Romanesque painting, and the church is part of a UNESCO World…

santa-maria-del-mar.s: Santa Maria del Mar is a Gothic basilica in the Ribera quarter of Barcelona, built between 1329 and 1383 with the support of the city's merchants and sailors. With its wide nave and slender octagonal pillars, it is the finest example of Catalan Gothic architecture.

schaan.s: Schaan is the largest municipality of Liechtenstein, just north of the capital Vaduz on the Rhine plain. An ancient settlement with Roman remains, it became the country's main industrial centre in the twentieth century, home to the construction-tool maker Hilti, founded there…

stelvio-pass.s: The Stelvio Pass is a mountain pass in northern Italy at 2,757 metres, one of the highest paved passes in the Alps, linking the Valtellina with the Vinschgau in South Tyrol. Until 1918 it lay on the border between Italy and Austria and was fought over in 1866 and in the First…

siret.s: Siret is a town in Suceava County, north-eastern Romania, near the border with Ukraine and on the river of the same name. In the fourteenth century it was one of the first centres of the Principality of Moldavia: a Catholic bishopric was founded there around 1371, and princes…

sucevita-monastery.s: Sucevița Monastery is a fortified Orthodox monastery in Suceava County, north-eastern Romania, founded in the 1580s by the Movilă family. Its church, painted inside and out around 1595–1596, has the best-preserved exterior frescoes of the Moldavian tradition, including a…

septuagint.s: The Septuagint is the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures, begun with the Torah in Alexandria in the third century BCE and completed over the following two centuries. The Letter of Aristeas tells that seventy-two scholars made it at the request of Ptolemy II…

serapis.s: Serapis was a Graeco-Egyptian god whose cult was promoted by Ptolemy I Soter in the early third century BCE, combining the Egyptian Osiris and the Apis bull with the appearance of Greek gods such as Zeus and Hades. His great temple, the Serapeum of Alexandria, was a centre of…

sattar-khan.s: Sattar Khan was a leader of the Iranian Constitutional Revolution, a former horse dealer from Tabriz who organised the city's defence after Mohammad Ali Shah closed the Majlis in 1908. His fighters held Tabriz against royalist forces for about ten months, keeping the…

supplementary-fundamental-law.s: The Supplementary Fundamental Law was the second part of the Persian Constitution, ratified in October 1907 by Mohammad Ali Shah. Modelled partly on the Belgian constitution, it set out civil rights, equality before the law and the separation of powers, and made Twelver…

siku-quanshu.s: The Siku Quanshu, or Complete Library of the Four Treasuries, was a vast compilation of Chinese literature ordered by the Qianlong Emperor in 1773 and completed in 1782. Arranged in the four categories of classics, history, philosophy and literature, it copied more than 3,400…

silahara-dynasty.s: The Silahara dynasty comprised three related lines of rulers in western India, in North Konkan around Thane, South Konkan and the Kolhapur region. They began as feudatories of the Rashtrakutas and then served the Western Chalukyas, while ruling their coastal and upland…

siyaka.s: Siyaka II, also called Harsha, was a Paramara king of Malwa in central India who turned his family from Rashtrakuta vassals into an independent power. In 972 he invaded the Deccan and sacked Manyakheta, the Rashtrakuta capital, an event recorded by the poet Dhanapala that…

slave-abolition-act-siam.s: The Slave Abolition Act of 1905 was the Siamese law that completed the abolition of slavery begun by King Chulalongkorn in 1874. It forbade any new enslavement and freed the children of slaves, while the remaining debt slaves had their redemption price reduced each month until…

sunthorn-phu.s: Sunthorn Phu was a Thai poet of the early Rattanakosin period, often called the Bard of Rattanakosin. A favourite of Rama II, he fell from favour under Rama III, became a monk and travelled widely, writing travel poems known as nirat.

sidi-fredj.s: Sidi Fredj, known to the French as Sidi Ferruch, is a small peninsula on the Mediterranean coast about 25 km west of Algiers. On 14 June 1830 a French army of more than 30,000 men under General de Bourmont landed there, defeated the dey's forces at Staouéli and advanced on…

stephen-decatur.s: Stephen Decatur was an officer of the United States Navy, famous for burning the captured frigate Philadelphia in Tripoli harbour in 1804 during the First Barbary War. In the War of 1812 he captured the British frigate Macedonian.

siglo-xx-mine.s: Siglo XX is a large tin mine at Llallagua in the department of Potosí, Bolivia, developed by Simón Patiño in the early twentieth century and nationalised in 1952. With the neighbouring Catavi complex it became the heartland of Bolivia's militant miners' unions.

simon-patino.s: Simón Iturri Patiño was a Bolivian mining magnate known as the 'King of Tin'. From the La Salvadora mine at Uncía, struck around 1900, he built a company that controlled much of Bolivia's tin output and acquired smelters in Europe.

second-battle-of-cancha-rayada.s: The Second Battle of Cancha Rayada was fought on the night of 19 March 1818 near Talca, when royalist forces under Mariano Osorio surprised the camp of the patriot army of San Martín and O'Higgins and scattered it. O'Higgins was wounded, but the patriots regrouped and…

salvador-allende.s: Salvador Allende was a Chilean Socialist physician and politician who won the presidential election of 1970 at the head of the Popular Unity coalition. His government nationalised copper, extended land reform and took over banks and industries, but faced inflation, shortages…

sebastian-pinera.s: Sebastián Piñera was a Chilean businessman and centre-right politician who served two terms as president, from 2010 to 2014 and from 2018 to 2022. His first term began with the 2010 earthquake and saw the rescue of 33 trapped miners; his second was shaken by the mass protests…

song-jiaoren.s: Song Jiaoren was a Chinese revolutionary and a founder of the Kuomintang, which he led to victory in China's first national parliamentary elections in 1912–1913. He championed a cabinet system that would limit presidential power.

southern-district-gran-colombia.s: The Southern District was one of the three great districts of Gran Colombia, comprising the departments of Quito, Guayaquil and Cuenca, roughly present-day Ecuador. It was incorporated after the patriot victory at Pichincha in 1822.

sacred-heart.s: The Sacred Heart is a Roman Catholic devotion to the physical heart of Jesus as a symbol of divine love, spread widely from the seventeenth century after the visions of Margaret Mary Alacoque in France. In the nineteenth century it became a symbol of Catholic and conservative…

sierra-ecuador.s: The Sierra is the Andean highland region of Ecuador, formed by two parallel mountain ranges enclosing a series of high basins, with the capital Quito at its northern end. Densely settled before the Inca conquest, it was the centre of the colonial Audiencia of Quito and of…

salvador-sanchez-ceren.s: Salvador Sánchez Cerén is a Salvadoran former schoolteacher and guerrilla commander of the FMLN during the civil war, and a signatory of the Chapultepec Peace Accords of 1992. He served as vice-president from 2009 and as president from 2014 to 2019, the first former guerrilla…

supreme-soviet-of-the-estonian-ssr.n: Supreme Soviet of the Estonian SSR
supreme-soviet-of-the-estonian-ssr.s: The Supreme Soviet of the Estonian SSR was the legislature of Soviet Estonia. On 16 November 1988 it declared Estonia's sovereignty and the supremacy of its laws over those of the Soviet Union.

skype.s: Skype was an internet telephony and video-calling service launched in 2003 by Niklas Zennström and Janus Friis, whose software was written by the Estonian developers Ahti Heinla, Priit Kasesalu and Jaan Tallinn. It became one of the most widely used communication services in…

state-elder.s: The State Elder (Riigivanem) was the head of government of interwar Estonia, who under the constitution of 1920 also acted as head of state, as there was no separate presidency. Dependent on the confidence of the Riigikogu, State Elders changed frequently.

sauli-niinisto.s: Sauli Niinistö (born 1948) is a Finnish politician of the National Coalition Party who served as president of Finland from 2012 to 2024. Earlier he was finance minister from 1996 to 2003, during the recovery from a deep recession and the introduction of the euro, and speaker…

sandro-botticelli.s: Sandro Botticelli (c. 1445–1510) was a Florentine painter of the early Renaissance, closely associated with the circle of Lorenzo de' Medici. His mythological paintings The Birth of Venus and Primavera, along with altarpieces and frescoes in the Sistine Chapel, made him one of…

storia-ditalia.s: The Storia d'Italia, or History of Italy, is a historical work by Francesco Guicciardini, written in the last years of his life and published after his death, from 1561. Covering the Italian Wars from 1490 to 1534, it treats Italy as a whole and explains events through the…

sack-of-rome-1527.s: The Sack of Rome took place on 6 May 1527, when mutinous and unpaid troops of Emperor Charles V, including German Landsknechte and Spanish soldiers, stormed the city during the War of the League of Cognac. Pope Clement VII took refuge in Castel Sant'Angelo and later…

signoria-of-florence.s: The Signoria was the chief executive body of the Republic of Florence, composed of the priors of the guilds and, from 1293, the Gonfaloniere of Justice. Its members were chosen by lot from bags of eligible citizens and served terms of two months, living in the Palazzo Vecchio…

strada-nuova.s: The Strada Nuova, now Via Garibaldi, is a street in Genoa laid out from 1550 for the city's leading noble families, who built a row of Renaissance and Baroque palaces along it. Many of these houses were on the Rolli, the official lists of private palaces required to lodge…

samana-peninsula.s: The Samaná Peninsula is a peninsula in the north-east of the Dominican Republic, enclosing Samaná Bay. In 1824–1825, while the whole island was under Haitian rule, free African American emigrants from the United States settled there at the invitation of President Jean-Pierre…

soto-cano-air-base.s: Soto Cano Air Base, formerly Palmerola, is a Honduran air base near Comayagua in central Honduras that has hosted a United States military presence, Joint Task Force-Bravo, since the 1980s. During the Central American wars it was a centre of the US military build-up in…

samuel-zemurray.s: Samuel Zemurray (1877–1961) was an American businessman, born in Kishinev in the Russian Empire, who built a banana empire in Honduras. His Cuyamel Fruit Company backed the invasion of 1910–1911 that restored Manuel Bonilla to power, winning large concessions.

san-juancito.s: San Juancito is a mining town in the mountains north-east of Tegucigalpa, Honduras. From 1880 it was the centre of operations of the New York and Honduras Rosario Mining Company, whose silver mines made it for decades one of the most important economic centres of the country.

san-pedro-sula.s: San Pedro Sula is the second-largest city of Honduras and its main industrial and commercial centre, in the fertile Sula valley of the north-west. Founded by the Spanish in 1536, it grew rapidly from the late nineteenth century with the railway and the banana companies, and…

sandinista-national-liberation-front.s: The Sandinista National Liberation Front (FSLN) is a Nicaraguan political party founded in 1961 as a guerrilla movement named after Augusto César Sandino. It overthrew the dictatorship of Anastasio Somoza Debayle in 1979 and governed until 1990, fighting the US-backed Contras,…

standard-fruit-company.s: The Standard Fruit Company was an American fruit company that grew out of the banana business founded on the north coast of Honduras in the 1890s by the Vaccaro brothers, Italian immigrants based in New Orleans. With its headquarters at La Ceiba, it built railways, ports and…

scheduled-castes.s: Scheduled Castes is the official term in India for the communities historically subjected to untouchability, listed in a schedule under the constitution. The constitution of 1950, drafted under B. R. Ambedkar, abolished untouchability and reserved seats in legislatures and…

scheduled-tribes.s: Scheduled Tribes is the official designation in India for indigenous communities, often called Adivasis, listed under the constitution of 1950. Like the Scheduled Castes, they receive reserved seats in legislatures and reserved places in education and public employment, and…

sino-indian-war.s: The Sino-Indian War was a border war fought between China and India in October and November 1962 over disputed Himalayan territory in Aksai Chin and the North-East Frontier Agency. Chinese forces overran Indian positions on both fronts, then declared a ceasefire and withdrew…

saeima.s: The Saeima is the single-chamber parliament of Latvia, made up of 100 members elected by proportional representation. First convened in 1922 under the Satversme, it was suspended after Kārlis Ulmanis's coup of 1934 and restored when the fifth Saeima met in July 1993.

skrunda-1.s: Skrunda-1 was a Soviet early-warning radar station near Skrunda in western Latvia, built from the 1960s with Dnepr radars to detect ballistic missiles approaching from the west. After Latvian independence Russia was allowed to keep operating it for four years under an…

seimas.s: The Seimas is the single-chamber parliament of Lithuania, with 141 members elected for four-year terms under a mixed system. The name, taken from the diet of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, was revived for the parliament of the interwar republic, which dominated government under…

soviet-lithuanian-peace-treaty.s: The Soviet–Lithuanian Peace Treaty was signed in Moscow on 12 July 1920, ending the war between Soviet Russia and Lithuania. Russia recognised Lithuanian independence and Lithuanian claims to a large territory including Vilnius, which the Red Army handed over in August after…

steponas-darius.s: Steponas Darius was a Lithuanian-American aviator who with Stasys Girėnas attempted a non-stop flight from New York to Kaunas in the aircraft Lituanica in July 1933. After crossing the Atlantic in about 37 hours, the plane crashed near Soldin in Germany, killing both men short…

stasys-girenas.s: Stasys Girėnas was a Lithuanian-American aviator who with Steponas Darius attempted a non-stop flight from New York to Kaunas in the aircraft Lituanica in July 1933. After crossing the Atlantic, the plane crashed near Soldin in Germany on 17 July, killing both men about 650…

san-juan-del-norte.s: San Juan del Norte, officially San Juan de Nicaragua, is a town at the mouth of the San Juan River on Nicaragua's Caribbean coast. Its position at the eastern end of a potential canal route made it a strategic prize: British forces seized it in 1848 and renamed it Greytown,…

sandinista-popular-army.s: The Sandinista Popular Army was the national army created by the Sandinista government of Nicaragua in 1979 to replace the defeated National Guard, under the command of Humberto Ortega. Built up with Soviet and Cuban support and conscription, it fought the US-backed Contra…

school-of-the-americas.s: The School of the Americas is a United States Army training institution for Latin American military and police officers, founded in the Panama Canal Zone in 1946. Moved to Fort Benning in Georgia in 1984 under the canal treaties, it was renamed the Western Hemisphere Institute…

seven-interpretive-essays-on-peruvian-re.n: Seven Interpretive Essays on Peruvian Reality
seven-interpretive-essays-on-peruvian-re.s: Seven Interpretive Essays on Peruvian Reality (Siete ensayos de interpretación de la realidad peruana) is a book by José Carlos Mariátegui published in Lima in 1928. Applying Marxist analysis to Peru, it treated the condition of the indigenous population as a problem of land…

secretary-general-of-the-united-nations.s: The Secretary-General of the United Nations is the chief administrative officer of the United Nations and head of its Secretariat, appointed by the General Assembly on the recommendation of the Security Council, usually for five-year terms. The office has also become an…

sutorina.s: Sutorina is a narrow strip of coast at the entrance to the Bay of Kotor, near Herceg Novi in present-day Montenegro. Under the Treaty of Karlowitz of 1699 it was left as an Ottoman corridor to the sea, which, with Neum to the north, separated the Republic of Ragusa from…

sool.s: Sool is an administrative region in northern Somalia, with its capital at Las Anod. Lying within the borders of former British Somaliland, it is claimed by Somaliland and Puntland, and much of its Dhulbahante population rejects Somaliland's rule.

ssc-khatumo.s: SSC-Khatumo is a political and military administration formed in 2023 by Dhulbahante leaders in the Sool, Sanaag and Cayn areas of northern Somalia, who reject Somaliland's authority and seek to remain part of Somalia. Its forces fought the Somaliland army around Las Anod and…

south-african-defence-force.s: The South African Defence Force (SADF) was the armed forces of South Africa from 1957 to 1994. It fought the South African Border War in Namibia and Angola against SWAPO, the Angolan government and Cuban forces, and conducted raids into neighbouring states.

sasol.s: Sasol is a South African chemicals and energy company founded by the state in 1950 to make fuel from coal, using the Fischer–Tropsch process at Sasolburg and later at Secunda. Its synthetic fuels reduced South Africa's dependence on imported oil during the apartheid-era…

south-african-communist-party.s: The South African Communist Party was founded in 1921 as the Communist Party of South Africa, banned in 1950 and re-formed underground in 1953. Closely allied with the ANC, it co-founded Umkhonto we Sizwe and supplied many leaders of the liberation struggle, including Joe…

swapo.s: SWAPO, the South West Africa People's Organisation, is the Namibian liberation movement founded in 1960. From 1966 its armed wing fought South African rule in the South African Border War, operating from Zambia and Angola.

steve-biko.s: Steve Biko was a South African anti-apartheid activist and founder of the Black Consciousness Movement, which urged black South Africans to free themselves from psychological dependence on whites. Banned from 1973, he was arrested in August 1977 and died in police custody in…

southern-movement-yemen.s: The Southern Movement, or al-Hirak, is a political movement in southern Yemen that began in 2007 with protests by retired southern officers and civil servants against discrimination after the 1994 civil war. It grew into a broad campaign, partly for autonomy and largely for…

south-yemen.s: South Yemen, from 1970 the People's Democratic Republic of Yemen, was the state formed in southern Arabia when Britain withdrew from Aden and the South Arabian protectorates in November 1967. Ruled by the Marxist Yemeni Socialist Party, it was the only communist state in the…

saada-governorate.s: Saada is a governorate in the far north of Yemen on the Saudi border, with its capital at the city of Saada, an old centre of Zaydi learning. It is the homeland of the Houthi movement, and from 2004 to 2010 it was the main battlefield of six wars between the movement and the…

southern-transitional-council.s: The Southern Transitional Council is a southern Yemeni separatist organisation formed in May 2017 under Aidarus al-Zoubaidi, the dismissed governor of Aden, and backed by the United Arab Emirates. It seeks an independent southern state.

seleucus-ii-callinicus.s: Seleucus II Callinicus was king of the Seleucid Empire from 246 to 225 BCE. His reign began with the Third Syrian War against Ptolemy III, and he then fought his own brother Antiochus Hierax for control of Asia Minor, while Parthia and Bactria broke away in the east.

syme.s: Syme (Symi) is a small, rocky Greek island in the Dodecanese, north of Rhodes and close to the coast of Turkey. In the Hellenistic period it belonged to the Rhodian state.

solway-firth.s: The Solway Firth is an inlet of the Irish Sea that forms part of the border between England and Scotland, between Cumbria and Dumfries and Galloway. Hadrian's Wall, begun around 122 CE, ran from the Tyne in the east to Bowness-on-Solway in the west, so the firth marked the…

sulis-minerva.s: Sulis Minerva was the goddess worshipped at the hot springs of Aquae Sulis, modern Bath, in Roman Britain. She combined the local Celtic goddess Sulis with the Roman Minerva, and a temple and bath complex were built around her spring from the late first century CE.

scetis.s: Scetis, the Wadi el-Natrun in the desert west of the Nile Delta in Egypt, was one of the main centres of early Christian monasticism. Macarius of Egypt settled there around 330, and the sayings of its monks were collected in the Sayings of the Desert Fathers.

serapeum-of-alexandria.s: The Serapeum of Alexandria was the great temple of the god Serapis, founded under Ptolemy III in the third century BCE and rebuilt in Roman times. It also housed a daughter library of the Library of Alexandria.

servian-wall.s: The Servian Wall was the defensive wall of ancient Rome, named after the king Servius Tullius but largely built in the early fourth century BCE after the Gallic sack of about 390 BCE. Made of large blocks of tufa from Grotta Oscura near Veii, it ran about 11 kilometres around…

socialist-realism.s: Socialist Realism was the officially approved style of art, literature and music in the Soviet Union, proclaimed in the early 1930s and imposed at the first Congress of Soviet Writers in 1934. It required realistic works that showed society in its revolutionary development and…

second-sho-dynasty.s: The Second Shō dynasty ruled the Ryukyu Kingdom from 1470 until Japan annexed it in 1879. It was founded by the royal treasurer Kanemaru, who took the throne as Shō En after the death of Shō Toku.

sho-shoken.s: Shō Shōken, also known as Haneji Chōshū, was a Ryukyuan prince and statesman who served as regent (sessei) of the Ryukyu Kingdom from 1666 to 1673. He cut court and ritual spending, reorganised the administration and promoted agriculture under the overlordship of Satsuma.

sho-en.s: Shō En, born Kanemaru, was the founder of the Second Shō dynasty of the Ryukyu Kingdom. A man of humble origins from Izena Island, he rose to become royal treasurer, and after the death of King Shō Toku in 1469 he was chosen king, reigning from 1470 to 1476.

sho-nei.s: Shō Nei was king of Ryukyu from 1589 to 1620, in the Second Shō dynasty. In 1609 the Shimazu clan of Satsuma invaded his kingdom; he surrendered Shuri Castle and was taken to Japan, where he was presented to the Tokugawa shoguns.

sho-sei.s: Shō Sei was king of Ryukyu from 1527 to 1555, the son and successor of Shō Shin in the Second Shō dynasty. He campaigned in the Amami Islands in 1537 to enforce royal authority in the north, and in his reign forts were built at the mouth of Naha harbour against wakō pirates.

sho-taikyu.s: Shō Taikyū was king of Ryukyu from 1454 to 1460, in the First Shō dynasty. His reign saw the conflict of 1458 in which the lords Gosamaru and Amawari were destroyed.

sho-toku.s: Shō Toku was the last king of the First Shō dynasty of Ryukyu, reigning from 1461 to 1469. He sent a military expedition that conquered the island of Kikai in 1466.

sonohyan-utaki-ishimon.s: The Sonohyan-utaki Ishimon is a stone gate before a sacred grove beside Shuri Castle on Okinawa, built in 1519 under King Shō Shin. Kings prayed there for safety before leaving Shuri on journeys.

saadian-tombs.s: The Saadian Tombs are the royal necropolis of the Saadi dynasty beside the Kasbah Mosque in Marrakesh. Built mainly under Ahmad al-Mansur in the late sixteenth century, they include the richly decorated Hall of the Twelve Columns with Carrara marble and carved cedar.

sistan.s: Sistan is a region in the basin of the Helmand river and Lake Hamun, divided today between south-eastern Iran and south-western Afghanistan. The ancient Drangiana, it took the name Sakastan, 'land of the Saka', after Saka nomads settled there in the late second century BCE.

syloson.s: Syloson was a brother of Polycrates, tyrant of Samos, who banished him. In exile in Egypt, according to Herodotus, he gave his cloak to the young Darius, who as king repaid the gift by sending Otanes to conquer Samos and install Syloson as tyrant around 517 BCE.

sarmatia.s: Sarmatia was the name used by Greek and Roman geographers for the lands of the Sarmatians, roughly the steppes between the Vistula, the Volga and the Caucasus. Ptolemy's Geography divided it at the Don into European and Asian Sarmatia.

siraces.s: The Siraces were a Sarmatian people of the plains of the Kuban river, north of the Caucasus, from about the fourth century BCE. Strabo records that they were ruled by kings and could field tens of thousands of horsemen.

sarmatism.s: Sarmatism was the ideology and culture of the nobility of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth from the sixteenth to the eighteenth centuries, based on the belief that the szlachta descended from the ancient Sarmatians. It celebrated noble liberty, equality among nobles,…

satakarni-i.s: Satakarni I was an early Satavahana king of the Deccan, successor of Kanha, generally placed in the second or first century BCE. He extended the kingdom over the western Deccan and probably Malwa, and performed Vedic horse sacrifices recorded in the Naneghat inscription of his…

saxnot.s: Saxnot was a god of the pagan Saxons, named with Thunaer and Woden in the Old Saxon baptismal vow of the late eighth or ninth century, which required converts to renounce them. He appears as Seaxneat, a son of Woden, at the head of the genealogy of the kings of Essex.

sidonius-apollinaris.s: Sidonius Apollinaris was a Gallo-Roman aristocrat, poet and bishop of Clermont from about 470. Son-in-law of the emperor Avitus, he wrote panegyrics for three emperors and a collection of letters that are a major source for fifth-century Gaul.

slavonic-bulgarian-history.s: The Slavonic-Bulgarian History is a short history of the Bulgarians written in 1762 by Paisius of Hilendar, a monk of the Hilandar Monastery on Mount Athos. Recalling the medieval Bulgarian tsars and saints, it urged Bulgarians to take pride in their language and past rather…

sharjah-fort.s: Sharjah Fort, known as Al Hisn, is a fort in the centre of Sharjah, United Arab Emirates, built around 1820 under Sultan bin Saqr Al Qasimi. For about 150 years it was the residence of the ruling family and the seat of government.

sultan-bin-muhammad-al-qasimi.s: Sultan bin Muhammad Al Qasimi has been ruler of Sharjah, one of the United Arab Emirates, since 1972, when he succeeded his brother Khalid after a failed coup. A historian with doctorates from British universities, he wrote The Myth of Arab Piracy in the Gulf (1986), which…

saqr-bin-sultan-al-qasimi.s: Saqr bin Sultan Al Qasimi was ruler of Sharjah from 1951 to 1965. Sympathetic to the Arab nationalism of Gamal Abdel Nasser, he was deposed by the British in 1965 and went into exile in Cairo, being replaced by his cousin Khalid bin Muhammad.

shaykh-haydar.s: Shaykh Haydar was head of the Safavid Sufi order of Ardabil from 1460 to 1488 and father of Shah Ismail I. Married to a daughter of the Aq Qoyunlu ruler Uzun Hasan, he turned the order's followers into a fighting force and is credited with the red headgear that gave them the…

sada-kaur.s: Sada Kaur was the leader of the Kanhaiya Misl, one of the Sikh confederacies, after the death of her husband Gurbakhsh Singh in 1785. She married her daughter to the young Ranjit Singh of the Sukerchakia Misl and supported him with troops, notably in his capture of Lahore in…

seondeok-of-silla.s: Seondeok was queen of Silla from 632 to 647, the first woman to rule a Korean kingdom. Facing attacks from Baekje and Goguryeo, she sought help from Tang China and promoted Buddhism, building the nine-storey wooden pagoda of Hwangnyongsa.

sinmun-of-silla.s: Sinmun was king of Silla from 681 to 692, son of King Munmu. He put down a rebellion of nobles early in his reign and built the institutions of Unified Silla, dividing the realm into nine provinces and five secondary capitals and founding the Gukhak, the national Confucian…

silla-tang-war.s: The Silla–Tang War was fought from 670 to 676 between the Korean kingdom of Silla and Tang China, its former ally against Baekje and Goguryeo. Silla resisted Tang plans to rule the conquered lands and supported Goguryeo rebels.

samsung.s: Samsung is a South Korean business group founded in 1938 by Lee Byung-chul as a trading company in Daegu. Its largest member, Samsung Electronics, became one of the world's biggest makers of smartphones, memory chips and televisions.

sino-vietnamese-war.s: The Sino-Vietnamese War was a brief war fought in February and March 1979, when China invaded northern Vietnam in response to Vietnam's invasion of Cambodia and its alliance with the Soviet Union. Chinese forces captured several provincial capitals, including Lạng Sơn, then…

sixth-national-congress-of-the-communist.n: Sixth National Congress of the Communist Party of Vietnam
sixth-national-congress-of-the-communist.s: The Sixth National Congress of the Communist Party of Vietnam met in Hanoi from 15 to 18 December 1986 and elected Nguyen Van Linh as general secretary. Facing hyperinflation and food shortages after a decade of central planning, it adopted the Doi Moi (renovation) policy,…

spratly-islands.s: The Spratly Islands are a scattered group of more than a hundred small islands, reefs and atolls in the southern South China Sea. They are claimed wholly by China, Taiwan and Vietnam and in part by the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei, all of which except Brunei occupy some…

sultan-of-sokoto.s: The Sultan of Sokoto is the ruler of the Sokoto Caliphate founded by Usman dan Fodio in 1804, styled Amir al-Mu'minin (Commander of the Faithful) and in Hausa Sarkin Musulmi. Dan Fodio's son Muhammad Bello was the first to rule from Sokoto.

shen-kuo.s: Shen Kuo was a Chinese scholar-official and polymath of the Northern Song dynasty who served under Wang Anshi's reform government. In his Dream Pool Essays (completed about 1088) he described the magnetic needle compass and magnetic declination, Bi Sheng's movable type,…

sunni-baru.s: Sunni Baru was the last ruler of the Sunni dynasty of Songhai, succeeding his father Sunni Ali in 1492. He reportedly refused to profess Islam publicly, which alienated the Muslim scholars and merchants of the towns, and in April 1493 he was defeated near Gao by his father's…

sand-river-convention.s: The Sand River Convention was an agreement signed on 17 January 1852 between British commissioners and Boer leaders headed by Andries Pretorius. Britain recognised the independence of the emigrant Boers living north of the Vaal River, undertook not to ally with African peoples…

salim-rubaya-ali.s: Salim Rubaya Ali was a Yemeni revolutionary who headed South Yemen's Presidential Council from 1969 to 1978 after the Corrective Move. A leader of the National Liberation Front, he leaned towards Maoist and more independent policies and sought better relations with Saudi…

sergei-prokofiev.s: Sergei Prokofiev was a Russian composer and pianist who left Russia after the revolution and returned to settle in the Soviet Union in 1936. His works include the ballet Romeo and Juliet, the children's tale Peter and the Wolf, the music for Eisenstein's film Alexander Nevsky,…

soviet-of-the-republics.s: The Soviet of the Republics was the upper chamber of the Supreme Soviet of the Soviet Union, created in September 1991 after the failed August coup, with delegates from the union republics. On 26 December 1991, the day after Mikhail Gorbachev resigned, it adopted a declaration…

sanctuary-of-artemis-orthia.s: The sanctuary of Artemis Orthia was one of the main religious sites of ancient Sparta, on the bank of the Eurotas. Excavated by the British School at Athens from 1906, it yielded thousands of votive offerings, including lead figurines, ivories and terracotta masks, from the…

spartiates.s: The Spartiates were the full citizens of ancient Sparta, also called homoioi (peers). They were trained from boyhood in the agoge, served as hoplites and had to contribute to a common mess, living from land worked by helots.

second-messenian-war.s: The Second Messenian War was a revolt of the Messenians against Spartan rule in the seventh century BCE, traditionally led by the hero Aristomenes. Its dates are uncertain.

sangrama-vijayatunggavarman.s: Sangrama Vijayatunggavarman was a ruler of Srivijaya in the early eleventh century, known from the Tanjore inscription of the Chola king Rajendra Chola I. When Rajendra's fleet raided Srivijaya and its ports, including Kadaram (Kedah), in 1025, the king was taken captive…

shen-baoxu.s: Shen Baoxu was a minister of the State of Chu who saved it after the invasion by Wu in 506 BCE. When Wu forces occupied the Chu capital Ying, he went to the court of Qin to ask for help and, according to the Zuo zhuan, wept day and night for seven days until Duke Ai of Qin…

shanrong.s: The Shanrong, or Mountain Rong, were a non-Zhou people of north-eastern China, in the region of present-day Hebei, during the Spring and Autumn period. Their attacks on the State of Yan led Duke Huan of Qi to campaign against them in 663 BCE, an expedition remembered as one of…

shen-dao.s: Shen Dao was a Chinese philosopher of the Warring States period, a native of Zhao who taught at the Jixia Academy in Qi. He stressed shi, the power that comes from position rather than personal virtue, and the impartial rule of law.

sun-bin.s: Sun Bin was a Chinese military strategist of the Warring States period, said to be a descendant of Sun Wu, author of The Art of War. Mutilated through the jealousy of the Wei general Pang Juan, he escaped to Qi and advised the general Tian Ji, defeating Wei at Guiling and Maling.

shuihudi.s: Shuihudi is an archaeological site in Yunmeng County, Hubei, China. In 1975 a tomb there belonging to a local Qin official named Xi yielded more than a thousand bamboo slips with Qin statutes, legal procedures, administrative rules, a chronicle and almanacs for choosing lucky…

sawankhalok-ware.s: Sawankhalok ware is the glazed stoneware made at the kilns of Si Satchanalai, near Sawankhalok in north-central Thailand, from about the fourteenth to the sixteenth century. It includes green celadons, brown and white wares and pieces painted in iron black under the glaze.

sharif-ul-hashim-of-sulu.s: Sharif ul-Hashim, also called Sayyid Abu Bakr, is credited in Sulu tradition as the founder and first sultan of the Sulu Sultanate in the mid-fifteenth century. Said in the Sulu genealogies to be an Arab scholar who came by way of Johor, he married the daughter of Rajah…

simunul.s: Simunul is an island and municipality in the province of Tawi-Tawi in the southern Philippines. According to Sulu tradition, the missionary Karim ul-Makhdum landed there in the late fourteenth century and founded a mosque at Tubig Indangan, regarded as the oldest in the…

sanghyang-siksa-kandang-karesian.s: The Sanghyang Siksa Kandang Karesian is an Old Sundanese manuscript dated 1518, from the Sunda Kingdom of western Java. Written as a book of instruction, it sets out religious duties, moral rules and the practical knowledge expected of different ranks and occupations, from…

sanghyang-tapak-inscription.s: The Sanghyang Tapak inscriptions are four stones found near Cibadak in Sukabumi, West Java, dated to 1030 CE. They record that the Sundanese king Sri Jayabupati declared a stretch of the river sacred, forbade fishing there and called down curses on anyone who broke the ban.

sri-jayabupati.s: Sri Jayabupati was a king of Sunda in western Java in the early eleventh century, known from the Sanghyang Tapak inscriptions of 1030 near Sukabumi. In them he declared a section of river sacred and forbade fishing there under threat of curses.

surawisesa.s: Surawisesa was king of Sunda in western Java from 1521 to about 1535, the son and successor of Sri Baduga Maharaja. He sought Portuguese help against the rising Muslim sultanates, but Banten and the port of Sunda Kalapa fell to forces from Demak and Cirebon in the 1520s.

sranan-tongo.s: Sranan Tongo is an English-based creole language that arose among enslaved Africans in Suriname in the seventeenth century, during the English period of the colony, and later absorbed many Dutch and Portuguese words. It became the common language of the country's many ethnic…

suriname-river.s: The Suriname River flows about 480 kilometres north from the interior of Suriname to the Atlantic, passing Paramaribo near its mouth, where it is joined by the Commewijne. The first lasting English colony was founded on its banks in 1650, and plantations and the Jewish…

second-anglo-dutch-war.s: The Second Anglo-Dutch War was a naval and colonial war between England and the Dutch Republic, fought from 1665 to 1667 over trade and overseas possessions. After English gains such as New Amsterdam in 1664, the Dutch won the Four Days' Battle, raided the Medway in 1667 and…

society-of-suriname.s: The Society of Suriname was a chartered company formed in 1683 by the Dutch West India Company, the city of Amsterdam and Cornelis van Aerssen van Sommelsdijck, each holding a third, to own and govern the colony of Suriname. Its directors in Amsterdam appointed the governor,…

southern-african-customs-union.s: The Southern African Customs Union, established in 1910 with the Union of South Africa, is the oldest existing customs union in the world. Its members are South Africa, Botswana, Lesotho, Namibia and Eswatini, which share a common external tariff and divide the pooled customs…

swaziland-conventions.s: The Swaziland Conventions were three agreements between Britain and the South African Republic (Transvaal) on the status of Swaziland, concluded in 1890, 1893 and 1894. The first set up a joint administration, while the third made Swaziland a protectorate of the South African…

swazi-language.s: Swazi, or siSwati, is a Bantu language of the Nguni group, closely related to Zulu. It is an official language of Eswatini alongside English and one of the official languages of South Africa, where it is spoken especially in Mpumalanga.

swiss-banking-act-of-1934.s: The Swiss Banking Act of 1934, the Federal Act on Banks and Savings Banks, was the first federal law regulating Swiss banks, passed after the banking crises of the early 1930s. Its article 47 made the disclosure of client information by bank employees a criminal offence,…

sonderbund.s: The Sonderbund was a defensive league formed in 1845 by seven Catholic and conservative Swiss cantons, Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Zug, Fribourg and Valais, against the liberal and Protestant majority. The federal Diet declared it contrary to the Federal Treaty and…

sonderbund-war.s: The Sonderbund War was a brief civil war in Switzerland in November 1847, in which the federal army under General Guillaume-Henri Dufour defeated the Sonderbund, a league of seven Catholic cantons, in under a month and with roughly a hundred dead. It was the last armed…

sweet-dew-incident.s: The Sweet Dew Incident was a failed attempt in 835 by the Tang emperor Wenzong and his officials Li Xun and Zheng Zhu to destroy the power of the palace eunuchs. The eunuchs were to be lured to view sweet dew, an auspicious omen, and killed, but they discovered the ambush and…

serengeti.s: The Serengeti is a vast ecosystem of grassland and savanna in northern Tanzania, extending into Kenya as the Maasai Mara. It is famous for the annual migration of more than a million wildebeest, together with zebras and gazelles, and for its lions and other predators.

solomon-mahlangu-freedom-college.s: The Solomon Mahlangu Freedom College was a school founded by the African National Congress in 1978 at Mazimbu near Morogoro in Tanzania, on land given by the Tanzanian government, to educate young South Africans who had fled after the Soweto uprising of 1976. It was named…

sierra-de-las-navajas.s: The Sierra de las Navajas is a range of hills near Pachuca in the Mexican state of Hidalgo, the main source of the distinctive green obsidian of Mesoamerica. Teotihuacan controlled and worked this obsidian, and green blades and points made from it travelled widely; the Aztecs…

spearthrower-owl.s: Spearthrower Owl is the name given by scholars to a powerful lord named in Maya inscriptions as the father of Yax Nuun Ayiin I, who became king of Tikal in 379 after the arrival of Siyaj K'ak'. His name glyph combines an owl and a spear-thrower, emblems associated with…

shantarakshita.s: Shantarakshita was an Indian Buddhist philosopher and abbot of the great monastery of Nalanda who was invited to Tibet by the emperor Trisong Detsen in the eighth century. He helped found Samye, the first Buddhist monastery in Tibet, around 779, and ordained the first Tibetan…

sharaf-al-din-ali-yazdi.s: Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi was a Persian historian and poet of the Timurid court, born in Yazd. His Zafarnama ('Book of Victory'), completed around 1425 for Shah Rukh's son Ibrahim Sultan, is a polished panegyric history of Timur's life and conquests.

shimabara-rebellion.s: The Shimabara Rebellion was an uprising of peasants, many of them Christians, and masterless samurai on the Shimabara Peninsula and the Amakusa islands of Kyushu in 1637–1638, provoked by heavy taxation, famine and persecution. Led nominally by the youth Amakusa Shirō, the…

shimoda.s: Shimoda is a port town at the tip of the Izu Peninsula in Shizuoka Prefecture, Japan. Under the Convention of Kanagawa of 1854 it was one of the two ports opened to American ships, and the first American consul to Japan, Townsend Harris, set up his consulate there in 1856.

sugita-genpaku.s: Sugita Genpaku was a Japanese physician and scholar of rangaku, or Dutch learning. After watching a dissection in Edo in 1771 that confirmed the accuracy of a Dutch anatomy book, he and his colleagues translated it as the Kaitai Shinsho, published in 1774.

saint-basils-cathedral.s: Saint Basil's Cathedral, formally the Cathedral of the Intercession of the Most Holy Theotokos on the Moat, stands on Red Square in Moscow. Ivan IV had it built in 1555–1561 to commemorate the capture of Kazan and Astrakhan, and its cluster of chapels crowned with colourful…

sea-of-okhotsk.s: The Sea of Okhotsk is a marginal sea of the north-western Pacific Ocean, enclosed by the Kamchatka Peninsula, the Kuril Islands, Hokkaido, Sakhalin and the Siberian coast. Cossacks under Ivan Moskvitin reached it in 1639, the first Russians to reach the Pacific, and the port…

semyon-dezhnev.s: Semyon Dezhnev was a Russian cossack explorer of Siberia. In 1648 he sailed from the mouth of the Kolyma River round the north-eastern tip of Asia into the Pacific, passing through the strait between Asia and America eighty years before Vitus Bering.

sobornoe-ulozhenie.s: The Sobornoe Ulozhenie was the law code of the Tsardom of Russia adopted by an assembly of the land in 1649 under Tsar Alexis, after the Salt Riot of 1648. Its 25 chapters codified criminal, civil and administrative law, abolished time limits on the recovery of runaway…

swarup-singh-of-mewar.s: Swarup Singh was Maharana of Mewar from 1842 to 1861. He tried to restore the state's finances and to curb the power of his nobles, and during the Indian Rebellion of 1857 he remained loyal to the British, sheltering European refugees from Neemuch on the island palace of Jag…

sahibdin.s: Sahibdin was a Muslim painter at the court of Mewar in the mid-seventeenth century and the leading artist of the Udaipur school under Maharana Jagat Singh I. His works include a Ragamala series of 1628 and illustrated manuscripts of the Bhagavata Purana and the Ramayana, among…

sanga-archaeological-site.s: Sanga is an archaeological site on the shores of Lake Kisale in the Upemba Depression of Katanga, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where excavations from 1957 uncovered large cemeteries of the Kisalian and Kabambian periods. Dating from about the eighth century…

shrinathji.s: Shrinathji is a form of the Hindu god Krishna depicted as a seven-year-old child lifting Govardhan Hill, worshipped as the principal deity of the Pushtimarg tradition founded by Vallabhacharya. The image, said to have been found on Govardhan Hill near Mathura, was moved in…

sisodia-dynasty.s: The Sisodias are a Rajput clan, a branch of the Guhila dynasty named after the village of Sisoda, that ruled Mewar from the recovery of Chittor by Hammir Singh around 1326 until 1949. Its rulers, among them Rana Kumbha, Rana Sanga and Maharana Pratap, reigned from Chittor and…

south-sudan.s: South Sudan is a landlocked country in east-central Africa with its capital at Juba. It became independent from Sudan on 9 July 2011 after a referendum held under the peace agreement of 2005 that ended Sudan's second civil war.

state-research-bureau.s: The State Research Bureau was the secret police and intelligence agency of Idi Amin's regime in Uganda from 1971 to 1979. Based at Nakasero in Kampala, it arrested, tortured and killed large numbers of suspected opponents, and with the Public Safety Unit and the Military…

sol-plaatje.s: Sol Plaatje was a South African journalist, writer and political leader, a founder and the first general secretary of the South African Native National Congress in 1912. He went with its delegation to Britain to protest against the Natives Land Act and described the law's…

south-africa-act-1909.s: The South Africa Act 1909 was the act of the British Parliament that united the Cape Colony, Natal, the Transvaal and the Orange River Colony as the Union of South Africa, which came into being on 31 May 1910. Based on a constitution drafted by a national convention of the…

south-african-party.s: The South African Party was a political party founded in 1911 by Louis Botha and Jan Smuts, whose leaders governed the Union of South Africa from 1910 to 1924. It sought reconciliation between Afrikaners and English-speaking South Africans within the British Empire and…

status-of-the-union-act-1934.s: The Status of the Union Act of 1934 was a law of the South African parliament that declared the Union a sovereign independent state and made its own parliament supreme, incorporating the Statute of Westminster into South African law. Passed by J. B. M. Hertzog's government, it…

south-east-england.s: South East England is one of the official regions of England, surrounding London and including counties such as Kent, Surrey, Sussex, Hampshire, Oxfordshire and Buckinghamshire. Prosperous and densely populated, it gained new industries and suburbs between the world wars and…

south-wales.s: South Wales is the southern part of Wales, including Cardiff, Swansea, Newport and the industrial valleys. From the nineteenth century its coalfield and its iron and steel works made it one of the most industrialised regions of Britain; the collapse of coal exports brought…

supermarine-spitfire.s: The Supermarine Spitfire was a British single-seat fighter aircraft designed by R. J. Mitchell and first flown in 1936. With the more numerous Hawker Hurricane it defended Britain in the Battle of Britain in 1940, and in successive versions it served with the Royal Air Force…

sheba-son-of-bichri.s: Sheba son of Bichri was a Benjamite who, according to the Hebrew Bible, led a revolt of the northern tribes of Israel against King David soon after the rebellion of Absalom. Pursued by David's commander Joab to the town of Abel-beth-maacah, he was beheaded by its inhabitants,…

saul.s: Saul was, according to the Hebrew Bible, the first king of Israel, a man of the tribe of Benjamin anointed by the prophet Samuel who ruled from Gibeah, traditionally in the late eleventh century BCE. He fought the Philistines, Ammonites and Amalekites, quarrelled with Samuel…

song-of-songs.s: The Song of Songs, also called the Song of Solomon, is a book of the Hebrew Bible consisting of love poems in the voices of a woman and her lover. Traditionally attributed to Solomon and read in Judaism and Christianity as an allegory of the love between God and Israel or…

sironj.s: Sironj is a town in the Vidisha district of Madhya Pradesh, India. Long a centre of trade and cotton printing on the route between northern India and the Deccan, it later formed a detached part of the princely state of Tonk in Rajputana, and under the States Reorganisation Act…

states-reorganisation-act-1956.s: The States Reorganisation Act 1956 was a law of the Indian Parliament that redrew the boundaries of India's states largely along linguistic lines, following the report of the States Reorganisation Commission. From 1 November 1956 it abolished the distinction between Part A, B…

second-continental-congress.s: The Second Continental Congress was the assembly of delegates from the thirteen American colonies that met from May 1775, after fighting had begun at Lexington and Concord. It created the Continental Army under George Washington, adopted the Declaration of Independence on 4…

shays-rebellion.s: Shays' Rebellion was an armed uprising in western Massachusetts in 1786–1787 by indebted farmers, led by the war veteran Daniel Shays, against high taxes and the seizure of property for debt. Its suppression by a state-funded militia exposed the weakness of the national…

siege-of-yorktown.s: The Siege of Yorktown, in Virginia, was the last major battle of the American Revolutionary War. From late September to 19 October 1781 a combined American and French army under George Washington and the Comte de Rochambeau, with a French fleet blocking relief by sea, besieged…

sin-leqi-unninni.s: Sin-leqi-unninni was a Babylonian scholar and incantation priest of Uruk, traditionally credited with compiling the Standard Babylonian version of the Epic of Gilgamesh in the late second millennium BCE. Scholarly families of Uruk in the Seleucid period claimed descent from…

santiago.s: Santiago is the capital and largest city of Chile, in the central valley at the foot of the Andes. It was founded on 12 February 1541 by the Spanish conquistador Pedro de Valdivia and became the seat of the governors and, from 1609, of the royal audiencia of Chile.

sadashiva-raya.s: Sadashiva Raya was emperor of Vijayanagara from 1542 to about 1570, the last ruler of the Tuluva dynasty. Placed on the throne as a youth, he had no real power: the regent Aliya Rama Raya governed in his name.

saluva-narasimha.s: Saluva Narasimha Deva Raya was a Vijayanagara general and governor of Chandragiri who seized the throne from the last weak Sangama ruler around 1485, founding the short-lived Saluva dynasty. He fought the Gajapatis of Odisha and the Bahmani Sultanate to restore the empire's…

sangama-dynasty.s: The Sangama dynasty was the first ruling house of the Vijayanagara Empire, founded around 1336 by the brothers Harihara I and Bukka I, sons of Sangama. Its kings conquered the Hoysala lands and the Madurai Sultanate, fought long wars with the Bahmani Sultanate and reached…

sayana.s: Sayana was a Sanskrit scholar and minister at the court of the early Vijayanagara kings, especially Bukka I and Harihara II. He and his collaborators wrote commentaries on all four Vedas, among them the Vedarthaprakasha on the Rigveda, which became the standard traditional…

sriranga-iii.s: Sriranga III was the last emperor of Vijayanagara, of the Aravidu dynasty, who came to the throne in 1642. He tried to reassert royal authority over the nayakas, but his own vassals and the armies of the Bijapur and Golconda sultanates defeated him, and by about 1646 he had…

suvar.s: Suvar was a medieval town of Volga Bulgaria, south of the Kama in present-day Tatarstan, named after the Suvar, one of the tribes that formed the Bulgar state. In the tenth century it was one of the main towns of the Bulgars, a centre of crafts and trade, and its rulers minted…

someshvara-i.s: Someshvara I, also called Ahavamalla, was king of the Western Chalukya Empire from 1042 to 1068. He made Kalyani his capital and fought a long series of wars with the Cholas, in which the Chola king Rajadhiraja I was killed at Koppam in 1054, but he was later defeated by…

someshvara-ii.s: Someshvara II was king of the Western Chalukya Empire from 1068 to 1076, the eldest son of Someshvara I. His reign was troubled by conflict with the Cholas and by the rivalry of his younger brother Vikramaditya, who held the southern provinces from Banavasi and allied with the…

someshvara-iii.s: Someshvara III, also called Bhulokamalla, was king of the Western Chalukya Empire from 1126 to 1138, the son of Vikramaditya VI. His reign was mostly peaceful, though the Hoysalas and other feudatories grew more independent.

son-of-heaven.s: Son of Heaven (tianzi) was a title of the Chinese ruler, first used by the kings of the Western Zhou, expressing the idea that the ruler held a mandate from Heaven to govern all under Heaven. Emperors of China used it until the end of the Qing dynasty in 1912, and it was also…

sadeq-khan-zand.s: Sadeq Khan Zand was a brother of Karim Khan Zand and his leading general. He commanded the siege of Basra in 1775–1776, which forced the Ottoman garrison to surrender, and governed the city until 1779.

senzangakhona.s: Senzangakhona was chief of the small Zulu chiefdom in what is now KwaZulu-Natal in the late 18th and early 19th centuries. He was the father of three Zulu kings, Shaka, Dingane and Mpande.

sulmona.s: Sulmona, the ancient Sulmo, is a town in the Peligna valley of Abruzzo, central Italy, originally one of the main towns of the Paeligni. It became a Roman municipium after the Social War and is best known as the birthplace of the poet Ovid in 43 BCE.

shwezigon-pagoda.s: The Shwezigon Pagoda is a gilded Buddhist stupa at Nyaung-U near Bagan in Myanmar, begun by King Anawrahta of Pagan and completed by Kyansittha around 1102. It is said to enshrine relics of the Buddha, and its bell-shaped form became the model for many later Burmese stupas.

savak.s: SAVAK was the secret police and intelligence service of Iran under Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi, founded in 1957 with American and Israeli help. It watched, imprisoned and tortured political opponents, and its reputation for brutality fuelled hatred of the regime.

simmern.s: Simmern is a small town in the Hunsrück hills of Rhineland-Palatinate, Germany. From 1410 it was the seat of the Palatinate-Simmern line of the Wittelsbachs, which in 1559 inherited the Electoral Palatinate.

shatrunjaya.s: Shatrunjaya is a sacred hill above Palitana in Gujarat, India, one of the holiest pilgrimage sites of the Jains. Its two summits are covered with more than 800 temples built over many centuries by merchant patrons, many of them rebuilt after the 16th century, and the main…

sirpur-chhattisgarh.s: Sirpur is a village on the Mahanadi river in Mahasamund district of Chhattisgarh, India, on the site of ancient Shripura, capital of the Panduvamshi kings of Dakshina Kosala from the 6th century. Excavations have uncovered Hindu temples, Buddhist monasteries, a Jain shrine and…

solunto.s: Solunto is an archaeological site on Monte Catalfano near Santa Flavia, east of Palermo in Sicily, on the site of ancient Soloeis or Solus. A Phoenician foundation, it was one of the Punic towns of western Sicily with Motya and Panormus, as Thucydides records.

surat-thani.s: Surat Thani is a city in southern Thailand, capital of Surat Thani province, near the mouth of the Tapi river on the Bay of Bandon. Formerly known as Ban Don, it received its present name, meaning 'city of good people', from King Vajiravudh in 1915.

sangramaraja.s: Sangramaraja was king of Kashmir from 1003 to 1028 and founder of the Lohara dynasty. A nephew of Queen Didda from the hill state of Lohara, he was chosen by her as heir.

selim-iii.s: Selim III was Ottoman sultan from 1789 to 1807. After defeats by Russia and Austria he launched the Nizam-ı Cedid, a programme of military and fiscal reform built around a new European-style army, and opened permanent embassies in European capitals.

souliotes.s: The Souliotes were an Orthodox Christian community of Albanian origin from the mountains of Souli in Epirus, in north-western Greece. Organised in clans, they kept a fierce autonomy under Ottoman rule and resisted Ali Pasha of Ioannina for years until they surrendered in 1803;…

sigehard-of-aquileia.s: Sigehard was Patriarch of Aquileia from 1068 to 1077. During the Investiture Controversy he supported Emperor Henry IV, who in 1077 rewarded him with the county of Friuli, followed soon after by Istria and Carniola.

sekhukhune-i.s: Sekhukhune I was king of the Pedi in the north-east of present-day South Africa from 1861 to 1879. From his mountain capital at Tsate he resisted the Boer South African Republic, whose army failed to defeat him in 1876.

sotho-tswana-peoples.s: The Sotho-Tswana peoples are a group of Bantu-speaking peoples of southern Africa, including the Sotho of Lesotho, the Tswana of Botswana and the Pedi of north-eastern South Africa. Their closely related languages form the Sotho-Tswana branch of the Bantu family.

steelpoort-river.s: The Steelpoort River is a river in Mpumalanga and Limpopo provinces of South Africa and a tributary of the Olifants. Its valley, in the region known as Sekhukhuneland, was the heartland of the Pedi kingdom from the 17th century.

stalinism.s: Stalinism is the system of rule and the policies associated with Joseph Stalin, leader of the Soviet Union from the late 1920s until 1953. It combined a one-party state and a personality cult with forced collectivisation of agriculture, rapid industrialisation through central…

sassacus.s: Sassacus was the grand sachem of the Pequot in south-eastern Connecticut, succeeding his father Tatobem in the mid-1630s. He led the Pequot during the Pequot War of 1636–1637 against the English colonists and their Mohegan and Narragansett allies.

saibai.s: Saibai was the first wife of Shivaji, founder of the Maratha state. A daughter of the Nimbalkar family of Phaltan, she married Shivaji as a child in 1640, linking his family to one of the oldest Maratha houses.

satara.s: Satara is a city in western Maharashtra, India, near the confluence of the Krishna and Venna rivers, overlooked by the hill fort of Ajinkyatara. In the 18th century it was the seat of the Maratha Chhatrapatis from Shahu onwards, while real power passed to the Peshwas at Pune.

syria-palaestina.s: Syria Palaestina was the Roman province formed when the emperor Hadrian renamed the province of Judaea after crushing the Bar Kokhba revolt in 135 CE. The new name, taken from the old Greek term for the coastal land of the Philistines, removed Judaea from the map, and Jews…

south-picene-language.s: South Picene is an extinct Sabellic language of the Italic family, known from about two dozen inscriptions of the 6th to 4th centuries BCE found in the Marche and Abruzzo, Italy. It was written in a distinctive alphabet adapted from Etruscan, and its texts, mostly on funerary…

seventh-day-adventist-church.s: The Seventh-day Adventist Church is a Protestant Christian denomination formally organised in the United States in 1863, which keeps Saturday as the Sabbath and emphasises the imminent Second Coming of Christ. It grew through missions into a worldwide church with millions of…

syarif-muhammad-alkadrie.s: Syarif Muhammad Alkadrie was sultan of Pontianak in West Kalimantan, Indonesia, from 1895 until his death in 1944. His long reign under Dutch rule saw the growth of Pontianak as a trading town.

sethlans.s: Sethlans was the Etruscan god of fire and metalworking, the counterpart of the Greek Hephaestus and the Roman Vulcan. He is shown on bronze mirrors and coins as a smith with hammer and tongs, often wearing a workman's cap.

salagama.s: The Salagama are a Sinhalese caste of the south-western coast of Sri Lanka, traditionally associated with weaving and later with peeling cinnamon. Under the Portuguese and then the Dutch, who drew great revenue from the island's cinnamon, they were required to collect and peel…

shama-ghana.s: Shama is a coastal town in the Western Region of Ghana, at the mouth of the Pra river. The Portuguese built a trading fort there in the 16th century, and the Dutch, who took it in 1640, rebuilt it as Fort San Sebastian.

samora-machel.s: Samora Machel was a Mozambican revolutionary who commanded FRELIMO's guerrilla army and became its leader after Eduardo Mondlane's assassination in 1969. He was the first President of independent Mozambique from 1975, building a one-party socialist state while supporting…

solor.s: Solor is a small island in the Lesser Sunda Islands of eastern Indonesia, east of Flores. Dominican friars built a fort there in 1566, and it became the Portuguese base for the sandalwood trade with Timor and for missionary work in the region.

sele-river.s: The Sele is a river of Campania in southern Italy, flowing about 64 kilometres from the Apennines to the Gulf of Salerno. The Greek colony of Poseidonia, later Paestum, stood on the plain south of its mouth, where an important sanctuary of Hera, the Heraion at Foce del Sele,…

second-temple-of-hera-paestum.s: The Second Temple of Hera at Paestum in southern Italy is a Doric temple built around 460 BCE, long known as the Temple of Neptune. Standing beside the older temple called the Basilica, it is among the best-preserved Greek temples anywhere, with almost all of its columns and…

strata-marcella-abbey.s: Strata Marcella Abbey was a Cistercian monastery on the River Severn near Welshpool in mid Wales, founded in 1170 by Owain Cyfeiliog, prince of southern Powys. It was a centre of Welsh religious life until its dissolution in 1536, and only its foundations survive.

sanctuary-of-fortuna-primigenia.s: The Sanctuary of Fortuna Primigenia was a great temple complex of the goddess Fortuna at Praeneste, modern Palestrina, east of Rome. It was famous for an oracle in which lots were drawn, and in the late 2nd century BCE it was rebuilt as a series of monumental terraces climbing…

souq-ukaz.s: Souq Ukaz was the most famous annual fair of pre-Islamic Arabia, held during the sacred months near Ta'if, south-east of Mecca. Besides trade, it hosted poetry contests among the tribes, where celebrated odes were recited.

saint-vitus.s: Saint Vitus was an early Christian martyr from Sicily, said to have died in the persecution under Diocletian. His relics were brought from Saint-Denis to the Saxon abbey of Corvey in 836, spreading his cult across central Europe, and he is the patron of Prague's cathedral.

sturmi.s: Sturmi, or Sturm, was a Bavarian-born disciple of Saint Boniface and the founder and first abbot of the abbey of Fulda, established in 744. He made Fulda a model Benedictine house and took part in Charlemagne's mission among the Saxons.

stade.s: Stade is a town on the lower Elbe in Lower Saxony, Germany, west of Hamburg. A Hanseatic port and a residence of the archbishops of Bremen, it was from 1648 the seat of the Swedish government of the duchies of Bremen and Verden.

saben-abbey.s: Säben Abbey is a Benedictine convent on a rock above Klausen in South Tyrol, Italy. The site was the seat of the earliest bishops of the region from late antiquity until they moved to Brixen around 990, and nuns have occupied it since 1686.

sigismund-archduke-of-austria.s: Sigismund, Archduke of Austria, ruled Tyrol and Further Austria from 1446 to 1490. Silver from the mines at Schwaz made him rich, earning him the name 'rich in coin'.

saxony-anhalt.s: Saxony-Anhalt is a state of central Germany, with Magdeburg as its capital. It was formed in 1947 from the Prussian Province of Saxony and the Free State of Anhalt, dissolved in 1952 and re-established in 1990.

stolpen.s: Stolpen is a small town east of Dresden in Saxony, Germany, crowned by a castle on a basalt hill. It was a residence of the bishops of Meissen until 1559, when it passed to the Electorate of Saxony, and Augustus the Strong's former mistress Countess Cosel was confined there…

st-stephens-cathedral-passau.s: St. Stephen's Cathedral in Passau, Bavaria, is the baroque cathedral of the bishops of Passau, rebuilt after a fire of 1662 by Italian architects led by Carlo Lurago. Its organ, with nearly 18,000 pipes, is one of the largest church organs in the world.

schonberg-mecklenburg.s: Schönberg is a small town in north-western Mecklenburg, Germany, near Lübeck. It was a residence of the bishops of Ratzeburg and, after the secularisation of the bishopric in 1648, the seat of government of the Principality of Ratzeburg, a detached part of Mecklenburg-Strelitz.

saverne.s: Saverne (German Zabern) is a town in Alsace, France, where the road from Strasbourg crosses the Vosges into Lorraine. After 1262 it was the main residence of the bishops of Strasbourg, whose great Château des Rohan was rebuilt there from 1779.

stanislaus-hosius.s: Stanislaus Hosius was a Polish churchman and theologian, bishop of Warmia from 1551 and a cardinal from 1561. A leading figure of the Counter-Reformation, he wrote a widely read defence of Catholic doctrine and presided as papal legate over the final sessions of the Council of…

schonborn-family.s: The Schönborn are a German noble family from the Rhineland who rose to great power in the church in the 17th and 18th centuries. Members of the family were electors of Mainz and Trier and prince-bishops of Würzburg, Bamberg, Speyer and Constance.

shkumbin.s: The Shkumbin is a river in central Albania, about 180 kilometres long, flowing west past Elbasan to the Adriatic. In Roman times the Via Egnatia followed its valley, making it the main route from the Adriatic coast into the Balkans.

shughnan.s: Shughnan is a mountain district of the western Pamirs on both banks of the Panj river, divided between Tajikistan, where Khorog is its main town, and Afghanistan. Its people speak Shughni, an Eastern Iranian language, and are mostly Ismaili Muslims.

sineus.s: Sineus is one of the three Varangian brothers who, according to the Russian Primary Chronicle, were invited by the Slavic and Finnic peoples of the north in 862 to rule over them. While Rurik settled at Novgorod and Truvor at Izborsk, Sineus is said to have taken Beloozero,…

sarre-department.s: Sarre was a department of the French Republic and Empire on the left bank of the Rhine, created in 1798 from occupied German lands, with its capital at Trier. It covered the Saar, the Hunsrück and the Moselle valley.

sofia.s: Sofia is the capital and largest city of Bulgaria, at the foot of Mount Vitosha. As Serdica it was a Thracian and then Roman city, where Emperor Galerius issued an edict of toleration for Christians in 311.

sophia-of-hanover.s: Sophia of Hanover was a princess of the Palatinate, daughter of Frederick V and Elizabeth Stuart, who married Ernest Augustus, later Elector of Hanover. The Act of Settlement of 1701 named her and her Protestant descendants heirs to the English throne.

schillingsfurst.s: Schillingsfürst is a small town in Middle Franconia, Bavaria, on a hill near Rothenburg ob der Tauber. It was the seat of the Catholic Hohenlohe-Schillingsfürst branch, raised to princely rank in 1744, whose baroque palace dominates the town.

saxony.s: Saxony is a name that has moved across Germany. It first meant the lands of the Saxons in the north-west, between the Rhine, the Elbe and the North Sea, conquered by Charlemagne and later ruled as the Duchy of Saxony.

shahrisabz.s: Shahrisabz is a city in southern Uzbekistan, south of Samarkand, in the Kashkadarya valley. Known in earlier times as Kesh, it was a Sogdian principality, and Timur was born nearby in 1336.

semen-olelkovich.s: Semen Olelkovich was the last Prince of Kiev, ruling from 1455 to 1470 as a vassal of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. A son of Olelko and a descendant of Algirdas, he kept an Orthodox court and rebuilt the Dormition Cathedral of the Kiev Pechersk Lavra.

saarbrucken.s: Saarbrücken is the capital of the German state of Saarland, on the Saar river near the French border. Seat of medieval counts, it passed in the 14th century to a line of the House of Nassau, whose 18th-century princes made it a baroque residence with the Ludwigskirche.

st-wendel.s: St. Wendel is a town in northern Saarland, Germany, named after Saint Wendelin, an early medieval hermit whose shrine in its Gothic basilica drew pilgrims. From 1816 to 1834 it was the capital of the Saxe-Coburg Principality of Lichtenberg, where unrest in 1832 led to military…

sophia-dorothea-of-celle.s: Sophia Dorothea of Celle was the only child of George William, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, and was married in 1682 to her cousin George Louis of Hanover, later George I of Great Britain. After her affair with Count Philip Christoph von Königsmarck, who vanished in 1694, the…

suceava.s: Suceava is a city in north-eastern Romania, in the historical region of Bukovina. It was the capital of the Principality of Moldavia from about 1388 until 1564, when the court moved to Iași, and its fortress withstood an Ottoman siege under Mehmed II in 1476.

strumica.s: Strumica is a town in south-eastern North Macedonia, in the valley of the Strumica river near the borders with Bulgaria and Greece. Known in antiquity as Astraion and in Byzantine times as Tiberiopolis, it changed hands repeatedly between Byzantium, Bulgaria and Serbia in the…

schleiz.s: Schleiz is a small town in the Saale-Orla district of Thuringia, Germany. From the 17th century it was the residence of a branch of the House of Reuss Younger Line, whose counts and later princes ruled Reuss-Schleiz from its palace until the lands were united in 1848.

suzdal.s: Suzdal is a small town in Vladimir Oblast, Russia, on the Kamenka river. First recorded in 1024, it became the seat of Yuri Dolgoruky in the 12th century, giving its name to the principality of Rostov-Suzdal and later Vladimir-Suzdal.

schola-medica-salernitana.s: The Schola Medica Salernitana at Salerno in southern Italy was the first great medical school of medieval Europe, flourishing from the 10th to the 13th century. It combined Greek, Latin and Arabic medical learning, helped by the translations of Constantine the African, and…

sichelgaita.s: Sichelgaita was a Lombard princess, daughter of Guaimar IV of Salerno, who married the Norman leader Robert Guiscard in 1058. She accompanied him on campaign, and Anna Komnene describes her riding armoured into battle at Dyrrhachium in 1081.

siconulf.s: Siconulf was the first Prince of Salerno. Brother of the murdered Prince Sicard of Benevento, he was proclaimed prince at Salerno in 839 and waged a decade-long civil war against Radelchis I.

samtskhe.s: Samtskhe is a historic upland region of southern Georgia on the upper Kura, centred on Akhaltsikhe and including the cave monastery of Vardzia. From the 13th century its Jaqeli atabegs ruled it as a largely independent principality; it then fell under Ottoman rule in the 16th…

sargis-i-jaqeli.s: Sargis I Jaqeli was the ruler of Samtskhe in southern Georgia in the second half of the 13th century and founder of the principality's independence. By securing direct recognition from the Mongol Ilkhanate, he placed his lands outside the authority of the Georgian kings, and…

steinhuder-meer.s: The Steinhuder Meer is the largest lake in north-western Germany, about 30 square kilometres in area but only a few metres deep, lying north-west of Hanover in Lower Saxony. Count William of Schaumburg-Lippe built the artificial island fortress of Wilhelmstein in it in the 1760s.

scheinfeld.s: Scheinfeld is a small town in Middle Franconia, Bavaria, in the Steigerwald hills. Above it stands Schwarzenberg Castle, from which the lords of Seinsheim took the name Schwarzenberg in the 15th century.

sretenje-constitution.s: The Sretenje Constitution was the first constitution of modern Serbia, adopted at Kragujevac on 15 February 1835, the feast of Sretenje (Candlemas). Drawn up to limit the autocratic rule of Prince Miloš Obrenović, it divided power between the prince, a state council and an…

serpukhov.s: Serpukhov is a city in Moscow Oblast, Russia, where the Nara joins the Oka, about 100 kilometres south of Moscow. First recorded in the will of Ivan Kalita in 1339, it became the seat of an appanage whose prince Vladimir the Bold fortified it and founded the Vysotsky Monastery.

sigebert-iii.s: Sigebert III was the Merovingian king of Austrasia, the eastern Frankish kingdom, from 633 or 634 until his death. Son of Dagobert I, he came to the throne as a child, and real power lay with his mayors of the palace, above all Grimoald.

stavelot.s: Stavelot is a small town on the Amblève in the province of Liège, Belgium. It grew around the abbey founded by Saint Remaclus around 650, whose abbots ruled the ecclesiastical principality of Stavelot-Malmedy until the French Revolution.

stavelot-triptych.s: The Stavelot Triptych is a portable reliquary altarpiece of gilded copper and enamel made by Mosan goldsmiths at the abbey of Stavelot around 1156 to 1158, probably for Abbot Wibald. It enclosed relics of the True Cross, and its enamel scenes tell the legend of the Cross under…
