sandilch.s: Sandilch was a ruler of the Utigurs, a nomadic people of the steppe east of the Don, in the mid-6th century. Known from the Byzantine historians Procopius and Agathias, he was persuaded by Emperor Justinian, with gifts and subsidies, to attack the related Kutrigurs in 551 and…

suyya.s: Suyya was a minister and engineer of King Avantivarman of Kashmir in the 9th century. According to Kalhana's Rajatarangini, he cleared rocks that blocked the Jhelum, drained marshes, built embankments and diverted streams to irrigate new land, so that rice became abundant and…

sharof-rashidov.s: Sharof Rashidov was an Uzbek writer and politician who led the Communist Party of the Uzbek SSR as first secretary from 1959 until his death in 1983. He built a powerful patronage network and promised Moscow ever larger cotton harvests.

strathspey.s: Strathspey is the valley of the River Spey in north-east Scotland, running from the Cairngorms through towns such as Grantown-on-Spey and Aviemore towards the Moray Firth. Long the country of the Clan Grant, it is known for its pine forests, cattle droving and whisky…

second-buddhist-council.s: The Second Buddhist Council was an assembly of monks held at Vaishali, according to Buddhist tradition about a century after the death of the Buddha. It was called to judge ten practices of the monks of Vaishali, among them accepting gold and silver, which the elders condemned…

setubandha.s: The Setubandha ('Building of the Bridge'), also called Ravanavaho, is an epic poem in Maharashtri Prakrit attributed to the Vakataka king Pravarasena II. In fifteen cantos it tells the episode of the Ramayana in which Rama's army builds a bridge to Lanka and defeats Ravana.

second-vatican-council.s: The Second Vatican Council was the 21st ecumenical council of the Catholic Church, held in St. Peter's Basilica from 1962 to 1965. Opened by Pope John XXIII and concluded by Paul VI, it allowed the Mass to be celebrated in local languages, recognised religious freedom, opened…

saint-paulien.s: Saint-Paulien is a small town in the Haute-Loire department of south-central France, north of Le Puy-en-Velay. Under Roman rule, as Ruessium, it was the chief town of the Gallic Vellavi and the capital of their civitas.

schoemansdal.s: Schoemansdal was a Boer settlement in the Soutpansberg in the far north of the Transvaal, founded in 1848 by Andries Hendrik Potgieter's followers and later named after the commandant Stephanus Schoeman. It became a frontier centre of the ivory trade and the seat of the…

stato-da-mar.s: The Stato da Mar ('State of the Sea') was the collective name for the overseas possessions of the Republic of Venice, as distinct from its Italian mainland territories, the Domini di Terraferma. Built up from the 11th century and especially after the Fourth Crusade of 1204, it…

salamanca.s: Salamanca is a city in Castile and León, Spain, on the River Tormes. As Salmantica it was a town of the Vettones that Hannibal attacked in 220 BCE and later a Roman settlement on the road known as the Via de la Plata.

silius-italicus.s: Silius Italicus was a Roman senator and poet, consul in 68 CE, who wrote the Punica, an epic in seventeen books on the Second Punic War and the longest surviving Latin poem. Pliny the Younger described his wealthy retirement in Campania and his death by starvation when he fell…

sharri-kushuh.s: Sharri-Kushuh, born Piyassili, was a son of the Hittite king Suppiluliuma I, who made him king of Carchemish after capturing the city around 1325 BCE. As viceroy he oversaw the Hittite possessions in Syria and helped his brother Mursili II hold them, and his descendants…

sesebi.s: Sesebi is an archaeological site on the Nile in northern Sudan, between the Second and Third Cataracts. It was a walled Egyptian temple town founded under Akhenaten in the 14th century BCE, with temples, houses and storerooms laid out on a grid, and was still in use under Seti I.

soleb.s: Soleb is a site on the west bank of the Nile in northern Sudan, between the Second and Third Cataracts, with a great temple built by Amenhotep III in the 14th century BCE. Dedicated to Amun and to the king himself as a god, it is the largest Egyptian temple known in Nubia, and…

sebastian-de-eslava.s: Sebastián de Eslava was a Spanish general and viceroy of New Granada from 1740 to 1749. He directed the defence of Cartagena de Indias against the British attack of Admiral Edward Vernon in 1741, together with the admiral Blas de Lezo, and was rewarded with the title Marquis…

sigmaringen.s: Sigmaringen is a town on the upper Danube in Baden-Württemberg, Germany, dominated by a castle on a rock above the river. Granted to the counts of Hohenzollern by the Habsburgs in the 1530s, it became the seat of the Catholic Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen line, whose members later…

sita.s: Sita is the heroine of the Ramayana, wife of Rama and daughter of King Janaka of Videha, who in the epic found her in a furrow while ploughing. Her abduction by Ravana and her rescue drive the story.

shatapatha-brahmana.s: The Shatapatha Brahmana ('Brahmana of a hundred paths') is a Sanskrit prose text of the White Yajurveda, composed in the first half of the 1st millennium BCE and traditionally attributed to Yajnavalkya. It explains the Vedic sacrificial rites in detail and contains myths such…

saluva-dynasty.s: The Saluva dynasty was the second ruling house of the Vijayanagara Empire. Its founder, the general Saluva Narasimha, seized the throne from the last weak Sangama king in 1485 to defend the empire against the Gajapatis and the Bahmani Sultanate.

sabarkantha-district.s: Sabarkantha is a district of north-eastern Gujarat, India, named after the Sabarmati river, with its headquarters at Himmatnagar. It was formed in 1949 from Idar and many small princely states of the former Mahi Kantha Agency, which had been merged into Bombay Province, and…

saint-quentin.s: Saint-Quentin is a town on the Somme in the Aisne department of northern France. As Augusta Viromanduorum it was the Roman chief town of the Viromandui, and in the Middle Ages it was the seat of the counts of Vermandois, growing around the shrine of the martyr Quentin.

septimania.s: Septimania was the coastal region of south-western Gaul between the Rhône and the Pyrenees, around Narbonne, roughly modern Languedoc-Roussillon. It was the only part of Gaul the Visigoths kept after Vouillé in 507, was taken by the Umayyads around 720, and was conquered by…

seneslau.s: Seneslau was a Romanian voivode of the mid-13th century, known only from King Béla IV of Hungary's charter of 1247 to the Knights Hospitaller. The charter left his land, east of the Olt in what became Wallachia, to the Romanians as a tributary of the Hungarian crown, and…

satricum.s: Satricum was an ancient town of Latium, at Borgo Le Ferriere near Latina south of Rome, contested between Latins and Volsci in the 5th and 4th centuries BCE. Its temple of Mater Matuta yielded the Lapis Satricanus, a Latin inscription of about 500 BCE naming the companions of…

sora-lazio.s: Sora is a town on the Liri river in southern Lazio, Italy. Originally a Volscian town, it changed hands between Rome and the Samnites during the Second Samnite War and received a Latin colony in 303 BCE.

sebastien-rale.s: Sébastien Rale (1657–1724) was a French Jesuit missionary who worked among the Abenaki of the Wabanaki Confederacy from the 1690s, based for decades at the village of Norridgewock on the Kennebec River in present-day Maine. He compiled a dictionary of the Abenaki language and…

sowams.s: Sowams was the chief village of the Wampanoag sachem Massasoit in the early 17th century, at the head of Narragansett Bay in what is now Warren and Barrington, Rhode Island. Envoys from Plymouth Colony, among them Edward Winslow, visited Massasoit there in the 1620s.

sanaag.s: Sanaag is a region of northern Somalia on the Gulf of Aden, with its capital at Erigavo. It includes the Cal Madow mountains and the historic port of Las Khorey, and was the homeland of the Warsangali Sultanate.

sambhupura.s: Sambhupura was a city of ancient Cambodia on the Mekong, at or near present-day Sambor in Kratié Province. Known from Khmer inscriptions, it was the seat of a local dynasty in the 8th century, after Chenla had broken up into rival principalities, and it remained a religious…

shawnee.s: The Shawnee are an Algonquian-speaking Native American people who in the 18th century lived mainly in the Ohio country. They were among the strongest opponents of American expansion north of the Ohio River, forming part of the Western Confederacy under leaders such as Blue…

shravanabelagola.s: Shravanabelagola is a town in Hassan district, Karnataka, India, and one of the most important pilgrimage centres of Digambara Jainism. Tradition holds that the Maurya emperor Chandragupta and the monk Bhadrabahu ended their lives there.

sanmenxia.s: Sanmenxia is a city in western Henan province, China, on the Yellow River near the gorge that gives it its name. In the Zhou period it was the site of Shangyang, capital of the State of Guo, whose Shangcunling cemetery has yielded rich burials.

shangcunling-cemetery.s: The Shangcunling cemetery is an archaeological site at Sanmenxia in Henan, China, belonging to the State of Guo of the late Western Zhou and early Spring and Autumn periods. Excavated in the 1950s and again in the 1990s, it holds hundreds of tombs and chariot pits, including…

sudarshana-lake.s: Sudarshana Lake was an ancient reservoir near Junagadh in Saurashtra, Gujarat, built under the Maurya emperor Chandragupta by his governor Pushyagupta and improved under Ashoka. Its history is recorded in inscriptions on the Girnar rock: Rudradaman I of the Western Satraps…

su-dingfang.s: Su Dingfang (592–667) was a general of the Tang dynasty. In 657 he defeated Ashina Helu, the last khagan of the Western Turkic Khaganate, bringing the western steppe under Tang control.

suyab.s: Suyab was a Silk Road city in the Chu valley of northern Kyrgyzstan, at the site of Ak-Beshim near Tokmok. It served as a seat of the khagans of the Western Turkic Khaganate, where the pilgrim Xuanzang met Tong Yabghu around 630, and later of the Turgesh.

su-chuo.s: Su Chuo (498–546) was a Chinese official who served as chief adviser to Yuwen Tai, the regent of the Western Wei. He drafted the Six Articles, a programme for honest and efficient local government, and introduced systems of budgeting and household registration.

stilsko.s: Stilsko is an early medieval hillfort near the village of the same name south of Lviv in western Ukraine. Dating mainly from the 9th and 10th centuries, it enclosed an exceptionally large area within earthen ramparts, with dwellings, sanctuaries and burial mounds nearby.

sarai.s: Sarai was the capital of the Golden Horde on the lower Volga, founded by Batu Khan in the 1240s near present-day Astrakhan; a second capital, New Sarai, was built further upstream in the 14th century. Rus' princes travelled there to receive their patents to rule, and it grew…

sauran.s: Sauran was a fortified medieval city on the middle Syr Darya in southern Kazakhstan, about 40 kilometres north-west of the town of Turkistan. It flourished from the 13th to the 16th centuries as a centre of the White Horde and later of the Kazakh Khanate, and travellers…

sima-qian.s: Sima Qian (c. 145–c. 86 BCE) was a historian of the Western Han dynasty who completed the Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), a history of China from the legendary sage kings to the reign of Emperor Wu. Castrated as punishment after defending a disgraced general, he chose…

soga-clan.s: The Soga clan was a powerful aristocratic lineage of the Yamato court in Japan in the 6th and 7th centuries. Its leaders, Soga no Iname and Soga no Umako, championed Buddhism after its arrival from Baekje and married their daughters into the royal line, dominating the court…

sumu-epuh.s: Sumu-epuh was the first known king of Yamhad, ruling from Halab (Aleppo) in northern Syria from about 1810 to 1780 BCE. Letters from Mari show him resisting Shamshi-Adad I of Upper Mesopotamia, who allied with the city of Qatna against him.

shibam.s: Shibam is a walled town in the Wadi Hadramawt of eastern Yemen, famous for its densely packed mud-brick tower houses, many of them five to eleven storeys high and dating mainly from the 16th century onwards. Often called the 'Manhattan of the desert', it was an ancient capital…

shibam-kawkaban.s: Shibam Kawkaban is a pair of towns in the highlands north-west of Sanaa, Yemen: Shibam at the foot of a mountain and the fortress town of Kawkaban on the cliff above it. In the 9th century Shibam was the base of the Yufirid dynasty, which seized it around 847 and soon took Sanaa.

shira-muren.s: The Shira Muren, or Xar Moron, is a river of eastern Inner Mongolia, China, the main upper source of the Liao River. Its valley was the homeland of the Yuwen Xianbei and later of the Khitan, whose Liao dynasty built its Supreme Capital in the river's basin.

saguamanchica.s: Saguamanchica (died c. 1490) was a zipa, ruler of the southern Muisca of Bacatá in the Colombian highlands. According to Muisca tradition he enlarged the realm by conquering neighbouring chiefdoms such as Fusagasugá and fought the Panche to the west.

ston.s: Ston is a small town on the isthmus joining the Pelješac peninsula to the Croatian mainland, north-west of Dubrovnik. It belonged to the principality of Hum until 1333, when the Republic of Ragusa bought it with Pelješac and fortified it with some five kilometres of walls,…

saada.s: Saada is a city in the far north of Yemen and capital of Saada Governorate. Yahya ibn al-Husayn founded the Zaydi imamate there in 897, and it remained the religious heart of Zaydism, with the mosque that holds his tomb.

sharaf-al-din-mahmud-shah.s: Sharaf al-Din Mahmud Shah was the founder of the Injuid dynasty in Fars, southern Iran. Appointed by the Ilkhanate in the early fourteenth century to manage its crown estates (inju) in the province, he built up his own power in Shiraz.

sharaf-al-dawla.s: Sharaf al-Dawla was a Buyid emir, the eldest son of Adud al-Dawla. After his father's death in 983 he ruled Fars and Kerman, then fought his brother Samsam al-Dawla for the inheritance, took Baghdad in 987 and became senior emir of the dynasty.

sinjar.s: Sinjar is a town in north-western Iraq at the southern foot of the Sinjar Mountains, west of Mosul. In the Middle Ages it was a fortified city on the route from Mosul to Syria, held by Zengid atabegs in the twelfth and early thirteenth centuries.

san-andres-de-sotavento.s: San Andrés de Sotavento is a town and municipality in the department of Córdoba in northern Colombia. It is the centre of the largest Zenú Indigenous reserve, established in the colonial period and later restored, and is known for the weaving of the sombrero vueltiao, the…

san-jorge-river.s: The San Jorge is a river of northern Colombia that rises in the Paramillo massif of the western Andes and flows north through the department of Córdoba to the wetlands of La Mojana, where it joins the Magdalena river system. Its floodplain was a heartland of the Zenú, whose…

stracimir-balsic.s: Stracimir Balšić was the eldest son of Balša I and, with his brothers Đurađ I and Balša II, one of the lords of Zeta after the death of Stefan Dušan. He held lands in the south of Zeta and died in 1373.

simtokha-dzong.s: Simtokha Dzong is a fortress-monastery just south of Thimphu, Bhutan, built by Ngawang Namgyal, the Zhabdrung, in 1629. It was the first dzong he built and is among the oldest surviving in the country, setting the pattern for the fortress-monasteries that combined government…

sun-jian.s: Sun Jian was a Chinese general of the late Han dynasty from the lower Yangtze. He made his name fighting the Yellow Turban rebels and joined the coalition against Dong Zhuo in 190, retaking Luoyang.

shang-zhixin.s: Shang Zhixin was the son of Shang Kexi, the Qing dynasty's feudatory prince in Guangdong. He took over his father's forces and joined the Revolt of the Three Feudatories in 1676, but submitted to the Qing again in 1677.

sagipa.s: Sagipa, also called Saquesazipa, was the last zipa of the Muisca realm of Bacatá in present-day Colombia. He succeeded Tisquesusa, who died resisting the Spanish conquistadors, and at first allied with Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada against the Panche.

sadeh.s: Sadeh is an ancient Iranian festival celebrated with great bonfires fifty days before Nowruz, at the end of January, to honour fire and mark the waning of winter. Associated with Zoroastrianism, it was celebrated lavishly at some medieval Muslim courts, notably by the Ziyarid…

soutpansberg.s: The Soutpansberg is a mountain range in Limpopo province in the far north of South Africa, named after a salt pan at its western end. Andries Hendrik Potgieter's Voortrekkers settled at its foot in 1848, founding Schoemansdal, the centre of a Boer republic later absorbed into…

sixth-crusade.s: The Sixth Crusade (1228–1229) was led by the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II, who sailed to the Holy Land while excommunicated by Pope Gregory IX. Without fighting a major battle he negotiated the Treaty of Jaffa (1229) with the Ayyubid sultan al-Kamil, which returned…

swedish-norwegian-war.s: The Swedish–Norwegian War was a short war in July and August 1814 between Sweden and Norway, which had declared independence after the Treaty of Kiel transferred it from Denmark to Sweden. Swedish forces under Crown Prince Charles John (Bernadotte) quickly gained the upper…

second-sino-japanese-war.s: The Second Sino-Japanese War was fought between China and Japan from 1937 to 1945. Beginning with the Marco Polo Bridge Incident, Japan occupied much of eastern China, including Beijing, Shanghai and Nanjing, where its troops committed a notorious massacre; Nationalists and…

scottish-norwegian-war.s: The Scottish–Norwegian War was fought from 1262 to 1266 between Alexander III of Scotland and Haakon IV of Norway over the Hebrides and the Isle of Man. Haakon's great expedition of 1263 ended indecisively at Largs, and he died in Orkney soon after; by the Treaty of Perth…

south-african-border-war.s: The South African Border War was fought from 1966 to 1990 in Namibia and southern Angola between South Africa and the Namibian liberation movement SWAPO, with Angolan and Cuban forces involved after 1975. It ended with the New York Accords of 1988, which linked Cuban…

sino-burmese-war-1765-1769.s: The Sino-Burmese War was fought from 1765 to 1769 between Qing China and the Konbaung dynasty of Burma. The Qianlong Emperor sent four invasions into Burma, all of which were repulsed, the last ending with the Treaty of Kaungton (1769); Burma kept its independence, but the war…

saintonge-war.s: The Saintonge War was a conflict of 1242 between Louis IX of France and a coalition of rebel nobles of Poitou led by Hugh X of Lusignan, supported by Henry III of England. Louis defeated the English and their allies at Taillebourg and Saintes in July 1242, ending Henry's…

sviatoslavs-invasion-of-bulgaria.s: Sviatoslav's invasion of Bulgaria was the campaign of 968–971 in which Sviatoslav I of Kiev, first invited by the Byzantines, conquered much of the First Bulgarian Empire and settled at Pereyaslavets on the Danube. The Byzantine emperor John I Tzimiskes then drove him out,…

second-french-intervention-in-mexico.s: The second French intervention in Mexico was the invasion of Mexico by France from 1861 to 1867, launched under Napoleon III after Benito Juárez suspended payment of foreign debts. Despite a defeat at Puebla on 5 May 1862, French troops took Mexico City and installed…

social-war-220-217-bce.s: The Social War of 220–217 BCE was fought between the Hellenic League led by Philip V of Macedon and the Aetolian League, joined by Sparta and Elis. Philip campaigned successfully in western Greece and the Peloponnese, and the war ended with the Peace of Naupactus (217 BCE),…

spanish-reconquest-of-santo-domingo.s: The Spanish reconquest of Santo Domingo was the campaign of 1808–1809 in which Dominican creoles led by Juan Sánchez Ramírez, with British naval help, drove the French from the eastern part of Hispaniola, ceded to France in 1795. After victory at Palo Hincado in November 1808…

spanish-conquest-of-iberian-navarre.s: The Spanish conquest of Iberian Navarre was the invasion of the Kingdom of Navarre south of the Pyrenees by Ferdinand II of Aragon, beginning in 1512. Navarrese and French attempts to restore the native monarchs, John III and Catherine, failed, notably at Noáin (1521), and the…

somali-civil-war.s: The Somali Civil War is the armed conflict in Somalia that grew out of resistance to the military regime of Siad Barre in the 1980s and became general after his overthrow in 1991. Clan militias, foreign interventions, including the UN operations of 1992–1995 and Ethiopian…

song-dai-viet-war.s: The Song–Đại Việt war was fought between the Song dynasty of China and the Lý dynasty of Đại Việt in 1075–1077. The Vietnamese general Lý Thường Kiệt struck first, raiding Song territory in Guangxi and destroying Yongzhou.

swabian-war.s: The Swabian War was fought in 1499 between the Old Swiss Confederacy and its allies and the Habsburg emperor Maximilian I with the Swabian League. The Swiss won a series of battles, including Calven and Dornach.

salvadoran-civil-war.s: The Salvadoran Civil War was fought from 1979 to 1992 between the military-led government of El Salvador, backed by the United States, and the Farabundo Martí National Liberation Front, a coalition of left-wing guerrilla groups. More than 75,000 people died, many in massacres…

swedish-novgorodian-wars.s: The Swedish–Novgorodian Wars were a series of conflicts between Sweden and the Novgorod Republic over Finland, Karelia and the trade routes of the Gulf of Finland and the Neva. Swedish expeditions and the building of Vyborg in 1293 and Landskrona in 1300 met Novgorodian…

sertorian-war.s: The Sertorian War was a Roman civil war fought in Hispania from 80 to 72 BCE between Quintus Sertorius, a supporter of the Marian party, and the government in Rome established by Sulla. Backed by Lusitanians and Celtiberians, Sertorius held off Metellus Pius and Pompey for years.

sullas-civil-war.s: Sulla's civil war was fought in 83–82 BCE between Lucius Cornelius Sulla, returning from the war against Mithridates, and the Marian faction governing Rome. Sulla landed at Brundisium, and with commanders such as Pompey and Crassus defeated the Marian and Samnite armies,…

soviet-japanese-border-conflicts.s: The Soviet–Japanese border conflicts were a series of clashes between the Soviet Union and Mongolia on one side and Japan and Manchukuo on the other along the Manchurian borders. The largest were the Battle of Lake Khasan in 1938 and the Battles of Khalkhin Gol in 1939, where…

spanish-portuguese-war-1776-1777.s: The Spanish–Portuguese War of 1776–1777 was fought over the borderlands of the Río de la Plata and southern Brazil. A large Spanish expedition under Pedro de Cevallos took the island of Santa Catarina and the colony of Sacramento in 1777.

sinhalese-portuguese-war.s: The Sinhalese–Portuguese War was a long series of conflicts in Sri Lanka between the Portuguese and the Sinhalese kingdoms of Sitawaka and Kandy. Portugal gained control of most of the coastal lowlands, but its invasions of the highland kingdom of Kandy were destroyed at…

spanish-conquest-of-the-muisca.s: The Spanish conquest of the Muisca was the subjugation of the Muisca Confederation of the Colombian highlands by conquistadors led by Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada from 1537. The Spaniards defeated the rulers of Bacatá and Hunza and founded Santa Fe de Bogotá in 1538.

somaliland-campaign-1900-1920.s: The Somaliland campaign was the series of British expeditions from 1900 to 1920 against the Dervish movement of Mohammed Abdullah Hassan in the Horn of Africa. Several British, Ethiopian and Italian expeditions failed to destroy his forces.

serbo-bulgarian-war.s: The Serbo-Bulgarian War was fought in November 1885 after Serbia attacked Bulgaria in protest against the union of Bulgaria with Eastern Rumelia. The young Bulgarian army defeated the Serbs at Slivnitsa and advanced to Pirot before Austro-Hungarian pressure halted it.

san-lorenzo-tenochtitlan.s: San Lorenzo Tenochtitlán is the collective name for three related Olmec archaeological sites in south-eastern Veracruz, Mexico: San Lorenzo, Tenochtitlán and Potrero Nuevo. San Lorenzo, on a plateau 50 metres above the Coatzacoalcos floodplain, was the major Olmec centre from…

spiro-mounds.s: Spiro Mounds is an archaeological site on the Arkansas River in eastern Oklahoma, a centre of the Caddoan Mississippian culture from about 800 to 1450. Craig Mound, one of its twelve earthen mounds, held a hollow burial chamber, the Great Mortuary, that preserved textiles,…

sidon.s: Sidon, or Saida, is a city on the Mediterranean coast of southern Lebanon, about 40 km south of Beirut, inhabited since prehistoric times. One of the most important Phoenician cities, it was known for its glass and purple dye, and under Persian rule it eclipsed Tyre as the…

sogdian-ancient-letters.s: The Sogdian Ancient Letters are private and business letters written in the early 4th century by Sogdians living in China, found by Aurel Stein in 1907 in an abandoned watchtower near Dunhuang. In two, Miwnay, left destitute in Dunhuang with her daughter by her husband, asks…

samuel-gompers.s: Samuel Gompers was a British-born American cigar maker and trade union leader who founded the American Federation of Labor and was its president, but for one year, from 1886 until his death. Born in London's East End, he emigrated with his family to New York in 1863 and joined…

seneca-falls-convention.s: The Seneca Falls Convention was the first women's rights convention, held in the Wesleyan Chapel at Seneca Falls, New York, on 19–20 July 1848. Organised by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and local Quaker women during a visit by Lucretia Mott, it adopted a Declaration of Sentiments…

solidarity-polish-trade-union.s: Solidarity is a Polish trade union that emerged at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk in August 1980, the first independent union in a Warsaw Pact country to be recognised by the state. Led by Lech Wałęsa, it had 10 million members at its peak in September 1981, a third of the…

sidereus-nuncius.s: Sidereus Nuncius, known in English as the Sidereal Messenger or Starry Messenger, is a short astronomical treatise in Latin by Galileo Galilei, published on 13 March 1610. It was the first published scientific work based on observations made through a telescope, reporting a…

selma-to-montgomery-marches.s: The Selma to Montgomery marches were three protest marches for African American voting rights, held in 1965 along the 54-mile (87 km) highway from Selma, Alabama, to Montgomery, the state capital. On 7 March, "Bloody Sunday", state troopers and a county posse attacked an…
